excerpt: MASISI March 7, 2026 - An AFC/M23 rebel position in the Mushaki area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, was targeted by an airstrike attributed to the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) on the morning of Saturday, March 7. Local sources reported that the strik
title_en: FARDC Conducts Airstrike on AFC/M23 Position Near Mushaki
excerpt_en: MASISI March 7, 2026 - An AFC/M23 rebel position in the Mushaki area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, was targeted by an airstrike attributed to the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) on the morning of Saturday, March 7. Local sources reported that the strik
body_en:
MASISI March 7, 2026 - An AFC/M23 rebel position in the Mushaki area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, was targeted by an airstrike attributed to the FARDC (Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo) on the morning of Saturday, March 7.
Local sources reported that the strike focused on a rebel position situated on the farm of businessman and former national deputy Edouard Mwangachuchu, a site reportedly used as a logistical base for the rebels. The operation was carried out using a military drone, part of the Congolese army’s ongoing campaign against AFC/M23 positions.
Residents heard a loud explosion followed by unusual activity near the target. While AFC/M23 political spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka claimed civilian casualties, local sources dispute this, noting no immediate confirmation of civilian injuries. The FARDC has not released an official statement regarding the strike.
This airstrike occurs amid a volatile security situation in Masisi and wider North Kivu, where clashes between government forces and AFC/M23 rebels have persisted for months. Mushaki, strategically located on the axis linking Masisi to Goma, has repeatedly been a focus of military operations.
Local populations continue to live under fear, with concern over further escalation and humanitarian consequences in an already conflict-affected area. Reports indicate ongoing troop movements from both sides near Mushaki, maintaining a tense atmosphere.

title: Parliament Ratifies Peace and Strategic Partnership Agreements with Rwanda and the United States
excerpt: KINSHASA March 7, 2026 - The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has adopted bills ratifying the peace agreement with Rwanda and the Strategic Partnership Agreement with the United States, two landmark accords signed under the Trump administration. The adoption w
title_en: Parliament Ratifies Peace and Strategic Partnership Agreements with Rwanda and the United States
excerpt_en: KINSHASA March 7, 2026 - The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has adopted bills ratifying the peace agreement with Rwanda and the Strategic Partnership Agreement with the United States, two landmark accords signed under the Trump administration. The adoption w
body_en:
KINSHASA March 7, 2026 - The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has adopted bills ratifying the peace agreement with Rwanda and the Strategic Partnership Agreement with the United States, two landmark accords signed under the Trump administration.
The adoption was carried out by Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Noëlla Ayeganato, on behalf of the Minister of Foreign Affairs. The bills come ahead of the March 2026 ordinary parliamentary session, scheduled for March 16, with the government emphasizing alignment with its legislative agenda.
The agreements were originally signed on December 4, 2025, in Washington, D.C., where President Félix Tshisekedi and President Paul Kagame endorsed the instruments in the presence of international dignitaries including Donald Trump, Faure Gnassingbé, João Lourenço, Évariste Ndayishimiye, William Ruto, Jessica Alupo, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Mohammed Al Khulaifi, and Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan.
The ratified instruments include:
The Washington Agreements for Peace and Prosperity between DRC and Rwanda, reaffirming the June 27, 2025 peace commitments and establishing the Regional Economic Integration Framework (REIF).
The United States-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement and related Memorandum of Understanding on Enhanced Security Cooperation.
The United States-Rwanda Framework for Shared Economic Prosperity, aiming to strengthen bilateral economic ties.
According to the U.S. State Department, these agreements aim to end decades of conflict, promote economic cooperation, and provide a roadmap for peace, security, and growth in the Great Lakes region. They also open opportunities for the U.S. private sector and reinforce regional integration.
The DRC government described the ratifications as a historic step toward sustainable peace, stability, and shared prosperity, in line with its commitments under the Washington Accords and related frameworks.
Conclusion
The period from February 22 to March 8, 2026, in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was marked by a complex interplay of persistent conflict, diplomatic tension, and internal governance reforms. While the country demonstrated significant international initiative-notably through the nomination of Juliana Lumumba for the OIF leadership and active participation in global mining forums-the security situation in the East remains its most pressing challenge.
The escalating conflict with the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion continues to destabilize North and South Kivu, resulting in mass displacements, humanitarian crises, and the discovery of mass graves in recently liberated areas such as Uvira. Despite international efforts under the Washington and Doha frameworks, diplomatic friction between Kinshasa and Kigali remains high, with both sides exchanging accusations regarding support for armed groups and the legitimacy of security concerns.
Domestically, the government is navigating a delicate political landscape, evidenced by internal divisions within the ruling coalition over constitutional reforms and growing opposition demands for a more inclusive and transparent national dialogue. At the same time, the presidency’s emphasis on government performance reviews and addressing fiscal pressures, including civil service salary delays, highlights a commitment to administrative efficiency and accountability.
In parallel, the DRC is making progress in areas such as agricultural transformation, industrial partnerships, and gender equality institutionalization. However, these gains remain fragile, and achieving lasting stability will require not only the effective implementation of regional peace agreements, but also a sustained effort to strengthen governance, ensure mineral traceability, and address the urgent health and humanitarian needs of the population.
In conclusion, while the DRC demonstrates resilience and strategic initiative, its future stability hinges on balancing security, diplomacy, and internal reforms to create a more peaceful, inclusive, and prosperous nation.
By Glad Musema
Jeff Buleli

title: EAC Calls on AU to Strengthen Mediation Efforts in Eastern DRC
excerpt: Arusha, March 9, 2026 - The East African Community (EAC) has urged the African Union (AU) to mobilize adequate financial and logistical resources to support ongoing mediation efforts aimed at resolving the escalating crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The appeal foll
title_en: EAC Calls on AU to Strengthen Mediation Efforts in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Arusha, March 9, 2026 - The East African Community (EAC) has urged the African Union (AU) to mobilize adequate financial and logistical resources to support ongoing mediation efforts aimed at resolving the escalating crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The appeal foll
body_en:
Arusha, March 9, 2026 - The East African Community (EAC) has urged the African Union (AU) to mobilize adequate financial and logistical resources to support ongoing mediation efforts aimed at resolving the escalating crisis in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The appeal follows the 25th Summit of Heads of State held on March 7 in Arusha, where regional leaders reviewed the deteriorating security and humanitarian situation marked by rising tensions between Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, as well as continued clashes involving the AFC/M23 rebellion.
In its final communiqué, the Summit emphasized the urgency of reinforcing the AU-led mediation framework. “The Summit urged the African Union to provide the necessary financial and logistical resources to the African Union-led mediation process in eastern DRC to ensure a swift and sustained commitment to its conclusion,” the statement read.
The mediation process, aligned with parallel diplomatic tracks in Washington and Doha, is led by Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who serves as the AU’s designated mediator for the eastern DRC crisis. The current structure stems from a high-level meeting convened in January 2026 in Lomé, aimed at harmonizing peace initiatives.
Under this framework, Gnassingbé is supported by a Togolese mediation team drawn from the presidency and foreign affairs ministry. Five co-facilitators-former African heads of state-have been assigned key thematic roles: Olusegun Obasanjo oversees military and security issues, Sahle-Work Zewde handles humanitarian concerns, Uhuru Kenyatta leads dialogue with armed groups, Mokgweetsi Masisi manages regional economic cooperation, and Catherine Samba-Panza is responsible for civil society, reconciliation, and women’s issues.
A joint secretariat-bringing together the AU, EAC, Southern African Development Community (SADC), and International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR)-has also been established to coordinate efforts, alongside international partners including the United Nations, the European Union, and Qatar.
Despite intensified diplomatic engagement, progress on the ground remains limited. The Washington track, backed by Donald Trump and endorsed by Félix Tshisekedi and Paul Kagame, has yet to translate into tangible security improvements. Mutual accusations between Kinshasa and Kigali over alleged violations continue to undermine trust and stability.
Meanwhile, the Doha negotiations-facilitated by Qatar between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 rebellion-have slowed significantly. Key provisions, including the ceasefire mechanism, declaration of principles, and framework agreement, remain unimplemented, stalling efforts to address root causes of the conflict such as state authority and armed group reintegration.
This diplomatic impasse has contributed to renewed violent clashes in eastern DRC, further complicating an already fragile humanitarian situation. Calls for a national dialogue to complement international mediation efforts have also gone unanswered. President Tshisekedi maintains that such an initiative must be led exclusively by his office, despite mounting pressure from socio-political actors and recent proposals from religious groups.
As mediation efforts struggle to gain momentum, regional leaders warn that without stronger institutional backing and coordinated implementation, prospects for lasting peace in eastern DRC remain uncertain.

title: Oakland Institute Criticizes Washington Agreement, Calls for Stronger Action Against Rwanda
excerpt: DRC March 13, 2026 - The Oakland Institute has sharply criticized the Washington Agreement, arguing that it contains “inherent contradictions” by allegedly rewarding Rwanda despite its continued involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. In a statement r
title_en: Oakland Institute Criticizes Washington Agreement, Calls for Stronger Action Against Rwanda
excerpt_en: DRC March 13, 2026 - The Oakland Institute has sharply criticized the Washington Agreement, arguing that it contains “inherent contradictions” by allegedly rewarding Rwanda despite its continued involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. In a statement r
body_en:
DRC March 13, 2026 - The Oakland Institute has sharply criticized the Washington Agreement, arguing that it contains “inherent contradictions” by allegedly rewarding Rwanda despite its continued involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
In a statement released on March 12, the organization called on the United States administration to take stronger measures to end what it describes as Rwandan aggression through the AFC/M23 rebellion, which it says fuels instability and illicit exploitation of natural resources at the expense of Congolese civilians.
The think tank also deemed U.S. sanctions imposed by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) and several senior officials as insufficient, arguing they fail to counter the financial gains derived from the conflict.
According to the report, the RDF has played a decisive role in supporting the M23 rebellion, including in the capture of key areas such as Goma and Bukavu, as well as strategic mining sites. The organization highlights that control over resources-particularly coltan and gold-has enabled the rebels to generate significant revenues, including an estimated $800,000 per month from coltan taxation and up to $2 billion in gold exports in 2025.
The Oakland Institute further notes that Rwanda continues to receive substantial international financial support, including U.S. bilateral aid and major funding from the World Bank, raising concerns about policy contradictions. It points to infrastructure contracts allegedly linked to entities associated with the RDF, suggesting a nexus between military influence and economic interests.
Frédéric Mousseau, policy director at the institute, argued that Rwanda’s actions undermine the credibility of the Washington Agreement. “Rwanda’s violations and continued presence in the DRC highlight the contradictions of a so-called peace agreement that effectively grants access to Congolese resources while failing to ensure accountability,” he said, warning that such an approach cannot lead to lasting peace.
The report echoes earlier findings published in the institute’s study “Shafted: The Race for Critical Minerals in the DRC,” which cautioned that diplomatic initiatives may be used to advance resource interests under the guise of peacebuilding.
Diverging Positions
In response to the sanctions, Rwanda rejected the measures as “unilateral” and “distorting the facts”, arguing they unfairly target one side of the conflict. Kigali accused Kinshasa of violating ceasefire agreements through drone strikes and military offensives, and reiterated concerns over the presence of armed groups, including the FDLR, alongside Congolese forces.
On its part, the Congolese government welcomed the sanctions as a “clear signal” in support of sovereignty and territorial integrity, stressing the need for consistency between diplomatic commitments and realities on the ground. Authorities in Kinshasa maintain that ending support for armed groups and respecting international law are essential to stabilizing eastern DRC.
Fragile Diplomatic Progress
Despite ongoing diplomatic efforts, including the Washington and Doha processes supported by the African Union, progress remains limited on the ground. Persistent tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali, combined with renewed clashes in North and South Kivu, continue to undermine hopes for a sustainable resolution to the conflict.
The Oakland Institute’s critique adds to growing international debate over whether current diplomatic frameworks can effectively address the root causes of the conflict or risk entrenching existing power dynamics in the region.

title: ICRC Meets Defense Minister as Prisoner Exchange Process Moves Forward
excerpt: DRC March 13, 2026 - Efforts to advance the prisoner exchange process between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebellion received renewed attention following a meeting in Kinshasa between the Deputy Prime Minister of Defense and François Moreillo
title_en: ICRC Meets Defense Minister as Prisoner Exchange Process Moves Forward
excerpt_en: DRC March 13, 2026 - Efforts to advance the prisoner exchange process between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebellion received renewed attention following a meeting in Kinshasa between the Deputy Prime Minister of Defense and François Moreillo
body_en:
DRC March 13, 2026 - Efforts to advance the prisoner exchange process between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebellion received renewed attention following a meeting in Kinshasa between the Deputy Prime Minister of Defense and François Moreillon, head of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) delegation.
The discussions focused on the release and transfer of prisoners of war in eastern DRC within the framework of the Doha mediation process, where the ICRC acts as a neutral intermediary. The Congolese Defense Minister commended the organization’s humanitarian commitment and expressed support for its role in protecting the lives and dignity of victims of armed conflict.
François Moreillon подчеркнул that the ICRC has been active in the country for more than 40 years, working closely with national institutions, including the Ministry of Defense, and facilitating operations linked to detainees and international humanitarian law. He reiterated that the organization stands ready to assist in any transfer operation, provided there is agreement between all parties.
This meeting comes days after the AFC/M23 announced the release of more than 5,000 FARDC soldiers, captured on various frontlines and handed over to the ICRC in Rumangabo, located in Rutshuru Territory. According to the group, these soldiers are to be repatriated to Kinshasa under ICRC supervision.
The ICRC confirmed its readiness to facilitate this transfer, recalling its previous role in May 2025, when more than 1,300 disarmed soldiers were successfully transferred from Goma to Kinshasa.
The prisoner exchange forms part of broader confidence-building measures agreed upon within the Doha process, aimed at easing tensions and promoting dialogue. However, the process remains fragile. The AFC/M23 accuses Kinshasa of refusing to release detained fighters, including individuals allegedly arrested arbitrarily, and of continuing ceasefire violations.
Despite these challenges, the involvement of the ICRC represents a significant step toward de-escalation, although the success of the process will depend on mutual trust and the effective implementation of commitments by both sides in a context of ongoing conflict.

title: UN Security Council to Hold Closed-Door Meeting After Deadly Drone Attack in Goma
excerpt: Kinshasa, DRC March 16, 2026 - The UN Security Council will hold closed-door consultations on Tuesday to discuss the escalating conflict in eastern DRC, following a deadly drone attack in Goma on March 11, which killed a UNICEF staff member. The meeting was requested by France. S
title_en: UN Security Council to Hold Closed-Door Meeting After Deadly Drone Attack in Goma
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DRC March 16, 2026 - The UN Security Council will hold closed-door consultations on Tuesday to discuss the escalating conflict in eastern DRC, following a deadly drone attack in Goma on March 11, which killed a UNICEF staff member. The meeting was requested by France. S
body_en:
Kinshasa, DRC March 16, 2026 - The UN Security Council will hold closed-door consultations on Tuesday to discuss the escalating conflict in eastern DRC, following a deadly drone attack in Goma on March 11, which killed a UNICEF staff member. The meeting was requested by France.
Several Council members are expected to condemn the attack and stress the need to protect civilians and humanitarian workers. MONUSCO, the UN mission in the DRC, has warned that attacks on UN personnel may constitute war crimes under the Rome Statute.
The strike was also condemned by Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson of the African Union Commission, and by the European Union, both calling for an impartial investigation. The Congolese government announced its own investigation on March 13.
The attack coincides with an escalation of drone use in the east, where the FARDC is conducting an offensive against the March 23 Movement (M23). Discussions at the Council are expected to focus on establishing a permanent ceasefire, in line with Security Council resolution 2808, adopted December 19, 2025, which renewed MONUSCO’s mandate.
The UN Secretary-General has recommended a “gradual, adaptable, and conditional” approach to supporting the ceasefire, including deploying light infantry battalions, a rapid deployment unit, and an advanced medical evacuation team, with 1,500-2,500 additional troops potentially needed in North and South Kivu.
Recent tensions were compounded by US sanctions on Rwandan military officials and the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) on March 2. Kinshasa welcomed the sanctions, while Kigali denounced them as unilateral.

title: DRC and Rwanda Agree on De-escalation Measures in Washington Talks
excerpt: Washington, D.C. March 19, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda have agreed on concrete measures to de-escalate tensions in eastern DRC, following talks held on March 17-18 in the United States capital. The announcement was made in a joint statement with the United
title_en: DRC and Rwanda Agree on De-escalation Measures in Washington Talks
excerpt_en: Washington, D.C. March 19, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda have agreed on concrete measures to de-escalate tensions in eastern DRC, following talks held on March 17-18 in the United States capital. The announcement was made in a joint statement with the United
body_en:
Washington, D.C. March 19, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda have agreed on concrete measures to de-escalate tensions in eastern DRC, following talks held on March 17-18 in the United States capital. The announcement was made in a joint statement with the United States.
The agreement outlines coordinated actions, including respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, the planned withdrawal of Rwandan forces, and the lifting of certain defensive measures in eastern DRC. It also includes renewed commitments by Kinshasa to neutralize FDLR rebels within a defined timeframe.
Both parties reaffirmed the protection of civilians as a priority and expressed commitment to achieving lasting peace in the Great Lakes region under the Washington Agreements framework.
The development comes amid ongoing tensions in eastern Congo, where fighting persists. Kinshasa recently welcomed US sanctions against the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) and several officials accused of supporting the M23 rebellion, calling the move a “clear signal” in defense of DRC sovereignty.
The Congolese government also emphasized the need for consistency between diplomatic commitments and realities on the ground, while expressing gratitude to Washington for its role in advancing peace efforts.

excerpt: Kolwezi, Lualaba - March 11, 2026 - The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), in coordination with the Congolese and Zambian authorities, convened the 9th meeting of the DRC-Zambia-UNHCR Tripartite Commission from March 10 to 12 in Kolwezi, the capital of Lualaba
title_en: DRC-Zambia-UNHCR: 9th Tripartite Commission Meeting on Refugee Repatriation
excerpt_en: Kolwezi, Lualaba - March 11, 2026 - The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), in coordination with the Congolese and Zambian authorities, convened the 9th meeting of the DRC-Zambia-UNHCR Tripartite Commission from March 10 to 12 in Kolwezi, the capital of Lualaba
body_en:
Kolwezi, Lualaba - March 11, 2026 - The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), in coordination with the Congolese and Zambian authorities, convened the 9th meeting of the DRC-Zambia-UNHCR Tripartite Commission from March 10 to 12 in Kolwezi, the capital of Lualaba Province.
The meeting aims to promote voluntary repatriation of Congolese refugees in Zambia and Zambian refugees in the DRC, ensure security in return areas, and support the reintegration of returnees.
Governor Fifi Masuka emphasized that the discussions would strengthen cooperation and develop constructive guidelines for the benefit of the affected populations. Éric Mukandila, Permanent Secretary of the National Commission for Refugees (CNR), warned that ongoing armed conflicts, including the AFC-M23 rebellion, continue to displace populations both internally and across borders.
Pierre Atchom, UNHCR Representative in the DRC, highlighted that 11,523 Congolese refugees (3,150 households) were repatriated from Zambia between 2023 and 2025, reaffirming UNHCR’s commitment to supporting returns and reintegration.
The DRC is undertaking initiatives to monitor borders, strengthen community protection, rehabilitate schools and health centers, and promote economic empowerment through value chains, contributing to peace and food security.
The meeting will culminate in the adoption of a response plan to facilitate the large-scale return of refugees, in accordance with the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees and the principle of non-refoulement.
body_fr:
Kolwezi, Lualaba - March 11, 2026 - The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), in coordination with the Congolese and Zambian authorities, convened the 9th meeting of the DRC-Zambia-UNHCR Tripartite Commission from March 10 to 12 in Kolwezi, the capital of Lualaba Province.
The meeting aims to promote voluntary repatriation of Congolese refugees in Zambia and Zambian refugees in the DRC, ensure security in return areas, and support the reintegration of returnees.
Governor Fifi Masuka emphasized that the discussions would strengthen cooperation and develop constructive guidelines for the benefit of the affected populations. Éric Mukandila, Permanent Secretary of the National Commission for Refugees (CNR), warned that ongoing armed conflicts, including the AFC-M23 rebellion, continue to displace populations both internally and across borders.
Pierre Atchom, UNHCR Representative in the DRC, highlighted that 11,523 Congolese refugees (3,150 households) were repatriated from Zambia between 2023 and 2025, reaffirming UNHCR’s commitment to supporting returns and reintegration.
The DRC is undertaking initiatives to monitor borders, strengthen community protection, rehabilitate schools and health centers, and promote economic empowerment through value chains, contributing to peace and food security.
The meeting will culminate in the adoption of a response plan to facilitate the large-scale return of refugees, in accordance with the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees and the principle of non-refoulement.

body_en:
Kinshasa - March 11, 2026 - The Kinshasa provincial government officially launched the issuance of biometric residence cards for foreign nationals residing in the city. The ceremony was held at Kinshasa City Hall, presided over by Provincial Minister Jeannot Canon Larose.
The initiative aims to strengthen public security, improve identification of foreigners, and modernize administrative management of their stay. Minister Larose emphasized that the system ensures a secure, regulated, and harmonized integration of foreigners in the city.
Financial oversight is also a priority: Minister Magloire Kabemba highlighted that the system will help mobilize revenues to support the city-province’s operations.
Key features of the program:
Validity: 2 years, with fees by category:
Category A: US$250
Category B: US$200
Category C: US$100
Category D: US$50
Spouse-specific fees also apply.
Electronic verification: Agents equipped with smartphone-like devices can scan cards and check authenticity via a dedicated database.
Digital procedures: Applications can be submitted online to streamline processing.
The government called on foreign communities to raise awareness and ensure compliance with this new administrative measure.

title: Kinshasa Seeks Strong EU Response to Rwanda-Backed AFC/M23 Rebellion

title_en: Kinshasa Seeks Strong EU Response to Rwanda-Backed AFC/M23 Rebellion
excerpt_en: Strasbourg, March 12-13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo, represented by Minister of Foreign Affairs Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, engaged with Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) to discuss the security and humanitarian crisis in eastern DRC, particularly the ongoing
body_en:
Strasbourg, March 12-13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo, represented by Minister of Foreign Affairs Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner, engaged with Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) to discuss the security and humanitarian crisis in eastern DRC, particularly the ongoing hostilities involving the Rwandan-backed AFC/M23 rebellion. The meeting was chaired by Belgian MEP Hilde Vautmans and included the EU Special Representative for the Great Lakes Region, Johan Borgstam, via videoconference.
Key Points from Kinshasa’s Appeal
Minister Kayikwamba Wagner emphasized that the conflict in eastern DRC has claimed over six million lives, making it one of the deadliest crises since World War II.
She denounced repeated violations of peace agreements and called for stronger international mobilization, including diplomatic pressure, regional mediation via the African Union, and concrete commitments from global partners.
The Congolese government specifically highlighted Rwanda’s continued support for the AFC/M23 as a major factor fueling instability.
EU Engagement and Advocacy
The non-profit United Front for the DRC urged the European Union to move beyond declarations, calling for:
Protection of civilians and promotion of peace and security in the Great Lakes region.
Respect for DRC territorial integrity.
Concrete actions against armed groups destabilizing eastern DRC, particularly Rwanda-backed rebels.
Dr. Audrey Mundine, president of the United Front for the DRC, stressed that the EU’s credibility in international law and human rights is at stake if it fails to act decisively.
Context and Challenges
Hostilities between AFC/M23 and government forces continue in North Kivu and South Kivu, including the increased use of drones, which both sides accuse the other of deploying against civilians.
International mediation processes-the Washington process (Kinshasa-Kigali) and the Doha process (Kinshasa-AFC/M23)-have recorded some progress on paper but struggle to produce tangible results on the ground, contributing to ongoing mistrust and violence.
Humanitarian needs are growing, with international aid funding falling short amid escalating hostilities.

title: Senator Dany Kabongo Files Petition Against Senate Vice-President Modeste Bahati for Alleged Incompetence
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 16, 2026 - Senator Dany Kabongo has officially filed a petition against Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, the Second Vice-President of the Senate, citing alleged incompetence in the exercise of his duties. The initiative reportedly garnered 83 signatures from fellow parliam
title_en: Senator Dany Kabongo Files Petition Against Senate Vice-President Modeste Bahati for Alleged Incompetence
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 16, 2026 - Senator Dany Kabongo has officially filed a petition against Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, the Second Vice-President of the Senate, citing alleged incompetence in the exercise of his duties. The initiative reportedly garnered 83 signatures from fellow parliam
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 16, 2026 - Senator Dany Kabongo has officially filed a petition against Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, the Second Vice-President of the Senate, citing alleged incompetence in the exercise of his duties. The initiative reportedly garnered 83 signatures from fellow parliamentarians.
Kabongo, a member of the Sacred Union of the Nation (USN), accuses Bahati, leader of the Alliance of Democratic Forces of Congo and Allies (AFDC-A), of failing to properly consult the Head of State, President Félix Tshisekedi, before making public statements on sensitive political issues, including constitutional discussions.
Bahati had previously appeared in the media, suggesting the opening of a debate on constitutional matters. This statement was perceived by some colleagues as a lack of respect toward the President. In response, Bahati issued an apology on March 10, asserting that his words had been misinterpreted and clarifying that he was not opposed to constitutional revision, but rather advocating for an internal debate within the USN.
The petition underscores rising tensions within the Senate and the ruling coalition, drawing attention to the scrutiny senior officials face over their public remarks.

title: Modeste Bahati Lukwebo Resigns as Second Vice-President of the Senate, Cites Desire to Avoid Power Struggle
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 18, 2026 - Modeste Bahati Lukwebo officially resigned from his position as Second Vice-President of the Senate on Wednesday, March 18, the day after a petition for his removal was filed by Senator Dany Kabongo Bondanya (UDPS) and signed by multiple elected officia
title_en: Modeste Bahati Lukwebo Resigns as Second Vice-President of the Senate, Cites Desire to Avoid Power Struggle
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 18, 2026 - Modeste Bahati Lukwebo officially resigned from his position as Second Vice-President of the Senate on Wednesday, March 18, the day after a petition for his removal was filed by Senator Dany Kabongo Bondanya (UDPS) and signed by multiple elected officia
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 18, 2026 - Modeste Bahati Lukwebo officially resigned from his position as Second Vice-President of the Senate on Wednesday, March 18, the day after a petition for his removal was filed by Senator Dany Kabongo Bondanya (UDPS) and signed by multiple elected officials.
In an interview following the submission of his resignation letter to Senate President Jean-Michel Sama Lukonde Kyenge, Bahati Lukwebo explained his decision:
“I figured there was no point in getting into a power struggle with my colleagues. In any case, when you receive a mandate, you have to be prepared to leave it at any time. Because there were misunderstandings following my statement, I thought I had been understood when I said that much work is needed on the individual, their mentality, and their behavior if we hope for the text to be properly implemented.”
The petition and public criticism had raised grievances against Bahati Lukwebo, including allegations of incompetence, lack of respect for institutions, and controversial remarks regarding a potential constitutional revision.
“I thought I had explained myself clearly, but there you have it. By nature, I don’t like confrontation, so I preferred to submit my resignation today,” he added.
The resignation also follows internal distancing within his own political platform, the AFDC-A, whose members had urged him to accept the political consequences of the controversy.
Bahati Lukwebo, who served as Senate President from 2019 to 2024, had held the position of Second Vice-President since the 2023 legislative elections. His departure closes a chapter marked by recent political tension within the Sacred Union of the Nation (USN) coalition.

title: DRC Launches “Country Window” Project to Boost Geoscience and Mining Sector Modernization
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 20, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo officially launched the “Country Window DRC” project on Thursday, March 19, a major initiative under the PanAfGeo+ program, aimed at modernizing the mining sector and strengthening geoscience cooperation. The launch, pre
title_en: DRC Launches “Country Window” Project to Boost Geoscience and Mining Sector Modernization
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 20, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo officially launched the “Country Window DRC” project on Thursday, March 19, a major initiative under the PanAfGeo+ program, aimed at modernizing the mining sector and strengthening geoscience cooperation. The launch, pre
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 20, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo officially launched the “Country Window DRC” project on Thursday, March 19, a major initiative under the PanAfGeo+ program, aimed at modernizing the mining sector and strengthening geoscience cooperation.
The launch, presided over by Minister of Mines Louis Watum Kabamba, took place in Kinshasa and formalized collaboration with the European Union. The project is coordinated by the French Geological Survey (BRGM) and supports the National Geological Survey of Congo (SGN-C) in enhancing its technical and scientific capacities.
“The Country Window DRC project represents a significant opportunity to improve our understanding of the subsoil, strengthen the capacities of our institutions, and reduce the risks associated with mining investment. Geoscientific data is a strategic decision-making tool,” said Minister Kabamba.
The initiative aims to modernize the acquisition, management, and use of geological data, providing tools to guide investment decisions, improve mining governance, and promote responsible and transparent exploitation of natural resources. Kabamba emphasized that the project is part of the DRC’s broader strategy to transition from a raw materials export model to one focused on local value creation, sustainability, and transparency.
EU Support and Strategic Cooperation
Fabrice Basile, acting head of the EU delegation in the DRC, hailed the project as a concrete milestone in the 2023 strategic partnership roadmap between the EU and the DRC. He outlined the project’s four main areas of focus:
Modernizing geoscientific data management and consolidating the national database.
Mapping and assessing resources in priority areas, including artisanal mining sites.
Supporting artisanal mining with innovative technologies for decarbonization and waste recycling.
Strengthening human and technical capacities in public institutions, including ESG training.
“Our ambition is clear: to have a reliable national geoscience database, integrate artisanal mining communities into sustainable value chains, and train a new generation of Congolese geoscientists,” Basile said.
Reducing Investment Risks
The project is also designed to reduce risks for investors. Jean-Claude Guillaneau, PanAfGeo+ coordinator, explained that the program builds on the previous AfricaMaVal phases, which trained 1,773 experts across Africa. PanAfGeo+ Invest aims to expand the scope, focusing on critical minerals, water resources, and fostering a pan-African network of geoscience experts.
Project Scope and Objectives
Running from 2026 to 2029, the PanAfGeo+ Country Window DRC targets:
Geological and mining reconnaissance in Tanganyika, Kasai Central, and Kongo Central.
Feasibility studies for artisanal mining in Lualaba and Haut-Katanga.
Digitization of geological archives in the DRC and abroad.
Mapping artisanal mining nationwide and promoting sustainable, low-carbon practices.
Strengthening human capital through training programs and technical equipment provision.
The project involves multiple partners, including CTCPM, SAEMAPE, CAMI, and CRGM, and represents a significant step toward enhancing state sovereignty over geoscientific data while promoting sustainable investment and governance in the mining sector.
“Improving our knowledge of the geological potential is essential to ensure responsible, transparent, and sustainable exploitation of mineral resources, contributing to national economic and social development,” concluded Minister Kabamba.

“Our ambition is clear: to have a reliable national geoscience database, integrate artisanal mining communities into sustainable value chains, and train a new generation of Congolese geoscientists,” Basile said.
Reducing Investment Risks
The project is also designed to reduce risks for investors. Jean-Claude Guillaneau, PanAfGeo+ coordinator, explained that the program builds on the previous AfricaMaVal phases, which trained 1,773 experts across Africa. PanAfGeo+ Invest aims to expand the scope, focusing on critical minerals, water resources, and fostering a pan-African network of geoscience experts.
Project Scope and Objectives
Running from 2026 to 2029, the PanAfGeo+ Country Window DRC targets:
Geological and mining reconnaissance in Tanganyika, Kasai Central, and Kongo Central.
Feasibility studies for artisanal mining in Lualaba and Haut-Katanga.
Digitization of geological archives in the DRC and abroad.
Mapping artisanal mining nationwide and promoting sustainable, low-carbon practices.
Strengthening human capital through training programs and technical equipment provision.
The project involves multiple partners, including CTCPM, SAEMAPE, CAMI, and CRGM, and represents a significant step toward enhancing state sovereignty over geoscientific data while promoting sustainable investment and governance in the mining sector.
“Improving our knowledge of the geological potential is essential to ensure responsible, transparent, and sustainable exploitation of mineral resources, contributing to national economic and social development,” concluded Minister Kabamba.

title: CENI Suspends Sankuru Governor Election Due to Financial Constraints
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 21, 2026 - The Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) announced on Friday, March 20, that it cannot continue operational activities for the election of the governor and vice-governor of Sankuru Province due to financial constraints. The election, initial
title_en: CENI Suspends Sankuru Governor Election Due to Financial Constraints
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 21, 2026 - The Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) announced on Friday, March 20, that it cannot continue operational activities for the election of the governor and vice-governor of Sankuru Province due to financial constraints. The election, initial
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 21, 2026 - The Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) announced on Friday, March 20, that it cannot continue operational activities for the election of the governor and vice-governor of Sankuru Province due to financial constraints.
The election, initially postponed and then rescheduled for Tuesday, April 7, 2026, is now on hold pending the availability of funds. In a statement signed by Deputy Rapporteur Paul Muhindo, CENI stressed that its legal obligation to hold the election within fifteen days after publishing the final candidate list (set for March 23) cannot be met without adequate resources.
CENI had earlier published a provisional list of 11 candidates on March 4, mostly men, sparking renewed debate over the low representation of women in provincial leadership. Following this, appeals against the list were scheduled from March 6-7, disputes from March 9-15, and publication of the final list on March 23. Campaign activities and accreditation of observers and journalists were planned from early to late April.
The postponement follows a formal request from Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior Jacquemain Shabani, who had urged CENI to organize elections quickly after the Constitutional Court upheld the removal of the previous governor on October 24, 2025. The ruling confirmed a vacancy at the head of the provincial executive and instructed that a new election be held in accordance with Article 198 of the Constitution.
CENI emphasized that the electoral process in Sankuru will resume once financial support is secured, underlining the critical role of resources in ensuring timely and lawful elections.

title: Delly Sesanga Condemns Any Attempt to Amend Constitution for Third Term
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 21, 2026 - Opposition leader Delly Sesanga issued a strong warning on Saturday against any efforts to amend the Constitution to allow President Félix Tshisekedi a third term. Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa, Sesanga described such initiatives as a “seri
title_en: Delly Sesanga Condemns Any Attempt to Amend Constitution for Third Term
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 21, 2026 - Opposition leader Delly Sesanga issued a strong warning on Saturday against any efforts to amend the Constitution to allow President Félix Tshisekedi a third term. Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa, Sesanga described such initiatives as a “seri
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 21, 2026 - Opposition leader Delly Sesanga issued a strong warning on Saturday against any efforts to amend the Constitution to allow President Félix Tshisekedi a third term.
Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa, Sesanga described such initiatives as a “serious breach of the republican order” and called for citizen mobilization to prevent what he labeled an “act of institutional violence.”
“Those who want to change the Constitution are breaking our republican pact and taking to the bush against the Republic. They must be treated and fought as such by all means,” he said.
Sesanga emphasized the historical role of the Congolese people in defending freedoms and reiterated that no leader is above the Constitution. “Changing the Constitution, transforming mandates into unlimited terms, and disregarding all the requirements of the rule of law is not part of the Republic. Establishing a personal power structure is a challenge to the republican pact,” he added.
He went further, categorizing any move to amend the Constitution for a third term as “high treason” and a red line that cannot be crossed. Drawing parallels with past authoritarian periods, Sesanga denounced such actions as a repetition of the dictatorial excesses experienced under the Second Republic.
This statement comes amid ongoing speculation about a possible constitutional revision in the Democratic Republic of Congo, a topic already sparking strong reactions across political and civil society circles.

title: Youth from Goma and Bukavu Urge Inclusive Dialogue to Resolve Kivu Crisis
excerpt: Bukavu, March 22, 2026 - Around one hundred young leaders from Goma and Bukavu, including students and members of local youth committees, have called on the DRC government and the AFC-M23 movement to engage in sincere and inclusive dialogue to end decades of conflict in eastern D
title_en: Youth from Goma and Bukavu Urge Inclusive Dialogue to Resolve Kivu Crisis
excerpt_en: Bukavu, March 22, 2026 - Around one hundred young leaders from Goma and Bukavu, including students and members of local youth committees, have called on the DRC government and the AFC-M23 movement to engage in sincere and inclusive dialogue to end decades of conflict in eastern D
body_en:
Bukavu, March 22, 2026 - Around one hundred young leaders from Goma and Bukavu, including students and members of local youth committees, have called on the DRC government and the AFC-M23 movement to engage in sincere and inclusive dialogue to end decades of conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The appeal followed a two-day workshop held in Bukavu from March 14 to 15, organized by the Kivu Social Festival under the theme: “Youth of North and South Kivu: Catalysts for Peace, Resilience, and Participatory Governance.” The event aimed to position youth as central actors in peacebuilding and regional development.
In a final declaration, participants urged authorities and M23 leaders to “prioritize sincere and inclusive dialogue,” promote social cohesion, and combat all forms of community stigmatization. They also called on young people across Kivu and the DRC to actively participate in governance and peace processes.
Regional, African, and international organizations were asked to support peace efforts responsibly and impartially, ensuring lasting results. The youth pledged to resist divisive and tribal rhetoric, instead fostering hope, resilience, and reconstruction in their communities.
Blaise Rugusha, Director General of the Kivu Social Festival, highlighted the positive energy and creativity of Kivu’s youth, emphasizing that the region is defined not only by conflict but also by a generation determined to transform its future.
The workshop comes amid recent diplomatic progress. Following persistent tensions between the DRC and Rwanda, a March 17-18 meeting in Washington, D.C., mediated by the United States, produced “concrete measures” to accelerate the implementation of the Washington Peace Agreement. The International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) welcomed these commitments, noting they are a step toward reducing tensions and strengthening trust while respecting each country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

title: Sessanga Questions $13 Billion Defense Spending, Calls for Accountability
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 23, 2026 - Opposition leader Delly Sessanga sharply criticized the Félix Tshisekedi government, claiming that over $13 billion allocated to national defense and security between 2019 and 2025 failed to improve conditions on the ground. Speaking at a press conferen
title_en: Sessanga Questions $13 Billion Defense Spending, Calls for Accountability
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 23, 2026 - Opposition leader Delly Sessanga sharply criticized the Félix Tshisekedi government, claiming that over $13 billion allocated to national defense and security between 2019 and 2025 failed to improve conditions on the ground. Speaking at a press conferen
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 23, 2026 - Opposition leader Delly Sessanga sharply criticized the Félix Tshisekedi government, claiming that over $13 billion allocated to national defense and security between 2019 and 2025 failed to improve conditions on the ground.
Speaking at a press conference in Kinshasa, Sessanga highlighted that, despite significant budget increases-over 30% of national expenditures going to security and defense-and the declaration of a state of emergency in 2021, there has been “no visible strengthening of the defense apparatus” and “no lasting security for the population.”
He questioned the use of these funds, asking: “Where have all these resources committed to defense, security, and the war gone? Who benefits from these war funds? If they haven’t strengthened operational capabilities or restored territorial integrity, this could very well be hiding a war business.”
Sessanga accused the government of “instrumentalizing the war” to buy time and avoid accountability, warning that any delay in the CENI’s electoral roadmap could threaten the scheduled October 23, 2028 elections. He rejected proposals by some loyalists to extend President Tshisekedi’s mandate under the pretext of national security.
“Having fought alongside the people in the streets against the electoral postponement between 2016 and 2018, Félix Tshisekedi and his supporters cannot now become the architects of another postponement under the guise of war,” he said.
The opposition leader also criticized the stalled national dialogue, which was meant to serve as a platform for truth-telling about the country’s multifaceted crises and for consolidating national cohesion, noting that Angola had been mandated to facilitate consultations with Congolese political actors.

title: Mukwege Warns Tshisekedi Against “Drummers,” Criticizes Purge of Dissenting Parliamentarians
excerpt: Kinshasa, March 23, 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dr. Denis Mukwege called on President Félix Tshisekedi to resist pressure from what he described as the “drummers” surrounding him, warning that these advisors pursue personal interests and could betray the President as others
title_en: Mukwege Warns Tshisekedi Against “Drummers,” Criticizes Purge of Dissenting Parliamentarians
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 23, 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dr. Denis Mukwege called on President Félix Tshisekedi to resist pressure from what he described as the “drummers” surrounding him, warning that these advisors pursue personal interests and could betray the President as others
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 23, 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dr. Denis Mukwege called on President Félix Tshisekedi to resist pressure from what he described as the “drummers” surrounding him, warning that these advisors pursue personal interests and could betray the President as others did during previous regimes.
In a statement issued Monday, Mukwege urged the President to listen to his conscience and the voice of the people rather than the ambitions of loyalists promoting a third term, despite elections scheduled for 2028.
“Tomorrow, they will be the first to stab you in the back, as certain bigwigs and leading figures of the previous regime did,” Mukwege warned. “Listen instead to your conscience and the voice of the people. Our freedom depends on it.”
Political Consequences of Opposing Constitutional Change
The Nobel laureate also criticized the resignations of two senior lawmakers who opposed the proposed constitutional amendment: Vital Kamerhe, former Speaker of the National Assembly, and Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, Second Vice-President of the Senate. Both stepped down after petitions were filed by colleagues aligned with the ruling party and the Sacred Union coalition.
“By daring to oppose the proposed constitutional amendment while our country is at war, you had the courage to speak the truth, a sign of nobility for a representative of the people,” Mukwege said in an analysis published Monday. He lamented what he called a reversal of democratic principles, in which dissenting deputies and senators are sanctioned by the President for exercising oversight.
Mukwege condemned the “hypocrisy” of colleagues who privately share the dissenting view but publicly align with the establishment.
Third Term Debate and Political Tensions
The DRC political landscape has become increasingly polarized over proposals to amend the Constitution of February 18, 2006, to allow a potential third term for President Tshisekedi. Opposition figures, including Delly Sessanga, have pledged to mobilize citizens and organize street protests to block any constitutional change.
Meanwhile, supporters of the ruling UDPS party insist the amendment is necessary, describing Tshisekedi’s mandate not merely as a term in office but as a “mission” to complete. This debate has intensified political tensions and drawn international attention, with civil society leaders warning of threats to democratic governance and institutional integrity.

excerpt: Butembo, North Kivu - March 12, 2026 - The war between the US-Israeli coalition and Iran is disrupting North Kivu’s gold market, leaving traders and miners struggling. Butembo, the main trading hub for artisanal gold from North Kivu and neighboring provinces, has seen a sharp slo
title_en: Middle East Conflict Paralyzes Gold Trade in North Kivu
excerpt_en: Butembo, North Kivu - March 12, 2026 - The war between the US-Israeli coalition and Iran is disrupting North Kivu’s gold market, leaving traders and miners struggling. Butembo, the main trading hub for artisanal gold from North Kivu and neighboring provinces, has seen a sharp slo
body_en:
Butembo, North Kivu - March 12, 2026 - The war between the US-Israeli coalition and Iran is disrupting North Kivu’s gold market, leaving traders and miners struggling. Butembo, the main trading hub for artisanal gold from North Kivu and neighboring provinces, has seen a sharp slowdown in operations as Dubai-the key destination for the region’s gold-reduces its purchases.
The crisis has left local gold buying offices short on cash and dependent on credit. Merchants who usually travel to Dubai to purchase goods have suspended their trips, further tightening the flow of funds in the region.
Artisanal miners are paying the heaviest price. In Manguredjipa, the price of gold per gram has fallen from $178 to between $90 and $100 since the outbreak of the conflict. The collapse in prices is severely affecting communities that rely almost entirely on artisanal mining for their livelihoods.
The disruption highlights the vulnerability of North Kivu’s gold trade, which depends heavily on international markets, and shows how geopolitical crises abroad can have immediate, devastating effects on local economies.
body_fr:
Butembo, North Kivu - March 12, 2026 - The war between the US-Israeli coalition and Iran is disrupting North Kivu’s gold market, leaving traders and miners struggling. Butembo, the main trading hub for artisanal gold from North Kivu and neighboring provinces, has seen a sharp slowdown in operations as Dubai-the key destination for the region’s gold-reduces its purchases.
The crisis has left local gold buying offices short on cash and dependent on credit. Merchants who usually travel to Dubai to purchase goods have suspended their trips, further tightening the flow of funds in the region.
Artisanal miners are paying the heaviest price. In Manguredjipa, the price of gold per gram has fallen from $178 to between $90 and $100 since the outbreak of the conflict. The collapse in prices is severely affecting communities that rely almost entirely on artisanal mining for their livelihoods.
The disruption highlights the vulnerability of North Kivu’s gold trade, which depends heavily on international markets, and shows how geopolitical crises abroad can have immediate, devastating effects on local economies.

title: Landslide at Safi Mine in Lualaba Kills at Least 10 Artisanal Miners
excerpt: Kakanda, Lualaba March 13, 2026 - At least ten artisanal miners have died and one person injured following a landslide at the Safi mining site near Kakanda in Lualaba’s Lubudi territory. Rescue teams also recovered the body of a child, approximately 13 years old, from the debris.
title_en: Landslide at Safi Mine in Lualaba Kills at Least 10 Artisanal Miners
excerpt_en: Kakanda, Lualaba March 13, 2026 - At least ten artisanal miners have died and one person injured following a landslide at the Safi mining site near Kakanda in Lualaba’s Lubudi territory. Rescue teams also recovered the body of a child, approximately 13 years old, from the debris.
body_en:
Kakanda, Lualaba March 13, 2026 - At least ten artisanal miners have died and one person injured following a landslide at the Safi mining site near Kakanda in Lualaba’s Lubudi territory. Rescue teams also recovered the body of a child, approximately 13 years old, from the debris.
Authorities have recommended the immediate suspension of mining activities in the affected area and a technical assessment of the unstable quarry sections. The landslide occurred in a pit where miners were working early in the morning, exposing unsafe mining conditions.
A technical review identified several factors contributing to the disaster, including excessively high slabs of up to 37 meters (compared to the recommended five meters), fragile sandy-clay soil, dangerously steep slopes reaching 70-80 degrees, and the absence of proper drainage. These conditions indicate a lack of proper oversight in the artisanal operations.
The Safi site, part of the Boss Mining company’s permit, allows artisanal miners to operate in specific areas under strict agreements with local cooperatives. However, the cooperative involved had not received formal approval for technical operations, raising questions about the legality of the work conducted.
Officials have also called for the withdrawal of military personnel overseeing miners, suggesting that the Mines and Hydrocarbons Police take over supervision. The affected area remains closed while safety assessments and security measures are implemented.
The tragedy highlights ongoing safety challenges in unregulated artisanal mining and the urgent need for stronger oversight and compliance with mining standards.

title: DRC Launches First Pilot Gold Refinery in Kalemie
excerpt: Kalemie, Tanganyika - March 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has inaugurated its first pilot gold refinery, marking a major milestone in the country’s efforts to process its mineral resources locally. The ceremony took place on Wednesday, March 11, with the attendance
title_en: DRC Launches First Pilot Gold Refinery in Kalemie
excerpt_en: Kalemie, Tanganyika - March 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has inaugurated its first pilot gold refinery, marking a major milestone in the country’s efforts to process its mineral resources locally. The ceremony took place on Wednesday, March 11, with the attendance
body_en:
Kalemie, Tanganyika - March 13, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has inaugurated its first pilot gold refinery, marking a major milestone in the country’s efforts to process its mineral resources locally. The ceremony took place on Wednesday, March 11, with the attendance of key government officials, including the Minister of Planning, Guylain Nyembo, Minister of Mines, Louis Watum Kabamba, and Minister of State Portfolio, Julie Shiku, alongside the Governor of Tanganyika Province and representatives of DRC Gold Trading S.A.
Named DRC Gold Refinery S.A., the facility has a production capacity of 500-600 kilograms of gold per month and manages the full value chain, from purchasing raw gold to refining and producing ingots. The refinery represents a strategic partnership between the state-owned DRC Gold Trading S.A. and Lunga Mining.
At the launch, the Minister of Mines emphasized that the refinery is a key step in President Félix Tshisekedi’s vision to transform the country’s natural resources into engines of economic development and national sovereignty.
“For the first time, the DRC can refine its own strategic minerals, ensuring fair prices and transparent conditions for artisanal miners, trading posts, and small to medium mining operations,” the minister said.
The refinery aims to produce gold with 99.9% purity, positioning the country as a competitive exporter of refined gold while creating local added value. Authorities also urged those involved in gold fraud or smuggling to use official channels established by the state through DRC Gold Trading S.A.
This initiative forms part of a broader reform of the Congolese gold sector, emphasizing transparency, traceability, and local processing, with the goal of ensuring that the nation fully benefits from its mineral wealth.

title: MP Questions Deputy Prime Minister on Fuel Supply Amid Middle East Crisis
excerpt: Kinshasa March 16, 2026 - Congolese National Deputy Flory Mapamboli Posa submitted a written question to the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of the National Economy regarding the potential impact of the Middle East crisis on the Democratic Republic of Congo’s fuel supply. The par
title_en: MP Questions Deputy Prime Minister on Fuel Supply Amid Middle East Crisis
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 16, 2026 - Congolese National Deputy Flory Mapamboli Posa submitted a written question to the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of the National Economy regarding the potential impact of the Middle East crisis on the Democratic Republic of Congo’s fuel supply. The par
body_en:
Kinshasa March 16, 2026 - Congolese National Deputy Flory Mapamboli Posa submitted a written question to the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of the National Economy regarding the potential impact of the Middle East crisis on the Democratic Republic of Congo’s fuel supply.
The parliamentary inquiry, formally submitted under Article 180 of the National Assembly’s Rules of Procedure, addresses concerns stemming from recent disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Suez Canal-two key global petroleum transit routes responsible for approximately 20% and 10% of daily oil consumption, respectively.
During a recent Council of Ministers meeting, the government assessed the effects of these disruptions on national fuel availability. Officials indicated that current stock levels are sufficient to meet the country’s needs until June and presented a series of measures designed to maintain the balance of the fuel supply system and limit budgetary impacts over the short, medium, and long term.
The National Assembly’s Bureau will now review the submission to ensure its admissibility before forwarding it to the Deputy Prime Minister for response.

title: National Assembly Affirms Vigilance Over Washington Accords and Investment Opportunities
excerpt: Kinshasa March 18, 2026 - The Speaker of the National Assembly, Aimé Boji Sangara, assured Parliament and the public that upcoming discussions on the ratification of the Washington Accords between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, as well as the Strategic Partnership A
title_en: National Assembly Affirms Vigilance Over Washington Accords and Investment Opportunities
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 18, 2026 - The Speaker of the National Assembly, Aimé Boji Sangara, assured Parliament and the public that upcoming discussions on the ratification of the Washington Accords between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, as well as the Strategic Partnership A
body_en:
Kinshasa March 18, 2026 - The Speaker of the National Assembly, Aimé Boji Sangara, assured Parliament and the public that upcoming discussions on the ratification of the Washington Accords between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, as well as the Strategic Partnership Agreement with the United States, will be conducted responsibly, without compromising national sovereignty or restricting other international investments.
Speaking at the opening of the March 2026 ordinary session, Boji emphasized that these agreements aim to strengthen the DRC’s capacity, promote transparent management of strategic resources, and foster mutually beneficial partnerships. “Our country remains open to all investors of good faith. Beyond mining, there are considerable opportunities in agriculture, industrial processing, tourism, energy, and telecommunications,” he said.
The Washington Accords, signed under U.S. auspices on June 27, 2025, and December 4, 2025, seek to end the cycle of insecurity in eastern DRC and encourage regional economic integration. Parliament is expected to review and vote on the ratification bills, as well as consider the draft law on the Inga Dam project during the current session.
Boji reassured that the National Assembly will act with “vigilance and responsibility” to ensure the agreements serve both national security and the long-term prosperity of the Congolese people.
The accords are part of a broader international framework designed to foster peace, regional stability, and economic growth in the Great Lakes region, while enabling DRC to attract additional foreign investment and develop local industries.

title: Two Years After Amendment 5: Progress on Infrastructure Amid Persistent Criticism
excerpt: Kinshasa March 18, 2026 - Two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo and a consortium of Chinese companies, progress on infrastructure is visible, but criticism from civil society and experts remains. The Congolese govern
title_en: Two Years After Amendment 5: Progress on Infrastructure Amid Persistent Criticism
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 18, 2026 - Two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo and a consortium of Chinese companies, progress on infrastructure is visible, but criticism from civil society and experts remains. The Congolese govern
body_en:
Kinshasa March 18, 2026 - Two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines agreement between the Democratic Republic of Congo and a consortium of Chinese companies, progress on infrastructure is visible, but criticism from civil society and experts remains. The Congolese government recently announced a technical and financial audit of the project, renewing debate over whether the nation is truly benefiting from its mineral wealth.
A Renegotiation Presented as a Turning Point
Signed in March 2024, Amendment 5 to the original 2008 Sicomines agreement aimed to correct long-standing imbalances. The agreement included increased infrastructure investment, greater involvement of Gécamines in marketing mining production, and a more structured institutional framework for energy projects such as the Busanga Dam.
Visible Infrastructure Gains
Some improvements are evident on the ground. Along National Route 1, between Nguba and Lubudi, formerly muddy roads have been paved, easing travel and trade. Four bridges are under construction on this 142-kilometer section, part of an 850-kilometer road network planned to connect Nguba to Mbuji-Mayi by 2027. Drivers and local traders note positive effects on transportation and commerce.
Persistent Concerns and Discrepancies
Despite these visible gains, many projects remain incomplete, and the cost of some works appears inflated. Reports highlight discrepancies such as Boulevard du 30 Juin in Kinshasa, billed at $142 million despite estimates of $28 million, and Triomphal Boulevard, billed at $61 million versus an actual $5 million.
Financial Mechanisms Under Scrutiny
Analysts also question the financial structure of Amendment 5. The fixed annual contribution formula limits the DRC’s benefits if copper prices rise while exposing the state to losses if prices fall. Critics argue this mechanism diminishes the potential gains from the country’s mineral wealth.
Electricity and Tax Exemptions
The Busanga Dam, a key component of the partnership, primarily powers mining facilities, with minimal electricity directed to households. Tax exemptions granted to Sicomines are estimated to have cost the state hundreds of millions of dollars annually, with projections suggesting losses could reach $7 billion over the remaining life of the project.
Audit Could Clarify Accountability
The government’s announced audit aims to clarify resource allocation, project costs, and financial mechanisms. Experts hope the process will identify irregularities and ensure the partnership delivers tangible benefits to Congolese citizens.
Public Debate Continues
Two years after Amendment 5, the question remains: who truly benefits from the Sicomines partnership? While some infrastructure improvements are apparent, civil society, analysts, and local stakeholders continue to call for renegotiation and greater accountability to ensure the DRC maximizes the value of its mineral resources.

title: IGF Confirms “Win-Win” Partnership and Increased Infrastructure Funding
excerpt: Kinshasa March 21, 2026 - Nearly two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines mining and infrastructure project, the Inspector General of Finance, Jules Alingete, defended the fifth amendment as a successful step toward eliminating corruption and ensuring a balanced partner
title_en: IGF Confirms “Win-Win” Partnership and Increased Infrastructure Funding
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 21, 2026 - Nearly two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines mining and infrastructure project, the Inspector General of Finance, Jules Alingete, defended the fifth amendment as a successful step toward eliminating corruption and ensuring a balanced partner
body_en:
Kinshasa March 21, 2026 - Nearly two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines mining and infrastructure project, the Inspector General of Finance, Jules Alingete, defended the fifth amendment as a successful step toward eliminating corruption and ensuring a balanced partnership between the Democratic Republic of Congo and its Chinese partners.
Speaking during the China-DRC Media Forum in Kinshasa, Alingete emphasized that the renegotiation, validated by the President and his cabinet, created a “win-win” arrangement, with $324 million annually earmarked for infrastructure development, in addition to $150 million in dividends for Gécamines. Out of the project’s $900 million in annual profits, roughly $470 million benefits the DRC each year, while the Chinese consortium receives about $400 million.
Major Infrastructure Projects Underway
Alingete highlighted several projects funded under the Sicomines program, totaling over $650 million disbursed in just two years:
Kinshasa ring roads: $145 million disbursed of $383 million planned
Mbuji-Mayi - Mwene-Ditu - Kasese - Nguba road: $325 million financed
Kananga-Kalambambuji road: $88 million financed
Nkamba road (8 km): financed
Bukavu-Kamanyola road: $78 million disbursed, delayed due to regional conflict
He noted that prior to the review, over 15 years, only $800 million had been delivered for infrastructure, averaging $50 million per year, compared to $350 million per year since Amendment 5. Alingete stressed that nearly 70% of current infrastructure works in the country are funded through Sicomines.
Audit and Transparency Measures
The government also announced a technical and financial audit of the Sicomines project, covering 17 years from the Kabila administration to the current Tshisekedi government. The audit, to be conducted by international firms, aims to provide clarity on project implementation and pave the way for a potential sixth amendment. Officials assured that the process will not target former regime officials or collaborators but will focus on verifying figures and ensuring transparency.
A Response to Criticism
Alingete urged the public to ignore critics who question the renegotiation, emphasizing that the project now neutralizes past inconsistencies and corruption. Kinshasa March 21, 2026 - Nearly two years after the renegotiation of the Sicomines mining and infrastructure project, the Inspector General of Finance, Jules Alingete, defended the fifth amendment as a successful step toward eliminating corruption and ensuring a balanced partnership between the Democratic Republic of Congo and its Chinese partners.
Speaking during the China-DRC Media Forum in Kinshasa, Alingete emphasized that the renegotiation, validated by the President and his cabinet, created a “win-win” arrangement, with $324 million annually earmarked for infrastructure development, in addition to $150 million in dividends for Gécamines. Out of the project’s $900 million in annual profits, roughly $470 million benefits the DRC each year, while the Chinese consortium receives about $400 million.
Major Infrastructure Projects Underway
Alingete highlighted several projects funded under the Sicomines program, totaling over $650 million disbursed in just two years:
Kinshasa ring roads: $145 million disbursed of $383 million planned
Mbuji-Mayi - Mwene-Ditu - Kasese - Nguba road: $325 million financed
Kananga-Kalambambuji road: $88 million financed
Nkamba road (8 km): financed
Bukavu-Kamanyola road: $78 million disbursed, delayed due to regional conflict
He noted that prior to the review, over 15 years, only $800 million had been delivered for infrastructure, averaging $50 million per year, compared to $350 million per year since Amendment 5. Alingete stressed that nearly 70% of current infrastructure works in the country are funded through Sicomines.

The government also announced a technical and financial audit of the Sicomines project, covering 17 years from the Kabila administration to the current Tshisekedi government. The audit, to be conducted by international firms, aims to provide clarity on project implementation and pave the way for a potential sixth amendment. Officials assured that the process will not target former regime officials or collaborators but will focus on verifying figures and ensuring transparency.

title: Five Killed, Two Injured in Landslide After Heavy Rains in Lushebere
excerpt: Masisi March 14, 2026 - At least five people were killed and two others injured following a landslide triggered by heavy rains in Lushebere, a village located about six kilometers from Masisi town in Masisi Territory. The disaster occurred overnight between Friday and Saturday af
title_en: Five Killed, Two Injured in Landslide After Heavy Rains in Lushebere
excerpt_en: Masisi March 14, 2026 - At least five people were killed and two others injured following a landslide triggered by heavy rains in Lushebere, a village located about six kilometers from Masisi town in Masisi Territory. The disaster occurred overnight between Friday and Saturday af
body_en:
Masisi March 14, 2026 - At least five people were killed and two others injured following a landslide triggered by heavy rains in Lushebere, a village located about six kilometers from Masisi town in Masisi Territory.
The disaster occurred overnight between Friday and Saturday after intense rainfall weakened the soil in this mountainous area, causing a sudden collapse that swept away several homes. Two houses were completely destroyed, burying their occupants under the mud.
Among the victims were twin children, while their father was seriously injured and rushed to the Masisi General Referral Hospital for treatment. In a related incident, a young man in his twenties was struck by lightning during the same storm and is also receiving medical care.
Residents described scenes of panic as the land gave way. “The rain fell all night. At dawn, we heard a loud noise before it collapsed onto the houses,” one witness said, recounting attempts to rescue those trapped beneath the debris.
Local inhabitants say the persistent heavy rains in recent days have destabilized the terrain, making landslides increasingly frequent in the area. “Our village is surrounded by hills. When the rains intensify, the soil becomes fragile and houses downhill are exposed,” another resident explained.
This tragedy comes just days after another deadly landslide at the Rubaya mining site, also in Masisi, highlighting the growing risks linked to extreme weather conditions in the region.
Faced with the recurrence of such disasters, residents are urging authorities to strengthen prevention measures and raise awareness among communities living in high-risk zones to prevent further loss of life.
