title: Government Announces New Measures to Tackle Rising Insecurity in Kinshasa
excerpt: Kinshasa March 22, 2026 - The government has unveiled a series of measures to address the resurgence of insecurity, crime, and robberies in the capital, Kinshasa, amid growing public concern. The announcement was made by Deputy Prime Minister Jacquemain Shabani during the 83rd Co
title_en: Government Announces New Measures to Tackle Rising Insecurity in Kinshasa
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 22, 2026 - The government has unveiled a series of measures to address the resurgence of insecurity, crime, and robberies in the capital, Kinshasa, amid growing public concern. The announcement was made by Deputy Prime Minister Jacquemain Shabani during the 83rd Co
body_en:
Kinshasa March 22, 2026 - The government has unveiled a series of measures to address the resurgence of insecurity, crime, and robberies in the capital, Kinshasa, amid growing public concern.
The announcement was made by Deputy Prime Minister Jacquemain Shabani during the 83rd Council of Ministers meeting. He confirmed that a high-level security meeting had been held on March 14, bringing together civilian, police, and military authorities to coordinate a response.
Key decisions include the intensification of arrests targeting criminal networks, particularly those involved in staged kidnappings, and the continuation of Operation “Ndobo”, which involves joint PNC-FARDC patrols to combat the Kuluna phenomenon.
Authorities also plan to convene inter-institutional meetings to address crimes involving men in uniform, as well as tighten oversight in the telecommunications sector, including a potential ban on pre-registered SIM cards and the re-identification of subscribers.
Despite ongoing operations, Kinshasa continues to face a rise in kidnappings and nighttime attacks, with many residents reporting little improvement in daily security.
President Félix Tshisekedi has acknowledged public concern, warning that these crimes are fueling a climate of fear, undermining state authority, and eroding public trust in security institutions. He has instructed security services to intensify operations to dismantle criminal networks responsible for kidnappings and armed robberies.

title: Residents Flee Bembele Village Amid Fears of Armed Presence
excerpt: Bafwasende, Tshopo March 23, 2026 - Residents of Bembele village, located 76 kilometers from Bafwasende, have begun fleeing their homes following reports of suspected armed men in nearby forests. Since March 23, families have been moving toward Nia-Nia (Ituri) and Bafwasende town
title_en: Residents Flee Bembele Village Amid Fears of Armed Presence
excerpt_en: Bafwasende, Tshopo March 23, 2026 - Residents of Bembele village, located 76 kilometers from Bafwasende, have begun fleeing their homes following reports of suspected armed men in nearby forests. Since March 23, families have been moving toward Nia-Nia (Ituri) and Bafwasende town
body_en:
Bafwasende, Tshopo March 23, 2026 - Residents of Bembele village, located 76 kilometers from Bafwasende, have begun fleeing their homes following reports of suspected armed men in nearby forests.
Since March 23, families have been moving toward Nia-Nia (Ituri) and Bafwasende town, though the exact number of displaced people remains unknown.
Local sources report that farmers spotted armed individuals, triggering fears of a possible ADF presence, especially after recent deadly attacks in Mambasa, where at least 50 people were killed in Muchacha and Babesua.
The renewed insecurity has already forced more than 7,000 people to flee Mambasa, many now living in precarious conditions with host families in Bafwasende and surrounding areas.
The situation highlights growing concerns over the spread of violence and the humanitarian impact of ongoing armed group activity in eastern DRC.
Conclusion
The period from March 9 to 22, 2026, revealed the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at a pivotal crossroads, navigating ambitious national development projects amid persistent security and political challenges.
On the security front, eastern provinces remain volatile. Despite international mediation efforts through the Washington and Doha tracks, which enabled gestures such as the release of over 5,000 FARDC soldiers, tangible improvements for local populations remain limited. Clashes involving the AFC/M23, Wazalendo militias, and the ADF continue, with civilian communities bearing the brunt of the violence. Humanitarian crises persist, exemplified by the destruction of judicial infrastructure in Goma and Bukavu and continued displacement.
Politically, the landscape is marked by polarization and high-stakes maneuvering. Resignations of senior parliamentary figures, such as Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, and rising opposition debates over constitutional amendments underscore a tense road toward 2028 electoral cycles. Meanwhile, legal reforms and institutional strengthening, including the establishment of the Economic and Financial Criminal Court, signal efforts to improve governance and combat corruption.
Economically, the DRC is pursuing strategic modernization, from infrastructure projects under Amendment 5 of the Sicomines agreement to the launch of a national gold refinery in Kalemie. Investments in energy, notably the Inga III development program, reflect a drive to transform the country into a continental energy hub. Yet these advances coexist with setbacks: the precarious state of Congo Airways, deadly landslides in Lualaba and Masisi, and the ongoing risks posed by irregular migration routes highlight continued vulnerabilities.
Overall, March 2026 underscores a nation striving for progress but constrained by conflict and institutional fragility. While the DRC lays foundations for long-term economic growth, energy expansion, and administrative modernization, persistent security threats and political tensions threaten to undermine these gains. Sustained stability will demand robust governance, inclusive dialogue, transparent resource management, and effective enforcement of the rule of law to ensure that economic and social progress reaches all Congolese citizens.
By Glad Musema
Jeff Buleli

Clashes involving the AFC/M23, Wazalendo militias, and the ADF continue, with civilian communities bearing the brunt of the violence. Humanitarian crises persist, exemplified by the destruction of judicial infrastructure in Goma and Bukavu and continued displacement.
Politically, the landscape is marked by polarization and high-stakes maneuvering. Resignations of senior parliamentary figures, such as Modeste Bahati Lukwebo, and rising opposition debates over constitutional amendments underscore a tense road toward 2028 electoral cycles. Meanwhile, legal reforms and institutional strengthening, including the establishment of the Economic and Financial Criminal Court, signal efforts to improve governance and combat corruption.
Economically, the DRC is pursuing strategic modernization, from infrastructure projects under Amendment 5 of the Sicomines agreement to the launch of a national gold refinery in Kalemie. Investments in energy, notably the Inga III development program, reflect a drive to transform the country into a continental energy hub. Yet these advances coexist with setbacks: the precarious state of Congo Airways, deadly landslides in Lualaba and Masisi, and the ongoing risks posed by irregular migration routes highlight continued vulnerabilities.
Overall, March 2026 underscores a nation striving for progress but constrained by conflict and institutional fragility. While the DRC lays foundations for long-term economic growth, energy expansion, and administrative modernization, persistent security threats and political tensions threaten to undermine these gains. Sustained stability will demand robust governance, inclusive dialogue, transparent resource management, and effective enforcement of the rule of law to ensure that economic and social progress reaches all Congolese citizens.
By Glad Musema
Jeff Buleli

title: Bamako Pays Tribute to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei
excerpt: Bamako, March 5, 2026 - Mali’s Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maïga, paid tribute to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei, describing him as a “martyr of the sovereignty of peoples,” during a visit to the residence of Iran’s ambassador in Bamako on Thursday

excerpt_en: Bamako, March 5, 2026 - Mali’s Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maïga, paid tribute to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei, describing him as a “martyr of the sovereignty of peoples,” during a visit to the residence of Iran’s ambassador in Bamako on Thursday
body_en:
Bamako, March 5, 2026 - Mali’s Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maïga, paid tribute to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei, describing him as a “martyr of the sovereignty of peoples,” during a visit to the residence of Iran’s ambassador in Bamako on Thursday.
Maïga signed the book of condolences following Khamenei’s reported death on February 28, 2026. The Malian leader was accompanied by Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister Abdoulaye Diop during the visit.
In his message, delivered on behalf of Mali’s transitional president General Assimi Goïta, Maïga praised Khamenei for what he described as a lifelong struggle in defense of Iran’s sovereignty and the interests of its people.
“He died a martyr, defending until his last breath the higher interests of the Iranian state and people, in line with the vision of Ayatollah Khomeini,” the message stated.
According to Maïga, the passing of the Iranian leader leaves “an immense void,” but his political legacy and advocacy for what he called a “more just and multipolar world that respects identities” would continue to inspire those fighting for national independence and sovereignty.
The Malian government also extended condolences to Khamenei’s family and to the authorities and people of Iran, emphasizing solidarity between the two nations during the mourning period.
Maïga reaffirmed Mali’s support for Iran and praised Khamenei’s life as one dedicated to opposing injustice and defending the sovereignty of nations.
“We pray for the eternal rest of his soul and for all Iranian martyrs,” the prime minister concluded in the message.
The tribute highlights growing diplomatic ties between Mali’s transitional authorities and partners outside traditional Western alliances, particularly countries advocating a multipolar international order.

title: Malian Ambassador Presents Credentials to Kazakhstan’s President Tokayev
excerpt: Astana, March 4, 2026 - Mali’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan, Seydou Kamissoko, officially presented his credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Wednesday during a ceremony marking the start of his diplomatic mission in the Central Asian country. Kamissoko, who is based in M
title_en: Malian Ambassador Presents Credentials to Kazakhstan’s President Tokayev
excerpt_en: Astana, March 4, 2026 - Mali’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan, Seydou Kamissoko, officially presented his credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Wednesday during a ceremony marking the start of his diplomatic mission in the Central Asian country. Kamissoko, who is based in M
body_en:
Astana, March 4, 2026 - Mali’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan, Seydou Kamissoko, officially presented his credentials to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Wednesday during a ceremony marking the start of his diplomatic mission in the Central Asian country.
Kamissoko, who is based in Moscow and concurrently accredited to Kazakhstan, delivered the credentials on behalf of Mali’s transitional authorities. Following the formal ceremony, the Malian diplomat held an audience with the Kazakh president.
During the meeting, Kamissoko conveyed the “warm greetings” of Mali’s transitional president, General Assimi Goïta, and briefed Tokayev on the political and security situation in Mali and within the broader confederal framework of the Sahel.
The ambassador reaffirmed his commitment to strengthening ties between Bamako and Astana, emphasizing cooperation grounded in solidarity, mutual respect, and shared interests.
Both sides highlighted the importance of expanding technical, economic, and trade cooperation across sectors of mutual interest, signaling a willingness to deepen bilateral relations.
Prior to the credential ceremony, Kamissoko had presented copies of his letters of credence on March 3 to Kazakhstan’s Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, Alibek Kuantyrov. The two officials discussed avenues for enhancing political dialogue and boosting economic and cultural exchanges between the two countries.
Kamissoko’s appointment reflects Mali’s ongoing efforts to broaden its diplomatic engagement and develop partnerships beyond its traditional allies.

title_en: Mali’s Foreign Minister Bids Farewell to Outgoing UNDP Representative
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 6, 2026 - Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdoulaye Diop, on Friday received the outgoing Resident Representative of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Mali, Maleye Diop, during a farewell audience marking the end of
body_en:
Bamako, March 6, 2026 - Mali’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Abdoulaye Diop, on Friday received the outgoing Resident Representative of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Mali, Maleye Diop, during a farewell audience marking the end of his diplomatic mission in the country.
During the meeting in Bamako, the Malian foreign minister praised the departing official for his professionalism, personal commitment, and innovative approach in supporting the UN agency’s development initiatives in Mali.
Diop highlighted the UNDP’s contributions to strengthening socio-economic governance, advancing institutional reforms, promoting innovative development financing, and supporting capacity-building efforts for development actors across the country.
For his part, Maleye Diop welcomed what he described as the Malian government’s strong commitment to cooperation with the UN agency. He pointed in particular to the regular payment of Mali’s contributions to the UNDP budget and the authorities’ leadership in developing a new cooperation program aligned with national priorities.
The outgoing representative also expressed gratitude to Malian authorities for their support throughout his tenure, describing Mali as a welcoming country committed to long-term development and economic emergence through a proactive strategic vision.

body_en:
Bamako, March 2, 2026 - The United States has lifted sanctions imposed on several Malian military officers, a move formally conveyed to Mali’s Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga during a meeting with the U.S. ambassador in Bamako on Monday.
During the audience, U.S. Ambassador Rachna Korkonen informed the head of government of Washington’s decision to remove the sanctions targeting members of the Malian armed forces.
Responding on behalf of Mali’s transitional president General Assimi Goïta, Maïga welcomed the decision and expressed the authorities’ appreciation for the measure.
According to the prime minister, the lifting of sanctions could contribute to improving diplomatic relations between Bamako and Washington.
Maïga also reiterated Mali’s commitment to maintaining constructive relations with international partners while emphasizing the country’s respect for national sovereignty.
The decision marks a potential easing of tensions between Mali’s transitional authorities and the United States, which had previously imposed restrictions following political and security developments in the country.

Bamako, March 13, 2026 - Mali’s Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maïga, received Hanaa Singer, the newly appointed United Nations Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator in Mali, on Friday for an introductory audience that quickly evolved into a working session.
During the meeting, Maïga praised ongoing government efforts to improve living conditions for Malians, highlighting the resilience and courage of the population amid ongoing social and economic challenges.

Key focus areas identified during the discussion included health, education, renewable energy, and food security, underscoring the UN’s commitment to supporting Mali’s long-term development and humanitarian objectives.

The minister highlighted the longstanding friendship and cooperation between Mali and China, citing cultural and educational initiatives such as the Confucius Centre, which promotes Chinese language and culture, and the Luban Workshop, which supports professional training for young Malians.

title: United States Nears Agreement with Mali to Resume Intelligence Flights
excerpt: Bamako, March 9, 2026 - The United States is reportedly close to reaching an agreement with Mali that would allow American aircraft and drones to resume intelligence-gathering operations over Malian territory, focusing on jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda. The potential resumpti
title_en: United States Nears Agreement with Mali to Resume Intelligence Flights
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 9, 2026 - The United States is reportedly close to reaching an agreement with Mali that would allow American aircraft and drones to resume intelligence-gathering operations over Malian territory, focusing on jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda. The potential resumpti
body_en:
Bamako, March 9, 2026 - The United States is reportedly close to reaching an agreement with Mali that would allow American aircraft and drones to resume intelligence-gathering operations over Malian territory, focusing on jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda.
The potential resumption of operations comes after Washington lifted sanctions against several high-ranking Malian officials, including the Defense Minister, who had previously faced restrictions for alleged ties to Russian mercenaries. The decision addresses a key demand from the Malian government and could pave the way for renewed security cooperation between the two countries.
Officials indicated that the U.S. is particularly motivated by the ongoing search for an American pilot, Kevin Rideout, 48, who was kidnapped in Niamey, Niger, while working with the missionary organization Serving In Mission. He is now believed to be held by armed groups linked to the Islamic State in the Sahel, and his recovery is a priority in Washington’s renewed engagement with Bamako.
The security situation in Mali remains precarious, with jihadist groups expanding in multiple regions and continuing attacks on roads, economic infrastructure, and some mining operations. The proposed agreement for intelligence flights is part of broader efforts to address these persistent threats.

Bamako, March 12, 2026 - General Assimi Goïta, President of the Transition and Head of State, presided over a ceremonial presentation of giant checks from the Local Mining Development Fund to nine municipalities on Thursday at Koulouba Palace.
The event was attended by Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga, the President of the National Transition Council, the Ministers of Territorial Administration, Mines, Economy and Finance, and other government and administrative officials, including the Minister-Commissioner in charge of mining affairs.

title: Malian Government Equips 14 Vocational Training Centers with 2 Billion CFA Investment
excerpt: Bamako, March 3, 2026 - The Malian government has provided new equipment worth 2 billion CFA francs to 14 vocational training centers across the country in an effort to strengthen technical education and boost employment opportunities. The handover ceremony was presided over on T
title_en: Malian Government Equips 14 Vocational Training Centers with 2 Billion CFA Investment
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 3, 2026 - The Malian government has provided new equipment worth 2 billion CFA francs to 14 vocational training centers across the country in an effort to strengthen technical education and boost employment opportunities. The handover ceremony was presided over on T
body_en:
Bamako, March 3, 2026 - The Malian government has provided new equipment worth 2 billion CFA francs to 14 vocational training centers across the country in an effort to strengthen technical education and boost employment opportunities.
The handover ceremony was presided over on Tuesday by Oumou Sall Seck, Minister of National Entrepreneurship, Employment, and Vocational Training.
According to the ministry, the equipment-fully financed through the national budget-aims to enhance the operational capacity of vocational institutions and improve practical training for young people.
The beneficiary centers are located in Sénou, Missabougou, Kéniéba, Keleya, Fana, Dioïla, Tominian, Saye, Yorosso, Yangasso, Sikasso, Bougouni, Yanfolila, and Badougou Djoliba.
Authorities say the equipment will support training in a wide range of technical and professional fields, including metal construction, building electricity, masonry, building painting, refrigeration and air conditioning, wood carpentry, tiling, automotive and motorcycle mechanics, photovoltaic electricity, electronics, as well as textile-related trades such as cutting, sewing, and dyeing.
The initiative is part of the government’s broader strategy to strengthen vocational education and equip young Malians with practical skills aligned with labor market needs.

body_en:
Bandiagara, March 8, 2026 - Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga, representing President of the Transition Assimi Goïta, laid the foundation stone for a new Traditional Authority Building in Bandiagara on Sunday, providing the 19th administrative region with dedicated facilities for local traditional leaders.
The building will feature a vestibule, offices, guest rooms, and parking, and is scheduled for completion within ten months. Construction will be carried out by La Falaise du Mali, with the architectural firm ALDI overseeing the project.
Prime Minister Maïga praised the presidential initiative to equip all regions with formal spaces for traditional authorities, emphasizing their vital role in maintaining national stability and preserving cultural heritage.
The Bandiagara project follows similar initiatives in Koulikoro, Ségou, Koutiala, San, and Timbuktu, reinforcing the government’s commitment to supporting traditional leadership across Mali.

body_en:
Bamako, March 9, 2026 - Colonel-Major Assa Badiallo Touré, Minister of Health and Social Development, met on Monday with representatives of the pharmacists’ unions SYNAPPO and SYNAPHARM to address procedural delays in reimbursements for services rendered.
The meeting, held at the Ministry of Health, provided a platform for union leaders to present challenges faced by pharmacists in receiving timely payments under the Mandatory Health Insurance system.
Union representatives highlighted the need to revise the reimbursement process to improve financial management between healthcare providers and insurers, aiming to ensure more efficient compensation for services delivered.
The discussions underscore the government’s ongoing efforts to strengthen Mali’s healthcare system and support frontline healthcare professionals.

title_en: Mali Registers Children of Terror Attack Victims as Wards of the Nation

body_en:
Bamako, March 13, 2026 - Thirty-one children of tanker truck drivers killed in terrorist attacks have officially been registered as Wards of the Nation in Mali, receiving their identity cards and bank accounts during a ceremony at the Prime Minister’s Office on Friday.
The event was chaired by Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga and attended by the Ministers of Health and Social Development, Labor, Public Service and Social Dialogue, and Transport and Infrastructure.
In a departure from the usual schedule, which typically sees such ceremonies held in October under the President of the Transition, these children were registered and provided their cards ahead of time, in recognition of the government’s commitment to supporting families affected by terrorism.
The initiative aims to provide financial support and social protection to children who lost their parents in violent attacks, reinforcing the state’s efforts to care for victims of insecurity and their families.

In a departure from the usual schedule, which typically sees such ceremonies held in October under the President of the Transition, these children were registered and provided their cards ahead of time, in recognition of the government’s commitment to supporting families affected by terrorism.
The initiative aims to provide financial support and social protection to children who lost their parents in violent attacks, reinforcing the state’s efforts to care for victims of insecurity and their families.

title: Mali’s Transition President Meets Legal Team After Court Victory Over Regional Sanctions
excerpt: Bamako, March 2, 2026 - Mali’s transitional president Assimi Goïta received the legal team that represented the country before regional courts following a ruling that declared sanctions imposed on Mali in 2022 illegal. The meeting took place on Monday in Bamako and followed the J

excerpt_en: Bamako, March 2, 2026 - Mali’s transitional president Assimi Goïta received the legal team that represented the country before regional courts following a ruling that declared sanctions imposed on Mali in 2022 illegal. The meeting took place on Monday in Bamako and followed the J
body_en:
Bamako, March 2, 2026 - Mali’s transitional president Assimi Goïta received the legal team that represented the country before regional courts following a ruling that declared sanctions imposed on Mali in 2022 illegal.
The meeting took place on Monday in Bamako and followed the January 28 decision by the Court of Justice of the West African Economic and Monetary Union, which ruled in favor of Mali in its dispute with the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU).
The sanctions had been imposed during a tense political period in early 2022 after Mali’s military authorities delayed a transition to civilian rule.
During the audience, Goïta praised the legal team for their work defending the country’s interests in the case.
The delegation included Justice and Human Rights Minister Mahamadou Kassogué, along with lawyers Ousmane Mama Traoré, Fatoumata Sidibé Diarra, and Amadou Tiéoulé Diarra, who took part in the legal proceedings.
Human Rights Concerns Raised in Azawad
Separately, the association Kal Akal released a report on March 1 documenting alleged human rights violations in Azawad and central Mali.
According to the report, the group recorded 11 cases of executions and massacres, 13 cases of arrests and disappearances, and six incidents involving destruction and looting.
The organization said civilians were killed and that many communities had their livelihoods severely affected.
The report attributes most of the alleged violations to the Malian armed forces and allied Russian fighters linked to the Afrika Korps group.

body_en:
Bamako, March 12, 2026 - Mamoudou Kassogue, Mali’s Minister of Justice and Human Rights, Keeper of the Seals, co-chaired the opening of a conference-debate on Thursday at the Bamako International Conference Center (CICB) to celebrate International Women’s Day.
Organized by the Network of African Women and Parliamentarians of Mali (REFAMP/Mali), the event focused on the theme: “Women’s and Girls’ Rights: Acting for a Safe and Equitable Future in a Resilient, Unified, and Sovereign Mali.” Minister Kassogue described the theme as highly relevant, highlighting the crucial role women play in shaping the country’s development and resilience.
In his address, the Minister paid tribute to the founders of REFAMP/Mali, noting that since its creation in 1996, the organization has played a key role in advocating for women’s empowerment and rights.
Before officially opening the ceremony, Kassogue assured participants of his and his ministry’s full commitment to supporting women in their ongoing efforts to protect and promote women’s rights across Mali.

body_en:
Bamako, March 12, 2026 - The 15th Ordinary Session of the Board of Directors of the National Institute for Judicial Training (INFJ) “Maître Demba Diallo” opened on Thursday under the chairmanship of Dr. Boubacar Sidiki Diarrah, Secretary General of the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights.
The ceremony, held at the institute’s premises, was attended by members of the General Directorate and invited resource persons, including former Minister of Justice Hamidou Younoussa Maiga and former INFJ Board member Alassane Diallo.
In his address, Dr. Diarrah praised the institute’s management and staff for their achievements in 2025 and provided a positive assessment of the institute’s performance.
The 2026 session will review three key documents: the 2025 annual performance report, the 2026 annual performance plan, and the 2026 annual performance contract, which serve as essential tools for evaluating results and guiding future actions.
The Secretary General highlighted the importance of these sessions in ensuring effective management and the continued professional development of Mali’s judicial personnel.

Soumountera presented the Bar Association’s vision for the coming years, highlighting priorities such as lawyer training, professional ethics, and the integration of digital tools to enhance efficiency and transparency in the justice system.

The meeting reflects a shared commitment between Mali’s judicial authorities and legal professionals to create a more efficient, accessible, and citizen-focused justice system.

body_en:
Bamako, March 5, 2026 - Traders in Bamako staged protests on Thursday to denounce what they describe as worsening living and working conditions, citing a series of fires in local markets and growing insecurity in the Malian capital.
Demonstrators said several markets have recently been destroyed by fires, causing significant financial losses for vendors and raising concerns about the safety of commercial areas. Many traders claim the repeated incidents have left them vulnerable and without sufficient protection.
The protesters also warned that insecurity in the capital is increasingly affecting their daily activities, making it difficult to operate businesses and protect their goods.
In response, groups of traders gathered in the streets to voice their frustration and call on authorities to take urgent action to secure markets and prevent further incidents.
Organizers of the protest said they are preparing a large nationwide demonstration in the coming weeks aimed at pressuring the government to implement stronger security measures and guarantee the safety of traders and their businesses.

Timbuktu Region, March 4, 2026 - The jihadist group Jama'at Nasr al‑Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) has claimed responsibility for an improvised explosive device (IED) attack targeting Malian military forces and Russian fighters in northern Mali.
According to the group, the explosion struck a military vehicle on Wednesday morning along the Niafunké-Tonka road in the Timbuktu Region.
JNIM said the device targeted a convoy involving soldiers from the Malian Armed Forces and members of the Africa Corps, the Russian paramilitary formation operating alongside Malian forces.
No immediate official statement from the Malian authorities regarding casualties or damage was available at the time of reporting.
The attack comes amid continuing insurgent activity in northern and central Mali, where jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State frequently target security forces and their allies.

excerpt_en: Kidal Region, March 3, 2026 - The jihadist group Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) has claimed responsibility for another improvised explosive device (IED) attack targeting Malian and allied forces in northern Mali. According to the group, the explosion struck a Malian ar
body_en:
Kidal Region, March 3, 2026 - The jihadist group Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) has claimed responsibility for another improvised explosive device (IED) attack targeting Malian and allied forces in northern Mali.
According to the group, the explosion struck a Malian army armored vehicle on Tuesday evening in the village of Karouroukh, near Aguelhok in the Kidal Region.
JNIM said the attack targeted soldiers from the Malian Armed Forces along with members of the Africa Corps, the Russian paramilitary formation operating alongside Malian troops.
Following the explosion, a Malian military helicopter reportedly deployed to the scene near Aguelhok.
Initial reports indicate that several Russian fighters were killed and others wounded in the blast. The injured were reportedly evacuated to the city of Kidal for treatment.
There has been no immediate official confirmation from Malian authorities regarding the casualties. The incident underscores the continuing insurgent threat in northern Mali, where armed groups frequently target military convoys using roadside bombs.

body_en:
Bamako, March 5, 2026 - The jihadist group Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) has reportedly established control over major routes connecting Kayes and Bamako, according to a video released by the group on March 5.
The footage shows armed fighters stopping vehicles traveling along the Kayes-Bamako and Nioro-Bamako roads, inspecting passengers and controlling who can continue their journey. Reports indicate that travelers originating from Kayes and Nioro are particularly affected, with some prevented from proceeding.
Local sources suggest that JNIM has maintained a presence and operational control over these routes since September 2025, raising ongoing concerns about security and the safe movement of civilians and goods.
Authorities have not yet provided an official response to the reported road closures and vehicle inspections. The situation underscores the persistent challenges posed by insurgent groups in Mali, especially along strategic transport corridors.

title: Drone Attack in Gao Sparks Conflicting Reports Between Azawad Front and Malian Forces
excerpt: Gao, March 11, 2026 - The city of Gao witnessed a drone strike targeting the Gao military airport within the Firhoun Ag Alinsar camp, one of Mali’s major military installations, on Wednesday morning. The incident has generated conflicting accounts from the Azawad Liberation Front
title_en: Drone Attack in Gao Sparks Conflicting Reports Between Azawad Front and Malian Forces
excerpt_en: Gao, March 11, 2026 - The city of Gao witnessed a drone strike targeting the Gao military airport within the Firhoun Ag Alinsar camp, one of Mali’s major military installations, on Wednesday morning. The incident has generated conflicting accounts from the Azawad Liberation Front
body_en:
Gao, March 11, 2026 - The city of Gao witnessed a drone strike targeting the Gao military airport within the Firhoun Ag Alinsar camp, one of Mali’s major military installations, on Wednesday morning. The incident has generated conflicting accounts from the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) and Malian military sources.
According to the FLA, the attack involved 25 kamikaze drones, causing significant casualties and material losses among Malian troops and Africa Corps forces stationed at the base. Sources close to the group added that the drones were deployed in two waves, with 18 drones in the first wave to overwhelm the Russian TOR-M2K air defense system, which intercepted 12 drones. A second wave, supported by mortar fire, reportedly damaged a Bayraktar TB2 drone command post, a Sukhoi-24 aircraft hangar, and several helicopters. The FLA claimed that 95% of the operation’s objectives had been achieved.
In contrast, the Malian army stated that a terrorist group had attempted a drone and projectile attack against its forces but reported no casualties or significant material damage. The army said a patrol was deployed to pursue the attackers and that investigations were ongoing to assess any possible damage outside the camp.
Russian elements of the Africa Corps have not issued an official statement, though unofficial channels suggested that the attack had no significant impact, with no losses reported among Russian personnel or within the base.
The incident highlights ongoing tensions and the persistent threat posed by drone and improvised attacks in northern Mali, while the differing accounts underscore the challenge of verifying operational impacts in conflict zones.

title: Bamako Faces Fuel Shortages, Power Cuts, and Water Disruptions Amid Public Discontent
excerpt: Bamako, March 14, 2026 - The Malian capital is grappling with a severe fuel supply crisis, particularly affecting diesel, which has disrupted electricity and water services and fueled growing public frustration. The shortages, ongoing for approximately two weeks, follow a persist
title_en: Bamako Faces Fuel Shortages, Power Cuts, and Water Disruptions Amid Public Discontent
excerpt_en: Bamako, March 14, 2026 - The Malian capital is grappling with a severe fuel supply crisis, particularly affecting diesel, which has disrupted electricity and water services and fueled growing public frustration. The shortages, ongoing for approximately two weeks, follow a persist
body_en:
Bamako, March 14, 2026 - The Malian capital is grappling with a severe fuel supply crisis, particularly affecting diesel, which has disrupted electricity and water services and fueled growing public frustration. The shortages, ongoing for approximately two weeks, follow a persistent hydrocarbon supply instability after the Jama'at Nasr al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) imposed a fuel embargo on the country in September 2025.
Residents report queues of up to three kilometers at gas stations, with trucks, buses, cars, and motorcycles waiting hours for diesel. While gasoline remains relatively available, the diesel shortage has worsened, echoing the crisis of last October and November when the armed embargo’s impact peaked.
The energy sector has been heavily affected, as Mali’s power plants rely on diesel. Many neighborhoods are now experiencing power outages exceeding 24 consecutive hours, while other areas receive electricity for only three to seven hours per day-far below the transitional authorities’ promise of roughly 19 hours of electricity daily during Ramadan.
Water supplies are also affected, as pumping stations depend on the national electricity grid operated by Énergie du Mali (EDM). Power outages have led to frequent water cuts in multiple districts, compounding public grievances.
Frustration has grown in the capital, expressed openly on social media and in traditional discussion forums known as “grins.” Citizens have also questioned taxes on mobile phone services and money transfers, introduced a year ago to fund energy sector improvements, citing a lack of transparency in the management of these funds. A widely shared social media slogan captures the mood:
“The blackness of night, the blackness of despair, the blackness of the new Mali, the blackness of propaganda.”
The government has attempted to downplay the crisis. Minister of Industry and Trade Moussa Alassane Diallo described the country’s petroleum supply as “regular,” attributing shortages to speculative practices and hoarding by some operators. Authorities have introduced measures such as limiting truck fuel to 600 liters per vehicle over 72 hours to better manage distribution.
Meanwhile, state media continue highlighting initiatives to distribute solar panels to artisans, promoted by President of the Transition Assimi Goïta as part of efforts to address the energy crisis. Despite these measures, observers warn that the fuel and electricity shortages highlight the fragility of Mali’s supply system, particularly amid ongoing security challenges and logistical difficulties, leaving the capital facing one of its most severe service crises in recent years.
Conclusion
The period from February 1 to March 15, 2026, illustrates a dual reality for Mali: a time of strategic diplomatic expansion alongside acute internal security and infrastructure challenges. While the transitional government has achieved notable international and legal milestones, the daily lives of citizens continue to be shaped by insecurity and disruptions to essential services.
Key Strategic Developments
Diplomatic Realignment: Mali has advanced a multipolar foreign policy, marked by high-level tributes to Iranian leadership, credential presentations in Kazakhstan, and strengthened cooperation with China.
Shifting Western Relations: Relations with the United States show signs of a pragmatic thaw, highlighted by the lifting of military sanctions and ongoing negotiations to resume intelligence-gathering flights.
Legal and Economic Milestones: Mali secured a major legal victory, with regional courts declaring the 2022 ECOWAS/WAEMU sanctions illegal. The government also advanced local development, including the allocation of 18.4 billion CFA francs from the Local Mining Development Fund to municipalities.
Persistent Challenges
Escalating Insecurity: Insurgent groups, including JNIM and the Azawad Army, have intensified attacks, using IEDs and drones against Malian forces and Africa Corps personnel. The seizure of key transport routes, such as Kayes-Bamako, underscores the ongoing struggle to maintain territorial control.
Humanitarian and Service Crisis: Bamako faces a severe fuel and diesel shortage, triggering widespread power and water outages. Public discontent has grown, with traders protesting fires, insecurity, and service disruptions across the capital.
Ultimately, the transitional authorities confront the challenge of transforming diplomatic and legal gains into tangible stability. The success of the National Strategy for Emergence (SNEDD 2024-2033) will hinge on securing strategic corridors, restoring reliable basic services, and addressing the urgent humanitarian and security needs of the population.
By Maïga Sidi Bonkana
(Boukari Zankey Sidi)
Jeff Buleli

Ultimately, the transitional authorities confront the challenge of transforming diplomatic and legal gains into tangible stability. The success of the National Strategy for Emergence (SNEDD 2024-2033) will hinge on securing strategic corridors, restoring reliable basic services, and addressing the urgent humanitarian and security needs of the population.

body_en:
On 23 February 2026, Sudan strongly criticized Uganda following a meeting between President Yoweri Museveni and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, leader of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), intensifying diplomatic tensions between the two countries.
Sudanese authorities described the visit of Dagalo, also known as “Hemedti,”, as an affront to human rights and to the Sudanese people, accusing the RSF leader of responsibility for widespread violence and civilian deaths during the ongoing Sudan conflict.
Officials in Khartoum argued that hosting the RSF leader constitutes a violation of international norms, which discourage support or engagement with armed groups opposing a recognized government.
During the meeting held on 20 February 2026, President Museveni emphasized the need for dialogue and political solutions as the only sustainable path toward peace in Sudan.
The visit comes as the Rapid Support Forces remain engaged in heavy fighting against Sudanese government forces, with the group facing serious accusations of war crimes and genocide.

title: Catholic Church Says Condemning Rwanda Will Not Resolve DRC Crisis
excerpt: KINSHASA, February 24, 2026 - The Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has stated that repeatedly condemning Rwanda is not a solution to the country’s ongoing security and political crisis, emphasizing instead the need for inclusive national dialogue among Co
title_en: Catholic Church Says Condemning Rwanda Will Not Resolve DRC Crisis
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, February 24, 2026 - The Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has stated that repeatedly condemning Rwanda is not a solution to the country’s ongoing security and political crisis, emphasizing instead the need for inclusive national dialogue among Co
body_en:
KINSHASA, February 24, 2026 - The Catholic Church in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has stated that repeatedly condemning Rwanda is not a solution to the country’s ongoing security and political crisis, emphasizing instead the need for inclusive national dialogue among Congolese stakeholders.
Church leaders say their current priority is to promote peace talks and national reconciliation, rather than focusing on accusations against Rwanda, which has frequently been blamed by authorities for its alleged support to the AFC/M23 rebellion operating in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.
Shift in Approach
The Catholic Bishops' Conference (CENCO) acknowledged that it had previously raised concerns about Rwanda’s alleged role in the conflict but concluded that continued condemnation would not help resolve the country’s internal challenges.
The Secretary General of CENCO, Bishop Donatien Nshole, explained that Church leaders had mentioned Rwanda in past statements but later decided to adopt a different strategy centered on national unity and dialogue.
According to Church officials, the new approach focuses on creating space for peace negotiations involving all Congolese actors, seen as a more effective path toward resolving the crisis.
Peace Dialogue Initiative
Since early 2025, the Catholic Church and the Anglican Church have been working on a joint initiative aimed at promoting inclusive peace talks between Congolese parties.
Church leaders argue that broad national dialogue, without excluding any stakeholders, offers the best chance for lasting stability in the country.
Government Opposition
The DRC government has expressed reservations about the initiative, maintaining that armed groups should not be included in political discussions.
Authorities insist that individuals who have taken up arms against the state must first lay down their weapons before being considered for participation in political negotiations.
The debate highlights continuing differences between the Catholic Church and the government over the best approach to resolving the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC, where insecurity linked to armed groups continues to affect civilian populations.

title: Rwandan Peacekeepers Provide Free Medical Care to Prisoners in Central African Republic
excerpt: Bria, February 25, 2026 - Rwandan peacekeepers deployed in the Central African Republic have provided free medical treatment to detainees at the Bria prison camp, as part of ongoing humanitarian assistance efforts under the United Nations peacekeeping mission. The operation was c
title_en: Rwandan Peacekeepers Provide Free Medical Care to Prisoners in Central African Republic
excerpt_en: Bria, February 25, 2026 - Rwandan peacekeepers deployed in the Central African Republic have provided free medical treatment to detainees at the Bria prison camp, as part of ongoing humanitarian assistance efforts under the United Nations peacekeeping mission. The operation was c
body_en:
Bria, February 25, 2026 - Rwandan peacekeepers deployed in the Central African Republic have provided free medical treatment to detainees at the Bria prison camp, as part of ongoing humanitarian assistance efforts under the United Nations peacekeeping mission.
The operation was carried out by members of the Rwandan Battle Group 8, supported by a Level II military hospital team, and aimed at addressing urgent healthcare needs among prisoners. Services included treatment for internal diseases, women’s health services, dental care, and other essential medical support.
Officials present during the operation included the Bria camp commander, the head of the Rwandan military hospital, and the commander of Rwandan Battle Group 8.
Local authorities welcomed the initiative, highlighting the longstanding cooperation between peacekeeping forces and local institutions. They emphasized that detainees often face serious challenges in accessing medical services, particularly due to shortages of medicines and limited healthcare resources.
The medical outreach was presented as part of the broader peacekeeping mandate, which focuses not only on security operations but also on the protection of civilians and the promotion of human dignity.
Peacekeeping officials stressed that access to healthcare remains a fundamental right and that humanitarian activities such as these contribute to improving living conditions for vulnerable populations, including detainees.
The initiative reflects the expanding role of peacekeeping missions, which increasingly combine security responsibilities with humanitarian support, reinforcing commitments to human rights, solidarity, and civilian protection in conflict-affected areas.

title: Bobi Wine Refuses to Negotiate with Uganda Government While in Hiding
excerpt: Uganda, February 25, 2026 - Opposition politician Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, popularly known as Bobi Wine, has rejected calls to negotiate with the Ugandan government while remaining in hiding, nearly six weeks after the country’s presidential elections. Bobi Wine went into hidi
title_en: Bobi Wine Refuses to Negotiate with Uganda Government While in Hiding
excerpt_en: Uganda, February 25, 2026 - Opposition politician Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, popularly known as Bobi Wine, has rejected calls to negotiate with the Ugandan government while remaining in hiding, nearly six weeks after the country’s presidential elections. Bobi Wine went into hidi
body_en:
Uganda, February 25, 2026 - Opposition politician Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, popularly known as Bobi Wine, has rejected calls to negotiate with the Ugandan government while remaining in hiding, nearly six weeks after the country’s presidential elections.
Bobi Wine went into hiding on January 15, 2026, following the controversial re-election of President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni. He has voiced concerns over the conduct of the elections and alleges that security forces are seeking to harm him, which he says is why he remains in seclusion.
In an interview with UK’s Channel 4, Bobi Wine stated that he would only come out of hiding if necessary to avoid being forced into government demands.
Asked about ongoing discussions and calls for him to meet with President Museveni or his son, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Bobi Wine said he could not negotiate under coercion. “You cannot negotiate with someone who has a gun to your neck and say ‘let’s talk.’ Only those who are free can truly discuss. That is what meaningful dialogue looks like,” he said.
The Ugandan Electoral Commission reported that President Museveni won with 71.65% of the vote, while Bobi Wine secured 24.72%. Despite the official results, Bobi Wine continues to question the transparency and fairness of the election process.

title: Rwanda and Singapore Strengthen Financial Sector Cooperation
excerpt: Singapore, February 25, 2026 - Rwanda and Singapore are expanding cooperation in the financial sector, focusing on banking, financial technology, and capacity building for government institutions. The Rwandan Ambassador to Singapore, Innocent B. Muhizi, held talks with representa
title_en: Rwanda and Singapore Strengthen Financial Sector Cooperation
excerpt_en: Singapore, February 25, 2026 - Rwanda and Singapore are expanding cooperation in the financial sector, focusing on banking, financial technology, and capacity building for government institutions. The Rwandan Ambassador to Singapore, Innocent B. Muhizi, held talks with representa
body_en:
Singapore, February 25, 2026 - Rwanda and Singapore are expanding cooperation in the financial sector, focusing on banking, financial technology, and capacity building for government institutions.
The Rwandan Ambassador to Singapore, Innocent B. Muhizi, held talks with representatives from Singapore’s banking sector and Ministry of Foreign Affairs, emphasizing opportunities for multi-sectoral collaboration, knowledge sharing, and partnerships to promote growth and innovation.
During a meeting with Ai Boon Ong-Ang, President of the Singapore Bankers Association, discussions centered on banking sector collaboration, particularly in fintech, as Singapore supports Rwanda’s goal of becoming a regional Fintech hub.
Ambassador Muhizi also met with Jolene Tan, Director General for Development Partnerships, to discuss continued cooperation in capacity building programs for civil servants, including knowledge development, institutional strengthening, and creating sustainable cooperation mechanisms.
Rwanda and Singapore already maintain partnerships in technology development, innovation, education, green technology, and capacity building. The countries also collaborate through FOSS, an organization established in 1992 to foster international cooperation.
In September 2023, the two countries signed a cooperation agreement to enhance population welfare and promote economic development, laying the groundwork for ongoing financial and technological collaboration.

title: Rwanda Receives Credentials of Three Newly Appointed Ambassadors
excerpt: The Rwanda Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (MINAFFET) has received copies of the credentials of three diplomats appointed by their respective governments to serve as Ambassadors to Rwanda. The documents were received on March 2, 2026, by Usta Kayitesi, S
title_en: Rwanda Receives Credentials of Three Newly Appointed Ambassadors
excerpt_en: The Rwanda Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (MINAFFET) has received copies of the credentials of three diplomats appointed by their respective governments to serve as Ambassadors to Rwanda. The documents were received on March 2, 2026, by Usta Kayitesi, S
body_en:
The Rwanda Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (MINAFFET) has received copies of the credentials of three diplomats appointed by their respective governments to serve as Ambassadors to Rwanda.
The documents were received on March 2, 2026, by Usta Kayitesi, Secretary of State at MINAFFET, during a formal ceremony in Kigali.
The diplomats who presented their letters of credence copies are Giles Cerutti, appointed as Ambassador of Switzerland to Rwanda, Brigadier General Boubacar Diallo, representing Mali, and Victorino-Nká Obiang Maye, representing Equatorial Guinea.
In international diplomatic practice, a government first appoints an individual to serve as ambassador to another country, after which the receiving state must approve the appointment before the diplomat assumes official duties.
Once approved, the envoy travels to the host country and presents copies of the credentials to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or an authorized official, confirming their designation.
Within a specified period, the ambassador then presents the original letters of credence to the Head of State, formally completing the process and officially beginning their diplomatic mission in the host country.

title: Rwanda’s Ambassador to UN Says DRC Insecurity Stems from Internal Problems
excerpt: Rwanda’s Ambassador to Switzerland and the United Nations in Geneva, Urujeni Bakuramutsa, told the UN Human Rights Council on March 3, 2026, that the ongoing insecurity in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is largely caused by internal governance and institutional problems w
title_en: Rwanda’s Ambassador to UN Says DRC Insecurity Stems from Internal Problems
excerpt_en: Rwanda’s Ambassador to Switzerland and the United Nations in Geneva, Urujeni Bakuramutsa, told the UN Human Rights Council on March 3, 2026, that the ongoing insecurity in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is largely caused by internal governance and institutional problems w
body_en:
Rwanda’s Ambassador to Switzerland and the United Nations in Geneva, Urujeni Bakuramutsa, told the UN Human Rights Council on March 3, 2026, that the ongoing insecurity in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is largely caused by internal governance and institutional problems within the country.
Speaking on the situation in the Great Lakes region, Ambassador Bakuramutsa noted that more than 160 armed groups operate in the DRC, particularly in the eastern provinces, where instability has persisted for over 30 years.
“In eastern DRC, the problem of insecurity has been ongoing for decades, driven by deep-seated internal and institutional issues,” he said. He added that insecurity is not confined to the east but has spread to other areas, including near Kinshasa, where groups such as Mobondo are active, illustrating systemic governance challenges.
Addressing accusations that Rwanda supports the M23 armed group, Ambassador Bakuramutsa emphasized that M23 is composed of Congolese fighters who have taken up arms due to political and security problems in the DRC, and that the primary responsibility to resolve these issues lies with the DRC government through political measures.
He also criticized the DRC government for continuing to support the FDLR terrorist group, formed by members of the defeated army (Ex-FAR) and Interahamwe, who were responsible for the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. Ambassador Bakuramutsa noted that despite the June 2025 peace agreement, reinforced in December 2025, the DRC has failed to dismantle the FDLR and has even integrated members into its military, contravening UN Security Council resolutions.
Ambassador Bakuramutsa called for a thorough analysis of the root causes of insecurity in the Great Lakes region to determine the responsibilities of each country and to guide solutions for lasting peace.

He added that insecurity is not confined to the east but has spread to other areas, including near Kinshasa, where groups such as Mobondo are active, illustrating systemic governance challenges.
Addressing accusations that Rwanda supports the M23 armed group, Ambassador Bakuramutsa emphasized that M23 is composed of Congolese fighters who have taken up arms due to political and security problems in the DRC, and that the primary responsibility to resolve these issues lies with the DRC government through political measures.
He also criticized the DRC government for continuing to support the FDLR terrorist group, formed by members of the defeated army (Ex-FAR) and Interahamwe, who were responsible for the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. Ambassador Bakuramutsa noted that despite the June 2025 peace agreement, reinforced in December 2025, the DRC has failed to dismantle the FDLR and has even integrated members into its military, contravening UN Security Council resolutions.
Ambassador Bakuramutsa called for a thorough analysis of the root causes of insecurity in the Great Lakes region to determine the responsibilities of each country and to guide solutions for lasting peace.

Rwanda and India have signed an agreement on cultural exchange aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation and deepening people-to-people ties between the two countries. The agreement was signed on March 3, 2026, during the second meeting of the bilateral commission monitoring cooperation.
The meeting took place in New Delhi, India, with the Rwandan delegation led by Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation Nduhungirehe Olivier, and the Indian delegation led by Secretary of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh.
Officials reviewed the status of cooperation in key sectors, including military, agriculture, trade and investment, education, science and technology, as well as culture and people-to-people exchanges. The cultural exchange agreement will guide initiatives between the two nations until 2030.
Minister Kirti highlighted that the discussions also included global and regional developments that could affect the interests of both countries.
Rwanda-India relations have grown steadily over the years. Rwanda was among the first African countries to open an Indian representative office, part of a plan to open 18 new offices across Africa to boost engagement.
Indian investment in Rwanda has also expanded, making India the second-largest investor in the country in 2024, after China. In that year, China invested $460 million (14.1% of total investment), while India invested $445.1 million (13.6%), reflecting its growing economic partnership with Rwanda.

Ambassador Santa Laker Kinyera, Uganda’s Deputy Ambassador to Rwanda, has died at Mulago Hospital in Kampala on the morning of March 3, 2026, the Ugandan Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced. The cause of death has not been disclosed.
Ambassador Kinyera had a diplomatic career spanning over 30 years, beginning in 1994, serving in various capacities including Minister of Foreign Affairs and representing Uganda in multiple international postings.
He played a key role in restoring and strengthening bilateral relations between Uganda and Rwanda, particularly in areas of trade, security, and cross-border cooperation, including efforts to reopen the border during periods of tension.
In Uganda, Kinyera is remembered as a dedicated diplomat whose work contributed significantly to peaceful and productive relations between the two neighboring countries.

title: US Senate Urges DRC Forces to Halt Attacks, Return to Negotiating Table
excerpt: The United States Senate has called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) forces to cease attacks on AFC/M23 positions in North and South Kivu provinces, emphasizing the need for a return to peace negotiations. The statement was made on March 4, 2026, by Senator Jim Risch, Ch
title_en: US Senate Urges DRC Forces to Halt Attacks, Return to Negotiating Table
excerpt_en: The United States Senate has called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) forces to cease attacks on AFC/M23 positions in North and South Kivu provinces, emphasizing the need for a return to peace negotiations. The statement was made on March 4, 2026, by Senator Jim Risch, Ch
body_en:
The United States Senate has called on the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) forces to cease attacks on AFC/M23 positions in North and South Kivu provinces, emphasizing the need for a return to peace negotiations. The statement was made on March 4, 2026, by Senator Jim Risch, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
Senator Risch highlighted that the Washington peace agreement signed between Rwanda and the DRC with US support offers a path to lasting peace and regional development if fully implemented.
“The DRC government and FARDC must stop pursuing a military solution in eastern DRC, respect the ceasefire, and work with partners, including the United States, to build a lasting solution to the security situation in the east of the country,” Risch said.
While AFC/M23 forces are expected to halt the expansion of their positions, the senator stressed that the FARDC and its allies, including Burundian troops, Wazalendo, mercenaries, and the FDLR, must also refrain from military actions and adhere to the ceasefire.
Despite a ceasefire agreement signed in Doha, Qatar, and the establishment of a monitoring mechanism, attacks by the DRC forces continue. AFC/M23 expressed regret that mediators remain silent while its fighters defend themselves and civilians in North and South Kivu, asserting that bias and misinformation persist in statements condemning the group.
On March 2, 2026, AFC/M23 announced it would continue defending its positions and protecting civilians while calling for renewed dialogue and compliance with the ceasefire.

body_en:
On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Embassy in Qatar announced that all its services would be temporarily moved online due to ongoing security concerns stemming from Iranian attacks in the region.
The embassy explained that the decision was made to ensure safety while continuing assistance to Rwandans and others in need.
“Due to the current security concerns, the Rwandan Embassy in Doha is operating online,” the statement read.
These attacks began after US and Israeli operations against Iran on February 28, 2026, prompting Iran to target allies of the US, including Qatar. The conflict has disrupted normal operations in Qatar, with companies and Qatar Airways suspending services amid the tense security situation.
The embassy reassured the public that, despite moving services online, it would continue to provide support remotely.

title: Burundians Mourn as Ruhwa Border with Rwanda Remains Closed
excerpt: On March 5, 2026, residents of Cibitoke commune in Bujumbura Province, Burundi, expressed frustration and mourning after the Burundian government failed to reopen its border with Rwanda, breaking earlier promises. The border closure has severely affected trade and daily life. Bef
title_en: Burundians Mourn as Ruhwa Border with Rwanda Remains Closed
excerpt_en: On March 5, 2026, residents of Cibitoke commune in Bujumbura Province, Burundi, expressed frustration and mourning after the Burundian government failed to reopen its border with Rwanda, breaking earlier promises. The border closure has severely affected trade and daily life. Bef
body_en:
On March 5, 2026, residents of Cibitoke commune in Bujumbura Province, Burundi, expressed frustration and mourning after the Burundian government failed to reopen its border with Rwanda, breaking earlier promises.
The border closure has severely affected trade and daily life. Before the closure, Burundians exported fruits and vegetables such as lemons, oranges, mangoes, tangerines, and tomatoes to Rwanda, earning significant income. Residents now report higher costs for basic necessities in Burundi compared to Rwanda.
“While the border was still open, we used to export products to Rwanda… This money helped us survive,” said a local resident of Ruhwa village.
The closure has also split families, preventing Burundians and Rwandans who are blood relatives from visiting one another across the border.
The head of Ruhwa village, Nsengiyumva Révocat, highlighted the human impact, emphasizing that many families remain separated due to the government’s decision.
Burundians in Ruhwa are calling on their government to negotiate with Rwanda to reopen the border, restore trade, and allow familial visits, hoping to return to previous levels of economic and social interaction.

title_en: Rwanda Denounces DRC for Destabilizing Regional Peace
excerpt_en: On March 5, 2026, before the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva, Rwanda condemned the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government for allegedly undermining peace in the Great Lakes region. Edmond Tubanambazi, First Counselor at the Rwandan Embassy in Switzerland and
body_en:
On March 5, 2026, before the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva, Rwanda condemned the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government for allegedly undermining peace in the Great Lakes region.
Edmond Tubanambazi, First Counselor at the Rwandan Embassy in Switzerland and at the UN offices in Geneva, emphasized that peace has been a cornerstone of Rwanda’s recovery over the past 32 years following the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. He said the country continues to prioritize unity, reconciliation, and a culture of peace in its national reconstruction.
Tubanambazi accused the DRC of harboring and collaborating with the FDLR terrorist group, instead of dismantling it, and of integrating FDLR fighters into the FARDC and allied groups, posing a threat to regional security. He stressed that these actions have been repeatedly highlighted by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the UN Security Council.
Rwanda, he added, is actively supporting regional security measures, including those under the African Union-led coalition and the Washington Peace Accords, and called for accountability and restraint to prevent armed groups from spreading hatred and committing crimes.

title: Prime Minister Nsengiyumva Attends East African Community Heads of State Summit
excerpt: Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva arrived in Arusha on March 6, 2026, where he is representing President Paul Kagame at the 25th Ordinary Summit of Heads of State of the East African Community (EAC) scheduled for March 7, 2026. Upon arrival at Kilimanjaro International Airport, N
title_en: Prime Minister Nsengiyumva Attends East African Community Heads of State Summit
excerpt_en: Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva arrived in Arusha on March 6, 2026, where he is representing President Paul Kagame at the 25th Ordinary Summit of Heads of State of the East African Community (EAC) scheduled for March 7, 2026. Upon arrival at Kilimanjaro International Airport, N
body_en:
Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva arrived in Arusha on March 6, 2026, where he is representing President Paul Kagame at the 25th Ordinary Summit of Heads of State of the East African Community (EAC) scheduled for March 7, 2026.
Upon arrival at Kilimanjaro International Airport, Nsengiyumva was received by Dennis Londo and Rwanda’s Ambassador to Tanzania, Patrick Nyamvumba.
The summit brings together leaders from eight EAC member states: Tanzania, Rwanda, Kenya, Uganda, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Somalia, South Sudan, and Burundi.
During the meeting, leaders are expected to appoint a new Director General and Secretary General of the EAC, select judges for the East African Court of Justice, and extend the mandates of deputy secretaries general.
One of the key outcomes anticipated from the summit is the launch of a common customs document known as the “EAC Customs Bond.” The new document will replace separate customs documentation currently used by each country for cross-border trade. Officials say the initiative will allow traders to conduct business across EAC member states using a single document, reducing administrative barriers and facilitating coordination between customs authorities, insurers, and financial institutions.
The reform is expected to lower operational costs for traders and accelerate trade and investment within the region.
The summit will also launch the seventh EAC Development Plan, covering the period 2026/27 to 2030/31, which outlines the region’s strategic vision for regional integration and development aimed at boosting social progress and economic growth over the next five years.
Despite an existing legal framework designed to accelerate joint projects, the EAC has acknowledged that intra-regional trade remains relatively low. Trade among member states has stagnated at around 15% over the past decade, significantly below the regional target of 30% to 50%.
Currently, intra-EAC trade accounts for roughly one-eighth of total exports. Regional trade increased only slightly from 11.5% in 2016 to 12.2% in 2024, reflecting the bloc’s continued reliance on external markets.

title_en: Rwanda’s Foreign Minister Criticizes DRC Ex-Minister Over US Statement on Peace in Great Lakes
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, March 8, 2026 - Rwandan Minister of Foreign Affairs, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, criticized former DRC Minister of Foreign Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister Léonard She Okitundu Lundula for distorting the US position on peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region. Okitundu L
body_en:
Kinshasa, March 8, 2026 - Rwandan Minister of Foreign Affairs, Amb. Olivier Nduhungirehe, criticized former DRC Minister of Foreign Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister Léonard She Okitundu Lundula for distorting the US position on peace efforts in the Great Lakes Region.
Okitundu Lundula, who served from December 2016 to 2019, claimed on social media that the United States had imposed sanctions on Rwandan troops supporting the AFC/M23, and urged Rwanda to withdraw its forces from DRC territory, suggesting this would restore peace.
Ambassador Nduhungirehe responded, emphasizing that the primary threat to peace in eastern DRC is not Rwandan troop presence but the FDLR terrorist group, composed of Rwandans involved in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, some of whom were incorporated into the FARDC.
“You are misrepresenting the US Department of State statement,” Nduhungirehe said. “You have overlooked the most important directive: the United States asked the DRC to destroy the FDLR group as soon as possible.”
He noted that this directive is not new. During ministerial peace talks in Luanda, Angola, the then DRC Foreign Minister Christophe Lutundula presented a plan to dismantle the FDLR on June 21, 2024, which was agreed upon by Rwanda and Angola. The plan was signed by the ministers on November 25, 2025, and ratified in Washington on June 27, 2025, during the Washington Peace Accords, attended by President Félix Tshisekedi, President Paul Kagame, and Donald Trump.
Ambassador Nduhungirehe expressed regret that nearly two years later, the DRC has yet to implement its commitments, while mediators continue to urge compliance. He highlighted that the government has not dismantled the FDLR, and in some cases continues to provide the group with weapons, food, and funding, which it uses in the ongoing conflict with AFC/M23 forces controlling parts of North and South Kivu.

title_en: Stephen Patrick Mbundi Appointed Secretary-General of the East African Community
excerpt_en: Arusha, March 7, 2026 - Ambassador Stephen Patrick Mbundi has been appointed Secretary-General of the East African Community (EAC), replacing Kenyan diplomat Veronica Nduva, who held the position since 2024. The appointment was made during the 25th General Assembly of the EAC, wh
body_en:
Arusha, March 7, 2026 - Ambassador Stephen Patrick Mbundi has been appointed Secretary-General of the East African Community (EAC), replacing Kenyan diplomat Veronica Nduva, who held the position since 2024.
The appointment was made during the 25th General Assembly of the EAC, where Mbundi was named for a five-year term from 2026 to 2031. The EAC statement highlighted that he is expected to strengthen diplomatic cooperation among member states and enhance the cohesion of the regional community.
Following the announcement, Mbundi was sworn in before the General Assembly of Heads of State and immediately assumed his duties. Prior to this appointment, he served as Permanent Secretary in charge of EAC Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tanzania.

title: Rwanda Plans $5 Billion Nuclear Power Plant to Boost Electricity Supply
excerpt: Kigali, February 24, 2026 - The Rwanda government estimates that more than $5 billion will be required to construct the country’s first nuclear power plant, a strategic project aimed at significantly increasing electricity production nationwide. Officials indicated that the plann
title_en: Rwanda Plans $5 Billion Nuclear Power Plant to Boost Electricity Supply
excerpt_en: Kigali, February 24, 2026 - The Rwanda government estimates that more than $5 billion will be required to construct the country’s first nuclear power plant, a strategic project aimed at significantly increasing electricity production nationwide. Officials indicated that the plann
body_en:
Kigali, February 24, 2026 - The Rwanda government estimates that more than $5 billion will be required to construct the country’s first nuclear power plant, a strategic project aimed at significantly increasing electricity production nationwide.
Officials indicated that the planned nuclear energy project is expected to strengthen the country’s energy capacity and support long-term industrial development. The initiative was highlighted during a meeting bringing together public institutions and private-sector stakeholders to discuss the investment opportunities linked to the construction of the facility.
Authorities emphasized that building the nuclear power station will require a major financial commitment, estimated between $5 billion and $6 billion, and stressed the importance of private sector participation. The project is expected to involve local industries, particularly companies producing cement, steel, and construction materials, which are among the country’s largest electricity consumers.
The project is also intended to promote local industrial involvement, with national companies encouraged to meet international quality standards in order to contribute to the construction and supply chain. Officials warned that relying exclusively on foreign contractors would represent a missed opportunity for domestic economic growth.
The future nuclear facility is expected to supply electricity across the country and improve industrial productivity, particularly in energy-intensive sectors.
According to projections, Rwanda’s first nuclear plant could become operational in the 2030s, with a specialized workforce of about 230 employees expected to be ready by 2028.
The installation is planned on a site covering between 15 and 50 square kilometers, located far from residential areas. The design includes advanced safety systems, allowing the plant to automatically shut down in the event of a malfunction, preventing the release of harmful radiation.
