title: Rwanda Registers Over 1.8 Million Citizens for Digital e-ID System
excerpt: Kigali, February 25, 2026 - More than 1.8 million citizens have been photographed and registered under Rwanda’s national electronic identity card (e-ID) program, a major digital transformation initiative designed to modernize public services and improve identity verification acro
title_en: Rwanda Registers Over 1.8 Million Citizens for Digital e-ID System
excerpt_en: Kigali, February 25, 2026 - More than 1.8 million citizens have been photographed and registered under Rwanda’s national electronic identity card (e-ID) program, a major digital transformation initiative designed to modernize public services and improve identity verification acro
body_en:
Kigali, February 25, 2026 - More than 1.8 million citizens have been photographed and registered under Rwanda’s national electronic identity card (e-ID) program, a major digital transformation initiative designed to modernize public services and improve identity verification across the country.
The e-ID system will serve as a single permanent identification document, issued to every Rwandan citizen from birth, securely linking interactions between individuals and both government institutions and private services.
Authorities reported that 1,828,763 people have already been registered across nine districts, including the pilot districts of Huye, Nyanza, and Gisagara, as well as Kamonyi, Muhanga, Ruhango, Nyarugenge, Gasabo, and Kicukiro. The project aims to eventually cover at least 15 million people, including citizens living abroad as well as refugees and migrants.
The digital ID project, which has already received more than $50 million in investment, is expected to complete the validation phase by the end of 2026, with the first electronic ID cards scheduled to be issued starting in August 2026.
Integrated Digital Identity System
The e-ID card will integrate multiple services throughout a citizen’s lifetime. For children, the system will be linked to birth registration, school enrollment, vaccinations, and medical care.
For young people, it will support identity verification for education, examinations, driver’s licenses, and employment records.
Among adults, the digital identity will connect services such as taxation, banking, healthcare, land ownership, marriage registration, business activities, and voting systems. It will also support pensions, social services, and asset management.
In the health sector, the system will link insurance coverage, medical records, medications, and vaccination histories. In education, it will provide a continuous identity record from early childhood to adulthood. The system is also expected to improve social protection programs by preventing identity fraud.
Privacy and Data Protection Measures
Officials emphasized that the digital ID system is designed to protect personal data and will not be used for daily surveillance. Access to personal information will require the explicit consent of the citizen.
Only limited information will be shared when verifying identity. For example, a financial institution may confirm that a person is over 18 years old without accessing the full date of birth. Citizens will be able to revoke access rights at any time.
Under data protection regulations, any misuse of information must be reported within 72 hours, and citizens retain the right to correct data and seek compensation if necessary.
Multiple Forms of Digital Identification
The electronic identity system will be available in three formats to ensure accessibility:
A mobile ID card with a QR code containing essential identity data
A secure electronic ID number for official verification
A Token system, allowing users to conduct electronic transactions without revealing their full ID number
These options are intended to ensure that every citizen can verify their identity even if one method is unavailable.
Inclusive Access to Digital Services
Authorities indicated that the system will remain accessible to citizens without smartphones, using mobile SIM cards and USSD services. Local officials will assist residents who lack access to digital technology, ensuring that no one is excluded from essential services.
Officials and lawmakers believe the national e-ID program will accelerate service delivery, simplify administrative procedures, and reduce the need to carry multiple documents.

title: Rwanda Secures $78.5 Million Grant for Kayonza Irrigation Project
excerpt: Kayonza, February 25, 2026 - The Government of Rwanda has received a $78.5 million grant from the International Fund for Agriculture and Livestock Development (IFAD) to boost agricultural development and irrigation infrastructure in Kayonza District. The grant agreement was signe
title_en: Rwanda Secures $78.5 Million Grant for Kayonza Irrigation Project
excerpt_en: Kayonza, February 25, 2026 - The Government of Rwanda has received a $78.5 million grant from the International Fund for Agriculture and Livestock Development (IFAD) to boost agricultural development and irrigation infrastructure in Kayonza District. The grant agreement was signe
body_en:
Kayonza, February 25, 2026 - The Government of Rwanda has received a $78.5 million grant from the International Fund for Agriculture and Livestock Development (IFAD) to boost agricultural development and irrigation infrastructure in Kayonza District.
The grant agreement was signed on February 24, 2026, with Rwanda represented by Minister of Finance and Economic Planning Yusuf Murangwa, and IFAD represented by its Country Director in Rwanda, Dagmawi Habte-Selassie.
The funding will support the irrigation of hills currently used for agriculture and the development of value-added small livestock sectors, aiming to reduce poverty, enhance food security, improve climate resilience, and increase rural household incomes.
Kayonza, one of the districts most vulnerable to droughts caused by extreme heat, experienced significant agricultural challenges in late 2025. The grant is expected to complement ongoing projects, including the Gishanda artificial pond, which will help irrigate 200 hectares of farmland.

title: 32 Rwandan Industries to Receive Licenses for Pan-African Trade
excerpt: For the first time, 32 Rwandan industries that have met common African standards will be granted trade licenses allowing them to export 72 product types to other African countries without additional requirements or obstacles. The licenses are scheduled to be issued on March 6, 20
title_en: 32 Rwandan Industries to Receive Licenses for Pan-African Trade
excerpt_en: For the first time, 32 Rwandan industries that have met common African standards will be granted trade licenses allowing them to export 72 product types to other African countries without additional requirements or obstacles. The licenses are scheduled to be issued on March 6, 20
body_en:
For the first time, 32 Rwandan industries that have met common African standards will be granted trade licenses allowing them to export 72 product types to other African countries without additional requirements or obstacles. The licenses are scheduled to be issued on March 6, 2026.
The announcement was made on March 3, 2026, during the three-day African Standards Organization (ARSO) meeting held in Kigali. The meeting, attended by 16 countries, focused on establishing 25 continental standards covering textiles, textile materials, and related products.
The licenses will initially cover products in agriculture and value addition, with plans to extend certification to other sectors, including garments and footwear.
Gatera Emmanuel, Director of Regulatory Affairs at the Rwanda Standards Board (RSB), said the certifications will expand markets, accelerate collaboration with exporting countries, and promote the ‘Made in Rwanda’ brand. He added, “If a garment is sewn and tested in Rwanda, it will pass quality checks in the destination country without delays, speeding up shipments.”
Gatera also highlighted the potential to boost intra-African trade, noting that current trade among African countries is only 15-18%, compared with over 60% on continents such as Asia and Europe.
Milagrosa Ntombikasiye, representing the National Standards Institute of Eswatini, said that most of Eswatini’s exports currently go to the European Union due to trade challenges within Africa. She welcomed the new regulations, stating they will facilitate continental trade and economic growth.
Dr. Hermogene Nsengimana, Secretary General of ARSO, explained that the initiative aims to harmonize regulations across Africa, reducing costs for inspections and compliance in different countries.
At the conclusion of the meeting, Rwanda will sign cooperation agreements with Zimbabwe and Congo-Brazzaville to further promote trade and streamline export processes with these countries.

Gatera Emmanuel, Director of Regulatory Affairs at the Rwanda Standards Board (RSB), said the certifications will expand markets, accelerate collaboration with exporting countries, and promote the ‘Made in Rwanda’ brand. He added, “If a garment is sewn and tested in Rwanda, it will pass quality checks in the destination country without delays, speeding up shipments.”
Gatera also highlighted the potential to boost intra-African trade, noting that current trade among African countries is only 15-18%, compared with over 60% on continents such as Asia and Europe.
Milagrosa Ntombikasiye, representing the National Standards Institute of Eswatini, said that most of Eswatini’s exports currently go to the European Union due to trade challenges within Africa. She welcomed the new regulations, stating they will facilitate continental trade and economic growth.
Dr. Hermogene Nsengimana, Secretary General of ARSO, explained that the initiative aims to harmonize regulations across Africa, reducing costs for inspections and compliance in different countries.
At the conclusion of the meeting, Rwanda will sign cooperation agreements with Zimbabwe and Congo-Brazzaville to further promote trade and streamline export processes with these countries.

title_en: Chamber of Deputies Urges MINAGRI to Reduce Agricultural Spoilage
excerpt_en: The Chamber of Deputies has requested the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MINAGRI) to develop strategies to monitor and reduce post-harvest spoilage, particularly for rice and maize, by March 3, 2026. The decision was taken during the Plenary Session of March 3, 2026, foll
body_en:
The Chamber of Deputies has requested the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MINAGRI) to develop strategies to monitor and reduce post-harvest spoilage, particularly for rice and maize, by March 3, 2026.
The decision was taken during the Plenary Session of March 3, 2026, following a study to be conducted by the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR). MINAGRI has been given three months to implement the measures.
The move comes after an audit by the Auditor General of Government Finance revealed post-harvest losses of 12.4% for rice and 13.8% for maize, exceeding the national target of reducing crop losses to 5% by 2029.
The audit highlighted insufficient and damaged infrastructure, with rice and maize drying facilities operating at 9% and 18% capacity, and storage facilities accommodating only 33% of production, of which 33% were damaged. In some districts, storage facilities were being misused; for example, Nyagatare’s Rwangingo rice cooperative stored hay instead of rice, while in Rusizi, some storage sheds remained unused.
Muzana Alice, Chairperson of the Commission on Land, Agriculture, Livestock and Environment, emphasized challenges such as limited market access, seasonal variations in production, and highly perishable crops, which affect both farmers and consumers. The audit found that of 14 maize cooperatives visited across Nyagatare, Gatsibo, Gisagara, and Rusizi, 12 lacked active markets for stored produce.
The Chamber urged MINAGRI to:
Establish quarterly and annual monitoring mechanisms for perishable crops, supported by NISR research every three years.
Accelerate the implementation of AMIS technology, which will improve the management of agricultural produce and connect farmers to markets.
Develop methods to better link rice and maize production with markets, ensuring farmers can cultivate with confidence even before AMIS technology is fully operational.
AMIS is a forthcoming agricultural information system designed to provide timely and comprehensive data to support farming decisions and market access across Rwanda.

title: IAEA Conducts Assessment to Support Rwanda’s Nuclear Power Ambitions
excerpt: Rwanda is undergoing an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) assessment to evaluate its readiness to build a nuclear power plant, the agency announced on March 4, 2026. The inspection, conducted by IAEA experts, began on March 2 and will run until March 9, 2026. The assessme
title_en: IAEA Conducts Assessment to Support Rwanda’s Nuclear Power Ambitions
excerpt_en: Rwanda is undergoing an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) assessment to evaluate its readiness to build a nuclear power plant, the agency announced on March 4, 2026. The inspection, conducted by IAEA experts, began on March 2 and will run until March 9, 2026. The assessme
body_en:
Rwanda is undergoing an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) assessment to evaluate its readiness to build a nuclear power plant, the agency announced on March 4, 2026. The inspection, conducted by IAEA experts, began on March 2 and will run until March 9, 2026.
The assessment focuses on 19 key areas, including Rwanda’s nuclear energy policy, funding sources, safety measures, and technical capacity to manage potential risks associated with nuclear plants.
Dr. Fidele Ndahayo, Director General of the Rwanda Atomic Energy Agency (RAEB), said the evaluation will identify areas where Rwanda needs to strengthen efforts. “This assessment will help us gain confidence in the international community and attract support to build these plants,” he explained.
The head of the IAEA Expert Group, Aline des Cloizeaux, clarified that the mission is advisory, not a decision-making process. “We are here to provide guidance on what needs improvement so Rwanda can continue its nuclear development plans,” she said.
Rwanda aims to have a nuclear power plant operational by the 2030s and has already invested in training programs, medical nuclear applications, and collaborations with international partners. In 2023, Rwanda signed an agreement with Dual Fluid Energy Inc. (Germany and Canada) to test a nuclear reactor, followed by projects with partners in Russia and the United States focusing on Small Modular Reactors (SMRs).
SMRs are compact plants capable of generating 100 megawatts of electricity, occupying 15-50 hectares, employing up to 230 workers, and being relocatable to remote areas. They are considered environmentally friendly, reducing up to 29 tons of CO₂ per gigawatt-hour (GWh) according to the World Nuclear Association.
The IAEA assessment is a critical step for Rwanda to demonstrate its commitment to safe, sustainable, and internationally compliant nuclear energy development.

title: Rwanda Sets New Fuel Prices Amid International Market Volatility
excerpt: The Regulatory Authority for Rwanda (RURA) has announced revised fuel prices, effective March 5, 2026, which will remain in force for the next two months. Petrol: 1,989 Frw per liter Diesel: 1,948 Frw per liter The new pricing, inclusive of Value Added Tax (VAT), reflects fluctua
title_en: Rwanda Sets New Fuel Prices Amid International Market Volatility
excerpt_en: The Regulatory Authority for Rwanda (RURA) has announced revised fuel prices, effective March 5, 2026, which will remain in force for the next two months. Petrol: 1,989 Frw per liter Diesel: 1,948 Frw per liter The new pricing, inclusive of Value Added Tax (VAT), reflects fluctua
body_en:
The Regulatory Authority for Rwanda (RURA) has announced revised fuel prices, effective March 5, 2026, which will remain in force for the next two months.
Petrol: 1,989 Frw per liter
Diesel: 1,948 Frw per liter
The new pricing, inclusive of Value Added Tax (VAT), reflects fluctuations in the international oil market, particularly following the US-Iran conflict that temporarily disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, a critical channel for 20% of global oil trade.
Minister of Finance and Economic Planning, Yusuf Murangwa, explained that the government is actively supporting fuel traders through financial facilitation, ensuring sufficient reserves to stabilize domestic supply. He noted that if the conflict is short-lived (up to two weeks), the economic impact on Rwanda will be minimal.
Murangwa emphasized contingency planning, stating, “If the war continues for more than two weeks or a month, additional measures will be taken to assist oil traders and other essential goods suppliers, preventing further disruption to the Rwandan economy.”
The move underscores Rwanda’s proactive approach to energy security and price stability, while mitigating the effects of international geopolitical tensions on domestic markets.

title: Rwanda Moves Toward Legalization of Virtual Assets
excerpt: On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet approved a draft law regulating virtual assets, marking the first step toward legalizing their use in the country. The Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning defines virtual assets as electronic values that can be exchanged or transferred
title_en: Rwanda Moves Toward Legalization of Virtual Assets
excerpt_en: On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet approved a draft law regulating virtual assets, marking the first step toward legalizing their use in the country. The Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning defines virtual assets as electronic values that can be exchanged or transferred
body_en:
On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet approved a draft law regulating virtual assets, marking the first step toward legalizing their use in the country.
The Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning defines virtual assets as electronic values that can be exchanged or transferred digitally. These assets can be used for payments and investments, but do not include official currencies such as the Rwandan franc, US dollar, or euro.
The Ministry highlighted that virtual assets promote innovation and economic growth globally, but also pose risks, including potential misuse for corruption and illegal activities.
The draft law aims to protect Rwanda’s financial sector, control these risks, and support the sector’s development. It is aligned with international standards set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to prevent financial crime.
Once approved and enacted, the law will be published in the Official Gazette, and the Capital Market Authority (AMC) and the National Bank of Rwanda (BNR) will issue regulations on implementation, licensing, and supervision of related service providers.
Social and Health

title: More Than 26,000 Refugee Children Integrated into the National Education System
excerpt: KIREHE, February 23, 2026 - More than 26,000 refugee children living in Mahama Camp in Kirehe District are currently enrolled in Rwanda’s education system, benefiting from access to primary, secondary and vocational education as part of the country’s broader refugee integration p
title_en: More Than 26,000 Refugee Children Integrated into the National Education System
excerpt_en: KIREHE, February 23, 2026 - More than 26,000 refugee children living in Mahama Camp in Kirehe District are currently enrolled in Rwanda’s education system, benefiting from access to primary, secondary and vocational education as part of the country’s broader refugee integration p
body_en:
KIREHE, February 23, 2026 - More than 26,000 refugee children living in Mahama Camp in Kirehe District are currently enrolled in Rwanda’s education system, benefiting from access to primary, secondary and vocational education as part of the country’s broader refugee integration policy.
Mahama Camp, the largest refugee settlement in Rwanda, hosts approximately 72,340 refugees from 14 countries, with the majority originating from the Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi. Among them, over 26,000 students attend schools across different educational levels.
Refugee families in the camp benefit from improved living conditions, including basic infrastructure, cooking gas distribution, and access to public services, while children attend both nearby public schools and technical and vocational training institutions.
Investment in Vocational Education
Under the Jyambere Project, authorities have invested heavily in vocational training infrastructure to support refugee education in Kirehe District. Two major technical secondary schools were constructed to expand opportunities for young refugees.
Musaza Technical Secondary School (TSS) received more than 2 billion Rwandan francs in funding, including modern equipment, while Bukora TSS benefited from investments exceeding 3.5 billion Rwandan francs.
These institutions provide training in fields such as electrical engineering, tailoring, and other technical professions, preparing students for employment or further studies.
Refugee Students Embrace Opportunities
Many refugee students say access to education has allowed them to build skills and plan for a better future.
An 18-year-old student studying electrical engineering at Musaza TSS explained that growing up in Rwanda allowed him to pursue his education without interruption or discrimination. He expressed confidence that his technical skills would help him secure employment or continue to university studies after graduation.
Another student enrolled in tailoring training highlighted the equal treatment between refugee and local students, noting that she hopes to use her education to help her family overcome poverty.
Equal Access to Public Services
Local authorities emphasize that refugees in Mahama Camp benefit from equal access to education, healthcare, and economic services under national regulations.
Officials say integrating refugees into public services not only improves living standards but also contributes to local development, as refugees bring valuable skills and economic potential to host communities.
Infrastructure Development
Over the past seven years, the Jyambere Project has supported infrastructure development in six refugee-hosting districts, including Gisagara, Nyamagabe, Karongi, Gicumbi, Gatsibo, and Kirehe.
In Kirehe alone, the project has:
Built Musaza TSS and Bukora TSS
Constructed a two-story building at Kirehe Hospital
Begun renovation of Nyarubuye Health Center into a district hospital
Upgraded facilities serving both refugees and host communities
Rising Number of Refugee Students
Recent education data shows a steady increase in the number of refugee students enrolled in Rwandan schools.
During the 2023-2024 academic year, refugee enrollment rose by 10.9%, increasing from 39,728 students in 2022-2023 to 44,051 students.
Of these students:
51.3% were boys
48.7% were girls
The continued expansion of education access, particularly in technical and vocational training, is seen as a key factor in improving self-reliance and long-term prospects for refugee communities in Rwanda.

title_en: Rwanda’s Prime Minister Calls for Public Support After Increase in Community Health Insurance Contributions
excerpt_en: On February 28, 2026, Prime Minister Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva called on citizens to better understand the recent increase in contributions to Rwanda’s Community Health Insurance scheme (Mutuelles de Santé), stressing that the measure aims to strengthen funding for the country’s hea
body_en:
On February 28, 2026, Prime Minister Dr. Justin Nsengiyumva called on citizens to better understand the recent increase in contributions to Rwanda’s Community Health Insurance scheme (Mutuelles de Santé), stressing that the measure aims to strengthen funding for the country’s health sector.
The Prime Minister made the remarks while participating in a community work activity (Umuganda) in Kigali City, specifically in Kicukiro District, Gatenga Sector, Nyarurama Cell. Residents gathered to clean and repair clogged water pipes that had caused flooding and obstructed homes for several days.
During the event, Nsengiyumva explained that the government’s decision to raise Mutuelles de Santé contributions was not taken lightly but reflects the need to increase resources dedicated to healthcare services.
He acknowledged that the adjustment comes at a time when citizens are also facing rising costs of living, including higher electricity tariffs, but emphasized that such decisions are part of broader efforts to manage limited national resources effectively.
Using a household analogy, the Prime Minister explained that the government budget operates much like a family budget, where limited income must be distributed among many competing needs such as education, healthcare, and public services.
According to him, just as families must prioritize spending when income is limited, the government must also balance national priorities while ensuring that essential services-particularly healthcare-remain accessible to the population.
He noted that the last adjustment of community health insurance contributions was made in 2011, despite growing demands on the healthcare system over the past decade. As the population grows and healthcare needs expand, additional funding has become necessary to maintain and improve health services nationwide.
The Prime Minister therefore urged citizens to view the increased contributions as a collective investment aimed at sustaining universal access to healthcare in Rwanda.
Beyond the issue of healthcare financing, Nsengiyumva also addressed urban sanitation and environmental management. He encouraged residents and local authorities to adopt better waste management practices, particularly by separating garbage before collection.
He suggested that households use different bags for plastic bottles, paper, and biodegradable waste, which would make waste collection more efficient and reduce unpleasant odors caused by mixed waste.
Meanwhile, Kigali City Mayor Samuel Dusengiyumva warned residents that weather forecasts indicate heavier rainfall this year. He urged communities to avoid practices that could block drainage systems, such as dumping waste in water channels and erosion control infrastructure.
The mayor also called on residents to take preventive measures against flooding and erosion, emphasizing that proper waste disposal and maintenance of drainage systems are essential to mitigating the impact of heavy rains in the capital.

title: Over Rwf 900 Million Invested in Rwanda’s Good Governance Program
excerpt: Trōcaire, the Irish Catholic organization supporting community development, has launched a good governance program in Rwanda aimed at promoting participatory and inclusive governance, prioritizing citizens’ needs, and improving service delivery. The program was officially launche
title_en: Over Rwf 900 Million Invested in Rwanda’s Good Governance Program
excerpt_en: Trōcaire, the Irish Catholic organization supporting community development, has launched a good governance program in Rwanda aimed at promoting participatory and inclusive governance, prioritizing citizens’ needs, and improving service delivery. The program was officially launche
body_en:
Trōcaire, the Irish Catholic organization supporting community development, has launched a good governance program in Rwanda aimed at promoting participatory and inclusive governance, prioritizing citizens’ needs, and improving service delivery. The program was officially launched on February 27, 2026, with a total investment of over Rwf 900 million.
The initiative, named the “Twiyubakire Programme”, is supported by the British Government’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) and focuses on education, agriculture, and citizen collaboration with government institutions.
The program had been piloted over the past nine months in eight districts: Rusizi, Gisagara, Kamonyi, Muhanga, Nyaruguru, Nyamagabe, Gatsibo, and Bugesera.
Marleen Levina Masclee, Director of Trōcaire in Rwanda, said the program’s main objective is to strengthen cooperation between citizens and government while prioritizing women, youth, and people with disabilities.
“The aim of this program is to promote collaboration in agriculture, education, and national unity, placing citizens at the forefront of development,” Masclee said.
The Director of Development at the British Embassy in Rwanda, Billy Stewart, commended the Rwandan Government’s commitment to good governance and its continued focus on people-centered initiatives.
The Twiyubakire Programme will run for one year, ending in March 2027, and will be implemented in partnership with the Rwandan Coalition of Community-Based Development Organizations (CCOAIB).
Trōcaire has been operating in Rwanda since 1994, following the Genocide against the Tutsi, contributing to poverty reduction, justice, and community development across the country.
According to the 2025 Rwanda Governance Scorecard conducted by the Rwanda Governance Board (RGB), Rwanda’s participatory and inclusive governance pillar scored 86.31%, highlighting the country’s long-standing commitment to good governance over the past 30 years.

title: Over 60 Convicted in Crackdown on Illegal Mining
excerpt: KARONGI, February 24, 2026 - Authorities in Karongi District have intensified efforts against illegal mining, leading to the conviction of more than 60 individuals over the past three months as officials seek to protect legal mining investments and curb environmental damage. Oper
title_en: Over 60 Convicted in Crackdown on Illegal Mining
excerpt_en: KARONGI, February 24, 2026 - Authorities in Karongi District have intensified efforts against illegal mining, leading to the conviction of more than 60 individuals over the past three months as officials seek to protect legal mining investments and curb environmental damage. Oper
body_en:
KARONGI, February 24, 2026 - Authorities in Karongi District have intensified efforts against illegal mining, leading to the conviction of more than 60 individuals over the past three months as officials seek to protect legal mining investments and curb environmental damage.
Operators in the legal mining sector say illegal miners continue to threaten their businesses by selling minerals at lower prices while avoiding tax obligations, creating what they describe as unfair competition.
Illegal mining activities are particularly widespread in the sectors of Rubengera, Rugabano, Gashari, Murambi, Bwishyura, and Mutuntu, where miners operate along several rivers, including Musogoro, Mashyiga, and Nyabahanga.
Environmental and Agricultural Damage
Residents report that illegal mining operations have caused significant environmental degradation, including the destruction of farmland, crop losses, and damage to riverbanks.
The affected waterways - including the Nyabahanga and Musogoro rivers, which flow into Lake Kivu, and the Mashyiga River, a tributary of the Nyabarongo River - play an important role in the region’s ecosystem and agriculture.
Legal Miners Report Economic Losses
Investors in licensed mining operations warn that illegal extraction activities are undermining their financial viability.
One long-time legal mining operator in Karongi District, who has worked in the sector for over 13 years, reported producing five to six tons of minerals per month and employing between 400 and 500 workers. He said illegal traders avoid paying taxes, allowing them to sell minerals at significantly lower prices, which weakens the formal market.
According to the investor, legally mined minerals are sold at approximately 35,000 Rwandan francs per kilogram, while illegally sourced minerals are sold for around 30,000 francs, making it difficult for licensed operators to remain competitive.
Authorities Intensify Enforcement
Local authorities say enforcement measures introduced since late 2025 are beginning to show results.
Officials have held meetings with landowners across the district to warn them about the legal consequences of allowing unauthorized mining on their property. Landowners who fail to report illegal activity risk being treated as accomplices under the law.
As part of the crackdown, more than 60 suspects have been prosecuted and convicted in court, contributing to a decline in illegal mining activities, according to district officials.
Local Official Under Investigation
Authorities have also detained a local administrative leader accused of collaborating with illegal miners.
The official is under investigation for allegedly leaking information to suspects and helping them evade arrest during enforcement operations.
Officials say the ongoing crackdown aims to protect natural resources, support legal mining investors, and reduce the economic and environmental impact of illegal mining in Karongi District.

title: Complaint Filed at ICC Against Congolese General Over Alleged Anti-Tutsi Remarks
excerpt: A group of Congolese Tutsi organizations has filed a complaint at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, accusing former Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) spokesperson Sylvain Ekenge of incitement and hate speech targeting the Tutsi commun
title_en: Complaint Filed at ICC Against Congolese General Over Alleged Anti-Tutsi Remarks
excerpt_en: A group of Congolese Tutsi organizations has filed a complaint at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, accusing former Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) spokesperson Sylvain Ekenge of incitement and hate speech targeting the Tutsi commun
body_en:
A group of Congolese Tutsi organizations has filed a complaint at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, accusing former Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) spokesperson Sylvain Ekenge of incitement and hate speech targeting the Tutsi community.
The complaint was submitted on February 17, 2026, by Belgian lawyer Bernard Maingain, who represents several Congolese Tutsi families and organizations. According to the filing, statements made by Gen. Maj. Ekenge could fuel discrimination and violence against the Tutsi minority in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The legal action stems from comments reportedly made by Ekenge in December 2025 during an appearance on the national broadcaster Radio‑Télévision Nationale Congolaise (RTNC). During the broadcast, he allegedly discouraged Congolese Tutsi women from having children with people from other ethnic groups and warned men to be cautious when marrying them.
The remarks sparked strong criticism from human rights groups and members of the Tutsi community, leading to Ekenge’s temporary suspension from his role as military spokesperson.
Lawyer Maingain argued in the complaint that the statements form part of a broader pattern of rhetoric targeting the Tutsi ethnic group in the DRC. He also claimed that certain individuals who promote such rhetoric have received political backing from figures within the government, including government spokesperson Patrick Muyaya.
According to Maingain, the situation creates a legal paradox, where Congolese law criminalizes hate speech, yet authorities have allegedly failed to enforce those provisions consistently.
The lawyer further recalled that Congolese families had previously filed a similar complaint in 2020, warning about the spread of anti-Tutsi rhetoric. He said that case was never fully investigated, despite evidence being submitted to national authorities.
In his letter to the ICC Prosecutor, Maingain urged the court to examine the evidence and determine whether the statements constitute crimes under international law, including incitement to persecution or violence against an ethnic group.
Under ICC procedures, once a complaint is received, the Prosecutor’s Office reviews the allegations and supporting evidence. If the information is considered credible and within the court’s jurisdiction, prosecutors may open a preliminary examination and potentially build a case for formal judicial proceedings.

title: Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment Questioned Over Rwf1.2 Billion Forest Loss
excerpt: The Chamber of Deputies has demanded an explanation from the Ministry of Environment regarding a Rwf1.2 billion loss caused by mismanagement of contracts between the Government of Rwanda and Sawmill East Africa Ltd (SEAL), the issue was raised during a plenary session on March 4,
title_en: Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment Questioned Over Rwf1.2 Billion Forest Loss
excerpt_en: The Chamber of Deputies has demanded an explanation from the Ministry of Environment regarding a Rwf1.2 billion loss caused by mismanagement of contracts between the Government of Rwanda and Sawmill East Africa Ltd (SEAL), the issue was raised during a plenary session on March 4,
body_en:
The Chamber of Deputies has demanded an explanation from the Ministry of Environment regarding a Rwf1.2 billion loss caused by mismanagement of contracts between the Government of Rwanda and Sawmill East Africa Ltd (SEAL), the issue was raised during a plenary session on March 4, 2026.
The concern stems from forest management agreements for the Shariyo and Ntobo I, II, III forests, which were reportedly not respected, leading to significant financial losses. A joint audit by the Ministry of Environment, Rwanda Forestry Authority (RFA), and SEAL, launched on February 17, 2025, revealed total losses of Rwf 1,238,244,838, including over Rwf 1.1 billion in unpaid timber harvests and Rwf 9.08 million in unpaid land leases.
The Ministry confirmed that SEAL has agreed to repay the losses, though payment has not yet been made. The Forest Service informed MPs that termination of the contract is nearly complete, with hopes of full repayment within 30 days.
The chairperson of the Commission on Land, Agriculture, Livestock and Environment, Muzana Alice, stated that measures are being taken to prevent future losses, including requiring contractors to pay 100% of tree costs before harvesting and strengthening contract monitoring.
Parliament also requested that the Ministry establish clear regulations for collaboration between RFA, districts, and Kigali City, ensuring continuous and timely reporting on forest management nationwide. This directive must be implemented within two months.
The case highlights the importance of accountability in state-forest contracts and the need for robust oversight to protect public resources.

The concern stems from forest management agreements for the Shariyo and Ntobo I, II, III forests, which were reportedly not respected, leading to significant financial losses. A joint audit by the Ministry of Environment, Rwanda Forestry Authority (RFA), and SEAL, launched on February 17, 2025, revealed total losses of Rwf 1,238,244,838, including over Rwf 1.1 billion in unpaid timber harvests and Rwf 9.08 million in unpaid land leases.
The Ministry confirmed that SEAL has agreed to repay the losses, though payment has not yet been made. The Forest Service informed MPs that termination of the contract is nearly complete, with hopes of full repayment within 30 days.
The chairperson of the Commission on Land, Agriculture, Livestock and Environment, Muzana Alice, stated that measures are being taken to prevent future losses, including requiring contractors to pay 100% of tree costs before harvesting and strengthening contract monitoring.
Parliament also requested that the Ministry establish clear regulations for collaboration between RFA, districts, and Kigali City, ensuring continuous and timely reporting on forest management nationwide. This directive must be implemented within two months.
The case highlights the importance of accountability in state-forest contracts and the need for robust oversight to protect public resources.

A joint audit by the Ministry of Environment, Rwanda Forestry Authority (RFA), and SEAL, launched on February 17, 2025, revealed total losses of Rwf 1,238,244,838, including over Rwf 1.1 billion in unpaid timber harvests and Rwf 9.08 million in unpaid land leases.
The Ministry confirmed that SEAL has agreed to repay the losses, though payment has not yet been made. The Forest Service informed MPs that termination of the contract is nearly complete, with hopes of full repayment within 30 days.
The chairperson of the Commission on Land, Agriculture, Livestock and Environment, Muzana Alice, stated that measures are being taken to prevent future losses, including requiring contractors to pay 100% of tree costs before harvesting and strengthening contract monitoring.
Parliament also requested that the Ministry establish clear regulations for collaboration between RFA, districts, and Kigali City, ensuring continuous and timely reporting on forest management nationwide. This directive must be implemented within two months.
The case highlights the importance of accountability in state-forest contracts and the need for robust oversight to protect public resources.

title_en: Rwanda Appoints Members of the Appeals Board for Refugees and Asylum Seekers

body_en:
On March 4, 2026, the Rwandan Cabinet appointed the leadership of the Appeals Board for Refugees and Asylum Seekers.
Chairpersons: Edda Mukabagwiza and Rusanganwa Jean Damascène
Registrars: Mukanyundo Patricie, Nyirinkwaya Immaculée, Rudasingwa Joseph, Mukama Augustin, and Ndabirora Kalinda Jean Damascène
The Appeals Board is mandated to review cases of migrants or asylum seekers who are dissatisfied with decisions made by the Immigration and Refugee Service. Appeals must be submitted in writing within 30 days of notification of the initial decision, and the Board is required to issue a ruling within six months. Decisions are communicated in writing within seven days of adoption. Article 15 allows appellants to submit any evidence supporting their case.
Edda Mukabagwiza brings extensive experience to the position:
Served as Minister of Justice and Deputy Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies
Rwanda’s Ambassador to Canada and Cuba (2007-2013)
Member of Parliament 2013-2018
Founder of EM Pathways Legal & Advisory Ltd, admitted to the bar in November 2025
Holds a Master’s in Diplomacy and a Bachelor of Laws
The establishment of this Appeals Board comes as Rwanda prepares to process migrants deported from the UK who will have the opportunity to appeal decisions regarding their refugee or asylum status.
This new structure is designed to strengthen due process and legal oversight in the country’s refugee and asylum system, ensuring that applicants have a formal mechanism to contest decisions fairly.

title: Rwanda to Launch Two New Mediation Centers to Resolve Disputes Outside Courts
excerpt: On March 4, 2026, the Ministry of Justice (MINIJUST) announced the establishment of two new mediation centers in the provinces to complement the existing center in Kigali City. These centers aim to provide out-of-court dispute resolution services and are part of Rwanda’s ongoing
title_en: Rwanda to Launch Two New Mediation Centers to Resolve Disputes Outside Courts
excerpt_en: On March 4, 2026, the Ministry of Justice (MINIJUST) announced the establishment of two new mediation centers in the provinces to complement the existing center in Kigali City. These centers aim to provide out-of-court dispute resolution services and are part of Rwanda’s ongoing
body_en:
On March 4, 2026, the Ministry of Justice (MINIJUST) announced the establishment of two new mediation centers in the provinces to complement the existing center in Kigali City. These centers aim to provide out-of-court dispute resolution services and are part of Rwanda’s ongoing effort to strengthen access to justice.
South Province: Center in Nyanza, opening in May 2026
Eastern Province: Construction expected to be completed by late 2026 or early 2027
The initiative was presented by Permanent Secretary Mbonera Théophile during the annual dialogue on access to justice organized by the Legal Aid Federation (LAF).
The centers will:
Receive clients seeking mediation instead of going directly to court
Provide advice and connect them with trained mediators
Serve as a line of first contact for disputes suitable for mediation
A judicial mechanism now allows judges to recommend mediation before cases enter the court system. According to the Judiciary report for 2024/2025:
Cases resolved through mediation increased by 32%, from 2,395 to 3,166
Cases settled via plea bargains rose by 20%, from 9,851 to 11,846
The non-judicial dispute resolution policy, launched in 2022, aims to reduce court backlogs from 62% at the policy’s start to 25% within five years.
These centers are part of Rwanda’s long-term plan for each province to eventually have at least one mediation facility, promoting faster, fairer, and more accessible justice for all citizens.

title: Two Ugandan Generals Removed Over Citizenship Document Dispute
excerpt: On 23 February 2026, the Ugandan Army reassigned two senior officers from the Immigration Service following allegations that Rwandan-origin Ugandans were being denied access to citizenship documents and passports. The officers affected are Maj Gen Apollo Kasiita-Gowa, former head
title_en: Two Ugandan Generals Removed Over Citizenship Document Dispute
excerpt_en: On 23 February 2026, the Ugandan Army reassigned two senior officers from the Immigration Service following allegations that Rwandan-origin Ugandans were being denied access to citizenship documents and passports. The officers affected are Maj Gen Apollo Kasiita-Gowa, former head
body_en:
On 23 February 2026, the Ugandan Army reassigned two senior officers from the Immigration Service following allegations that Rwandan-origin Ugandans were being denied access to citizenship documents and passports.
The officers affected are Maj Gen Apollo Kasiita-Gowa, former head of the Citizenship Inspection Service, and Brig Gen Johnson Abaho Namanya, former Commissioner for Passports. Both have been returned to Army Headquarters for reassignment to other military duties.
The decision follows earlier orders by Chief of Defence Forces Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who announced the dismissal of officials accused of obstructing Rwandans living in Uganda from obtaining official documents.
The issue concerns the legal status of Rwandan-origin communities, recognized as a constitutionally protected ethnic group whose presence predates 1926. Many members of the community have long complained about delays and refusals in obtaining national identification and travel documents, despite being born and raised in Uganda.
Authorities have reiterated that the 1995 Constitution guarantees citizenship rights to eligible residents, and efforts are ongoing to review pending cases and facilitate access to official documentation.

title: MONUSCO and ICGLR Assess Security Situation
excerpt: UVIRA, February 24, 2026 - A joint assessment mission by MONUSCO and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) has been deployed to Uvira, South Kivu, to evaluate the security situation and the feasibility of future peacekeeping operations. The five-day missi
title_en: MONUSCO and ICGLR Assess Security Situation
excerpt_en: UVIRA, February 24, 2026 - A joint assessment mission by MONUSCO and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) has been deployed to Uvira, South Kivu, to evaluate the security situation and the feasibility of future peacekeeping operations. The five-day missi
body_en:
UVIRA, February 24, 2026 - A joint assessment mission by MONUSCO and the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) has been deployed to Uvira, South Kivu, to evaluate the security situation and the feasibility of future peacekeeping operations.
The five-day mission, running from February 23 to 27, 2026, follows consultations with President Félix Tshisekedi, who currently chairs the ICGLR. The joint team is tasked with assessing the credibility, security conditions, and operational feasibility of potential peacekeeping deployments in the area.
Focus on Ceasefire Monitoring
Officials say the assessment will help determine how ceasefire monitoring mechanisms could contribute to reducing violence and creating conditions for a sustainable political solution in South Kivu.
The acting head of MONUSCO, Vivian van de Perre, emphasized that effective monitoring of the ceasefire could help stabilize the region and support long-term peace efforts.
Limited Mandate in South Kivu
Unlike in North Kivu and Ituri, the MONUSCO mandate in South Kivu does not include civilian protection, according to mission officials. The assessment aims to clarify what role peacekeeping forces could realistically play under the current mandate.
Phased Deployment Planned
Senior United Nations peacekeeping officials have indicated that any future MONUSCO deployment in South Kivu will be carried out in phases.
Before deploying troops, authorities intend to verify the reliability of security arrangements for peacekeepers operating in the region. The plan also includes the use of surveillance drones to gather security intelligence and support operational planning.
The joint mission is expected to provide key recommendations on the future role of MONUSCO and the ICGLR in supporting stability efforts in Uvira and surrounding areas.

title: Rwanda Welcomes 22 Citizens Returning from Democratic Republic of Congo
excerpt: Rusizi, February 25, 2026 - Rwanda welcomed 22 of its citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), including individuals who had lived in exile for over 30 years, expressing regret over the years lost during displacement and the impact on their education and fa
title_en: Rwanda Welcomes 22 Citizens Returning from Democratic Republic of Congo
excerpt_en: Rusizi, February 25, 2026 - Rwanda welcomed 22 of its citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), including individuals who had lived in exile for over 30 years, expressing regret over the years lost during displacement and the impact on their education and fa
body_en:
Rusizi, February 25, 2026 - Rwanda welcomed 22 of its citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), including individuals who had lived in exile for over 30 years, expressing regret over the years lost during displacement and the impact on their education and family life.
The returnees arrived via the Rusizi I Border on February 24, 2026, marking the second group this year to come back from the DRC. The group includes two men, four women, and 16 children. They were first received at the Nyarushishi temporary camp before being reunited with their families.
Speaking to local media, the returnees described years spent in the DRC as a period of hardship, noting that their children were unable to attend school and grew up under difficult conditions in a war zone. One returnee said, “This is a great loss because we kept running away and our children were unable to study and were always in trouble.” Another added, “My older brother returned first and told me that Rwanda was safe, so we decided to come back.”
The returnees were warmly received by the Rusizi District Administration, UNHCR staff, and security forces. The Mayor of Rusizi District, Sindayiheba Phanuel, described the return as a significant step toward leaving behind a history of conflict and hatred, encouraging others still in exile to consider returning. He said, “Their arrival is good news as they come to join other Rwandans in rebuilding the country. We want to show others that Rwanda is peaceful and encourage them to make their own decision to return.”
The repatriation reflects Rwanda’s ongoing efforts to support displaced citizens, promote reconciliation, and facilitate family reunification.

title: Rwanda Welcomes 32 Former Armed Group Members from DRC for Rehabilitation
excerpt: Musanze, February 25, 2026 - Rwanda received 32 former members of armed groups from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), along with 31 of their family members, as part of the country’s ongoing demobilization and reintegration efforts. The group was handed over by the Unite
title_en: Rwanda Welcomes 32 Former Armed Group Members from DRC for Rehabilitation
excerpt_en: Musanze, February 25, 2026 - Rwanda received 32 former members of armed groups from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), along with 31 of their family members, as part of the country’s ongoing demobilization and reintegration efforts. The group was handed over by the Unite
body_en:
Musanze, February 25, 2026 - Rwanda received 32 former members of armed groups from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), along with 31 of their family members, as part of the country’s ongoing demobilization and reintegration efforts.
The group was handed over by the United Nations Peacekeeping Mission in the DRC (MONUSCO), under the Disarmament, Demobilization, Reintegration, and Security (DDR&S) program, and received at the National Demobilization and Rehabilitation Commission (RDRC) facility in Mutobo, Musanze District. They will undergo early training to support their reentry into civilian life and social integration.
The returning fighters include former members of FDLR-FOCA, CNRD, and Nyatura CMC, groups historically linked to the Genocide ideology. Most of the returnees are young adults aged 18 to 30, although the oldest is a 53-year-old woman, Odette, formerly part of the FDLR special forces unit CRAP. The group also includes more than 10 women and one child who had participated in Nyatura CMC operations.
Since 2001, Rwanda has received 12,602 former combatants from armed groups aiming to destabilize the country, reintegrating them into civilian life. Authorities emphasize that Rwanda remains willing to accept individuals who lay down arms, though the DRC government reportedly continues to restrict returns, and the FDLR-FOCA still maintains 7,000 to 10,000 fighters, blending with civilian populations when threatened.
The initiative reflects Rwanda’s ongoing commitment to peacebuilding, rehabilitation, and the reintegration of former combatants, contributing to regional stability and security in the Great Lakes region.

excerpt: Eastern DRC, February 25, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition expressed deep disappointment at the international community’s silence amid escalating attacks by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government forces, which have targeted both civilians and rebel positions using drones a
title_en: AFC/M23 Condemns International Silence as DRC Forces Escalate Attacks
excerpt_en: Eastern DRC, February 25, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition expressed deep disappointment at the international community’s silence amid escalating attacks by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government forces, which have targeted both civilians and rebel positions using drones a
body_en:
Eastern DRC, February 25, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition expressed deep disappointment at the international community’s silence amid escalating attacks by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government forces, which have targeted both civilians and rebel positions using drones and heavy weaponry.
AFC/M23 spokesman Lawrence Kanyuka reported that large-scale attacks occurred in Rutigita, Rugezi, and border areas of Minembwe and Kitazungura communes in Kalehe territory, causing deaths, mass displacement, and a worsening humanitarian crisis.
Bertrand Bisimwa, AFC/M23 Deputy Director for Political, Diplomatic, and Governance Affairs, criticized the DRC government for violating the ceasefire agreement, accusing it of choosing war over diplomacy. He highlighted the lack of concrete international measures to prevent continued fighting, contrasting the silence of global actors with the attention given when AFC/M23 defends itself.
The attacks on February 25 followed previous drone strikes by DRC forces in central Masisi and surrounding areas on February 24, illustrating a pattern of escalating military operations.

excerpt: Bugesera, February 26, 2026 - The Government of Rwanda received 164 refugees and migrants who had been stranded in Libya, as part of ongoing humanitarian efforts to assist vulnerable populations. The group includes 143 individuals from Sudan, affected by nearly three years of con
title_en: Rwanda Welcomes 164 Refugees and Migrants from Libya 🕊️
excerpt_en: Bugesera, February 26, 2026 - The Government of Rwanda received 164 refugees and migrants who had been stranded in Libya, as part of ongoing humanitarian efforts to assist vulnerable populations. The group includes 143 individuals from Sudan, affected by nearly three years of con
body_en:
Bugesera, February 26, 2026 - The Government of Rwanda received 164 refugees and migrants who had been stranded in Libya, as part of ongoing humanitarian efforts to assist vulnerable populations.
The group includes 143 individuals from Sudan, affected by nearly three years of conflict, 19 from Eritrea, one from Ethiopia, and one from South Sudan.
This initiative is part of the Emergency Transit Mechanism (ETM), established through an agreement between Rwanda, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), and the African Union (AU). The program provides temporary accommodation for refugees and migrants in Libya while they await permanent resettlement in third countries.
The new arrivals were received at the Gashora temporary camp in Bugesera District, where they are processed before being relocated to countries that have agreed to host them.
Since the launch of the ETM in 2019, Rwanda has hosted 2,760 refugees and migrants from Libya, with over 2,500 successfully resettled in other countries.

title: Rwandan Author Richard Hategekimana Launches Book on the Diversity and Values of the RDF

title_en: Rwandan Author Richard Hategekimana Launches Book on the Diversity and Values of the RDF
excerpt_en: On February 28, 2026, Rwandan author and President of the Rwanda Writers' Guild, Richard Hategekimana, officially launched a new book examining the diversity, history, and values of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF). The publication highlights the role of the Rwandan military in the
body_en:
On February 28, 2026, Rwandan author and President of the Rwanda Writers' Guild, Richard Hategekimana, officially launched a new book examining the diversity, history, and values of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF). The publication highlights the role of the Rwandan military in the country’s security, unity, and development agenda.
Titled “The Force Behind the Vision: RDF and Rwanda’s Development Agenda,” the 400-page book explores the evolution of the Rwandan armed forces from the Rwandan Patriotic Army (RPA)-the movement credited with liberating the country and ending the Genocide against the Tutsi-to the modern RDF.
In the book, Hategekimana revisits not only the wars fought by the RPA and RDF, but also the core values that have shaped the force, including patriotism, courage, discipline, and vision. He argues that these principles have contributed significantly to Rwanda’s governance, economic development, social welfare, and justice systems.
According to the author, the book was written to preserve the history of the Rwandan armed forces while also sharing lessons that could inspire leadership and professionalism across other sectors of society.
Hategekimana emphasized that the diversity and institutional culture of the RDF serve as an example that could be adopted in government institutions, ministries, and public administration. He describes the RDF as an army guided by a mindset of “I know, I do, and I strive for,” reflecting a commitment to discipline and achieving objectives.
The author also explained that he chose to write the book in English to allow international readers to better understand the structure, diversity, and achievements of the Rwandan military.
He noted that the work aims to highlight Rwanda’s positive experiences, particularly the strong public trust in the RDF, which surveys have shown to be among the most respected national institutions in the country. By sharing these lessons globally, Hategekimana believes other countries can learn from Rwanda’s approach to security, leadership, and national unity.
Looking ahead, the author revealed plans to translate the book into Kinyarwanda, French, and Swahili to ensure that its contents are accessible to a broader audience across Rwanda and the wider African region.
During the launch event, Tito Rutaremara, Chairman of the Rwandan Armed Forces Advisory Board, praised the initiative, describing the book as an important contribution to preserving the historical record of the RDF.
Rutaremara also highlighted the importance of leadership in shaping the armed forces, pointing to President Paul Kagame, the Commander-in-Chief of the RDF, as a central figure in guiding the institution and contributing to the country’s broader development.
He further encouraged Rwandans to cultivate a culture of reading, stressing that support for literature and scholarship helps encourage authors to continue documenting national history and achievements.
Hategekimana dedicated the book to President Paul Kagame, Tito Rutaremara, and the Rwanda Defence Force, acknowledging their role in shaping the institution that the book seeks to document.
Participants at the launch described the RDF as a pillar of Rwanda’s development, welcoming the publication as an important effort to record and share the history and values of the country’s armed forces.

title: AFC/M23 Confirms Death of Spokesperson Col. Willy Ngoma in North Kivu
excerpt: The AFC/M23 coalition has confirmed the death of Colonel Willy Ngoma, a senior officer and spokesperson of its military wing, the Congolese Revolutionary Army (ARC), who was killed in North Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The announcement was made on the ev
title_en: AFC/M23 Confirms Death of Spokesperson Col. Willy Ngoma in North Kivu
excerpt_en: The AFC/M23 coalition has confirmed the death of Colonel Willy Ngoma, a senior officer and spokesperson of its military wing, the Congolese Revolutionary Army (ARC), who was killed in North Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The announcement was made on the ev
body_en:
The AFC/M23 coalition has confirmed the death of Colonel Willy Ngoma, a senior officer and spokesperson of its military wing, the Congolese Revolutionary Army (ARC), who was killed in North Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The announcement was made on the evening of February 28, 2026, by AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka, who stated that the officer died on February 24, 2026 during ongoing fighting in the region.
According to Kanyuka, Col. Willy Ngoma was killed at around 9:00 a.m. when a drone strike attributed to the Congolese army targeted positions where he and other fighters were engaged in combat against forces aligned with the DRC government.
Kanyuka accused the government of violating a ceasefire agreement and escalating hostilities, alleging that attacks involving drones and military operations have targeted both AFC/M23 fighters and civilians.
“This violation of the ceasefire has cost us one of our senior officers,” he said, adding that the situation continues to result in casualties among what he described as innocent civilians.
The coalition said clashes have intensified in several conflict-affected areas of North and South Kivu, including Mweso, Rutigita, Kitazungura, Rugezi, Rubaya, Walikale, Masisi, Kalehe, Minembwe and Gasheke, where fighting and drone strikes have been reported in recent weeks.
Particularly heavy fighting has been reported around Rubaya, where armed groups associated with the Wazalendo coalition, including CMC-FDP, Raia Mutomboki and PARECO-FFF, have been involved in clashes with AFC/M23 forces. The coalition said reinforcements were deployed to the area in response to the attacks.
Kanyuka stated that the alliance remains committed to protecting civilians in territories under its control while continuing to participate in peace efforts aimed at ending the conflict.
Colonel Willy Ngoma became widely known as the spokesperson of the M23 movement when the group resumed armed operations in November 2021 following the collapse of negotiations with the DRC government.
During that period, he regularly communicated the movement’s position, arguing that Kinyarwanda-speaking Congolese communities, particularly those of Tutsi origin, were facing violence and displacement.
Ngoma was also among senior commanders who appeared publicly in areas captured by the movement in eastern Congo to reassure local populations during military advances.
At the start of the renewed rebellion, Ngoma held the rank of Major. He was promoted to Colonel in January 2024, a promotion the movement said recognized his leadership and operational performance during the conflict.

title: Over 160 Killed in Armed Attack in South Sudan
excerpt: At least 169 people, including security personnel, were killed when unidentified gunmen attacked the Abiemnom district in Ruweng State, South Sudan, in the early hours of March 1, 2026. According to Ruweng State Information Minister James Monyluak Mijok, the attackers are believe
title_en: Over 160 Killed in Armed Attack in South Sudan
excerpt_en: At least 169 people, including security personnel, were killed when unidentified gunmen attacked the Abiemnom district in Ruweng State, South Sudan, in the early hours of March 1, 2026. According to Ruweng State Information Minister James Monyluak Mijok, the attackers are believe
body_en:
At least 169 people, including security personnel, were killed when unidentified gunmen attacked the Abiemnom district in Ruweng State, South Sudan, in the early hours of March 1, 2026.
According to Ruweng State Information Minister James Monyluak Mijok, the attackers are believed to be fighters linked to the Sudan-based SPLA-IO, who launched a coordinated assault on the area.
Mijok said the militants engaged in intense clashes with local security forces for several hours, with the fighting lasting between four and five hours. During the attack, homes and shops were set on fire, causing widespread destruction.
Among the 169 victims were children, women, elderly civilians and members of the state’s security forces, including police officers, the minister said.
The United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) reported that the violence forced around 1,000 civilians to flee their homes, while 23 injured people have been treated following the attack.
UNMISS said that after the fighting subsided, it began working with South Sudanese security forces to help restore stability and security in the Abiemnom area.

title: AFC/M23 Vows Retaliation After Death of Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma
excerpt: The AFC/M23 coalition has vowed to continue attacks on Bangoka Airport in Kisangani and to avenge the death of its former military spokesperson, Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, amid escalating tensions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. In a statement issued on March 3, 2026, the coa
title_en: AFC/M23 Vows Retaliation After Death of Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma
excerpt_en: The AFC/M23 coalition has vowed to continue attacks on Bangoka Airport in Kisangani and to avenge the death of its former military spokesperson, Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, amid escalating tensions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. In a statement issued on March 3, 2026, the coa
body_en:
The AFC/M23 coalition has vowed to continue attacks on Bangoka Airport in Kisangani and to avenge the death of its former military spokesperson, Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, amid escalating tensions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
In a statement issued on March 3, 2026, the coalition confirmed that it carried out a drone strike on Bangoka Airport on March 1, 2026, saying the operation targeted drones allegedly being prepared by the Congolese army to strike AFC/M23 positions and civilian areas.
The group said a similar attack had already been conducted on February 1, 2026, with the same objective of destroying facilities used to coordinate drone operations against its bases.
Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Political, Diplomatic and Governance Affairs within the coalition, said the group considers the attacks part of its responsibility to protect civilians, particularly as mediation efforts have not stopped ongoing hostilities.
“While mediators in the peace process have not been able to compel Kinshasa to respect its commitments or stop attacks against innocent people, we must fulfill our duty to protect the population,” he said.
The escalation follows the death of Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, who was killed on February 24, 2026, during a drone strike attributed to Congolese government forces near Rubaya centre in Masisi territory, North Kivu.
According to the coalition, the strike targeted AFC/M23 fighters engaged on the front line, resulting in several casualties including Ngoma, who served as the movement’s military spokesperson.
Lawrence Kanyuka, the coalition’s political spokesperson, said the deaths of fighters and civilians would not be forgotten and that those responsible must be held accountable.
He stated that the coalition remains determined to seek justice for its members and supporters, including Ngoma.
The developments come despite a ceasefire agreement signed between the DRC government and AFC/M23 during talks in Qatar, which was intended to reduce hostilities in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.
However, continued military operations and drone strikes in the region have contributed to renewed clashes and heightened tensions, with fighting reported in several areas over recent days.
body_fr:
The AFC/M23 coalition has vowed to continue attacks on Bangoka Airport in Kisangani and to avenge the death of its former military spokesperson, Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, amid escalating tensions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
In a statement issued on March 3, 2026, the coalition confirmed that it carried out a drone strike on Bangoka Airport on March 1, 2026, saying the operation targeted drones allegedly being prepared by the Congolese army to strike AFC/M23 positions and civilian areas.
The group said a similar attack had already been conducted on February 1, 2026, with the same objective of destroying facilities used to coordinate drone operations against its bases.
Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Political, Diplomatic and Governance Affairs within the coalition, said the group considers the attacks part of its responsibility to protect civilians, particularly as mediation efforts have not stopped ongoing hostilities.
“While mediators in the peace process have not been able to compel Kinshasa to respect its commitments or stop attacks against innocent people, we must fulfill our duty to protect the population,” he said.
The escalation follows the death of Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, who was killed on February 24, 2026, during a drone strike attributed to Congolese government forces near Rubaya centre in Masisi territory, North Kivu.
According to the coalition, the strike targeted AFC/M23 fighters engaged on the front line, resulting in several casualties including Ngoma, who served as the movement’s military spokesperson.
Lawrence Kanyuka, the coalition’s political spokesperson, said the deaths of fighters and civilians would not be forgotten and that those responsible must be held accountable.
He stated that the coalition remains determined to seek justice for its members and supporters, including Ngoma.
The developments come despite a ceasefire agreement signed between the DRC government and AFC/M23 during talks in Qatar, which was intended to reduce hostilities in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.
However, continued military operations and drone strikes in the region have contributed to renewed clashes and heightened tensions, with fighting reported in several areas over recent days.

title: RDF Pledges Partnership with Ethiopian Army on AI and Advanced Technologies
excerpt: The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) leadership held high-level talks with the Ethiopian Ministry of Defence on March 2, 2026, to explore cooperation in military and technological areas, including the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The RDF delegation, led by Brigadier General Ro
title_en: RDF Pledges Partnership with Ethiopian Army on AI and Advanced Technologies
excerpt_en: The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) leadership held high-level talks with the Ethiopian Ministry of Defence on March 2, 2026, to explore cooperation in military and technological areas, including the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The RDF delegation, led by Brigadier General Ro
body_en:
The Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) leadership held high-level talks with the Ethiopian Ministry of Defence on March 2, 2026, to explore cooperation in military and technological areas, including the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI).
The RDF delegation, led by Brigadier General Ronald Rwivanga, RDF Spokesperson, was in Ethiopia to join celebrations marking the 130th anniversary of the Battle of Adwa, a historic victory in 1896 where Ethiopian forces defeated the Italian army, preserving the country’s independence during the reign of Emperor Menelik II. The celebrations ran from February 28 to March 1, 2026.
Following the commemorations, the RDF leaders were received by Ethiopia’s Minister of Defense, Eng. Aisha Muhammed, where they discussed ways to strengthen bilateral military cooperation, particularly in intelligent and advanced technologies.
The RDF emphasized on social media that the discussions aimed to deepen existing collaboration in the military sector and expand it to emerging fields such as AI.
Rwanda and Ethiopia have a history of cooperation spanning more than 20 years, including training of soldiers and police forces, as well as collaboration in security, agriculture, trade, and education.
In March 2025, a military cooperation agreement was signed during a visit by the Chief of Staff of the Rwandan Armed Forces, Gen. Mubarakh Muganga, formalizing joint efforts.
In addition to defense cooperation, both countries recently signed agreements on air travel services, allowing RwandAir and Ethiopian Airlines to operate smoothly between their nations, further strengthening bilateral relations.

title: AFC/M23 Says It Is Not Bound by Washington Peace Accords
excerpt: The AFC/M23 alliance has asserted that it is not bound by the Washington peace agreement signed between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in Washington, D.C., on March 3, 2026. The statement was delivered by Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Politics, Diplomac
title_en: AFC/M23 Says It Is Not Bound by Washington Peace Accords
excerpt_en: The AFC/M23 alliance has asserted that it is not bound by the Washington peace agreement signed between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in Washington, D.C., on March 3, 2026. The statement was delivered by Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Politics, Diplomac
body_en:
The AFC/M23 alliance has asserted that it is not bound by the Washington peace agreement signed between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) in Washington, D.C., on March 3, 2026.
The statement was delivered by Bertrand Bisimwa, Deputy Director for Politics, Diplomacy and Governance of AFC/M23, in response to claims by US Senator Jeanne Shaheen that the group was violating the accords.
Senator Shaheen, a member of the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, had stated: “After three months of Rwanda-backed M23 violating the Washington Peace Accords, the US has finally imposed sanctions on the RDF and four leaders.”
Bisimwa countered, saying the alliance cannot breach an agreement it did not sign or observe, and urged the senator to familiarize herself with the realities of the conflict in eastern DRC.
“How could M23 violate an agreement it did not sign and does not observe? The real problem lies in the way Washington understands this war,” Bisimwa said, emphasizing that the Washington agreement concerns the DRC and Rwanda, with the DRC tasked to dismantle the FDLR terrorist group and Rwanda required to adjust border security measures.
He added that ongoing talks in Doha, Qatar, are aimed at resolving the conflict permanently, but claimed that the DRC government under President Félix Tshisekedi has sought to shift discussions to Washington, which he suggested misrepresents the nature of the conflict.

body_en:
Rwandan peacekeepers (Rwanbatt-1) serving with the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) were awarded UN medals on March 3, 2026, in recognition of their contribution to peacekeeping operations.
The ceremony took place at UNMISS Tomping headquarters in Juba, the capital of South Sudan, and was led by Major General Robert Yaw Affram, Deputy Force Commander of UNMISS, who described the medals as a symbol of professionalism, dedication, and commitment to duty.
“The UN Medal you received today reflects professionalism, good conduct, dedication, and courage in challenging conditions. It is earned through days of hard work, nights on guard duty, and steadfast commitment to peacekeeping,” Maj Gen Affram said.
He also commended the Government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) for continuously deploying soldiers of competence and professionalism to the UNMISS mission.
Lt Col Paul Ndushabandi, Commander of Rwanbatt-1, praised his unit for their dedication, perseverance, and courage over ten months of service, encouraging them to maintain this commitment for the remainder of the mission.
The ceremony featured military parades and cultural performances, including traditional Rwandan dances, celebrating the peacekeepers’ achievements and their role in protecting humanity.

body_en:
Lt. Col. Willy Ngoma, widely remembered as the founder of “Les Lions de Sarambwe”, led the M23 armed group in defending Congolese Tutsis who faced killings, expulsions, and forced displacement to Rwanda and neighboring countries.
Ngoma earned the nickname “Quickly Quickly!”, a phrase he famously shouted at mercenaries from Romania in early 2025, during operations that expelled them from DRC territory. His decisive leadership forced these mercenaries to return to Europe, showcasing his courage and tactical skill.
Those familiar with the M23 of 2012-2013 recognized Ngoma as a loyal and capable leader, seen as a worthy successor to Col. Kazarama Vianney. He was respected across all ranks, from junior fighters to senior commanders, for his dedication and commitment to the cause.
Ngoma’s legacy is remembered for his courage, leadership, and sacrifice in the defense of vulnerable communities in eastern Congo, cementing his place as a symbol of resilience and loyalty within the M23 movement.
