title: US Sanctions on RDF Criticized as Attack on African Interests, Says Zimbabwean Watchdog
excerpt: Rutendo Matinyarare of Zimbabwe Human Rights Watch has said that recent US sanctions on the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) reflect Rwanda’s defense of African interests, rather than wrongdoing, and accused international actors of misrepresenting the situation in eastern DRC. On the
title_en: US Sanctions on RDF Criticized as Attack on African Interests, Says Zimbabwean Watchdog
excerpt_en: Rutendo Matinyarare of Zimbabwe Human Rights Watch has said that recent US sanctions on the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) reflect Rwanda’s defense of African interests, rather than wrongdoing, and accused international actors of misrepresenting the situation in eastern DRC. On the
body_en:
Rutendo Matinyarare of Zimbabwe Human Rights Watch has said that recent US sanctions on the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) reflect Rwanda’s defense of African interests, rather than wrongdoing, and accused international actors of misrepresenting the situation in eastern DRC.
On the evening of March 2, 2026, the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on the RDF and several senior military officers, alleging their involvement in security disruptions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo-claims repeatedly denied by Rwanda.
Matinyarare, who visited Rwanda in February 2025 to make a feature film about the M23 movement, said he initially believed Rwanda was a tool of Western powers. However, his visit revealed a country committed to African pride and self-determination.
“When I arrived in M23-controlled areas, I learned how Belgian colonialists divided Kinyarwanda-speaking communities and how the DRC government sought to displace them. Sharing this truth on platforms like TikTok was censored,” he said.
He argued that the RDF’s actions are aimed at defending African communities, and that sanctions from the West often target countries protecting the continent’s interests, rather than those violating human rights.
“I think as Africans, we know that when the West sanctions you, it is because you are serving Africa, hindering international efforts. Let us congratulate Rwanda for being a revolutionary society,” Matinyarare said.
The Rwandan government condemned the sanctions, calling them biased and contrary to the realities in eastern DRC, and reaffirmed that the RDF remains committed to national and regional security.

title: Belgian Analyst Says US Misplaced Sanctions Over FDLR Issue in DRC
excerpt: Alain Destexhe, former Belgian Senator and Secretary General of Doctors Without Borders (MSF), has criticized the United States for sanctioning the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) instead of holding the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government accountable for its ties to the FD
title_en: Belgian Analyst Says US Misplaced Sanctions Over FDLR Issue in DRC
excerpt_en: Alain Destexhe, former Belgian Senator and Secretary General of Doctors Without Borders (MSF), has criticized the United States for sanctioning the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) instead of holding the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government accountable for its ties to the FD
body_en:
Alain Destexhe, former Belgian Senator and Secretary General of Doctors Without Borders (MSF), has criticized the United States for sanctioning the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF) instead of holding the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government accountable for its ties to the FDLR terrorist group, in remarks made on March 4, 2026.
Destexhe’s comments followed US sanctions imposed on March 2, 2026, targeting RDF and senior Rwandan officers accused of supporting the AFC/M23 coalition and destabilizing eastern DRC. He argued that the DRC government, not Rwanda, is responsible for continuing insecurity in the region.
“The DRC should be punished, not Rwanda. Despite UN Security Council Resolution 2773 and peace agreements, the DRC has refused to distance itself from the FDLR, which remains a major security threat. Meanwhile, Wazalendo extremists’ funds continue to fuel terrorism,” Destexhe wrote on X on March 3.
He further accused the DRC of collaborating with foreign mercenaries and conducting drone attacks on civilians, including in Minembwe, South Kivu, noting that such attacks have persisted for several days.
Destexhe, who has long monitored the Great Lakes region, highlighted that the FDLR’s capabilities doubled after receiving support from the DRC government, making it difficult to dismantle the group entirely. “Their numbers increased after the FDLR received weapons and material support from President Félix Tshisekedi to fight M23,” he said.
UN expert reports estimate the FDLR has between 1,500 and 3,000 fighters, though the group’s military spokesman claimed in November 2025 that their numbers were significantly higher.
Destexhe called on the United States to reassess its approach and hold the DRC government responsible for enabling continued violence in eastern DRC.

“The DRC should be punished, not Rwanda. Despite UN Security Council Resolution 2773 and peace agreements, the DRC has refused to distance itself from the FDLR, which remains a major security threat. Meanwhile, Wazalendo extremists’ funds continue to fuel terrorism,” Destexhe wrote on X on March 3.
He further accused the DRC of collaborating with foreign mercenaries and conducting drone attacks on civilians, including in Minembwe, South Kivu, noting that such attacks have persisted for several days.
Destexhe, who has long monitored the Great Lakes region, highlighted that the FDLR’s capabilities doubled after receiving support from the DRC government, making it difficult to dismantle the group entirely. “Their numbers increased after the FDLR received weapons and material support from President Félix Tshisekedi to fight M23,” he said.
UN expert reports estimate the FDLR has between 1,500 and 3,000 fighters, though the group’s military spokesman claimed in November 2025 that their numbers were significantly higher.
Destexhe called on the United States to reassess its approach and hold the DRC government responsible for enabling continued violence in eastern DRC.

title_en: The Deadly February Attack on AFC/M23 Leadership in Masisi: What Really Happened
excerpt_en: Since late February 2026, the DRC army and allied Wazalendo groups have intensified attacks on AFC/M23 positions in Masisi territory, targeting the coltan-rich Rubaya area. These operations have involved heavy weapons and drones, as clashes continue in the region. On February 23,
body_en:
Since late February 2026, the DRC army and allied Wazalendo groups have intensified attacks on AFC/M23 positions in Masisi territory, targeting the coltan-rich Rubaya area. These operations have involved heavy weapons and drones, as clashes continue in the region.
On February 23, senior AFC/M23 officers, including Gen Maj Sultani Makenga, Brig Gen Gaceri Musanga, Col Japhet Gakufe, and Lt Col Willy Ngoma, visited Rubaya to boost the morale of their fighters. That day ended with the DRC coalition failing to capture Rubaya, though they continued attacks in Bahunde chiefdom, including Gatoyi, Gasenyi, and Kinigi.
According to AFC/M23 sources, the leaders decided to spend the night near Rubaya at barracks located in the pasture of Brig Gen Innocent Gahizi. Around 8:00 a.m. on February 24, Gen Maj Makenga rested at Mater Dei Catholic Church in Matanda, while other officers remained in the pasture barracks.
Lt Col Willy Ngoma, the military spokesman, was killed during a targeted attack on the barracks. The coalition’s deputy spokesman, Dr. Oscar Balinda, stated: “They came to shoot at our military spokesman, they shot him in the barracks where he was. It was a house, not on the road-a place where they were staying to stop attacks coming from Walikale.”
Rumors circulated that Gen Maj Makenga had been injured or killed, but AFC/M23 sources confirmed he was alive and on duty. Dr. Balinda emphasized, “He arrived at the battlefield, left, and went to other duties. He was not there when this happened. He is alive, he is on duty.”
On March 2, Gen Maj Makenga was seen at Rumangabo military base in Rutshuru, where he inducted 1,518 new fighters into AFC/M23. Addressing them, he stressed that their mission was to remove incompetent leaders in Kinshasa, restore stability, and support displaced Congolese. “Are you ready to remove Tshisekedi and these ignorant people working with him? Do you refuse to lead with bandits?” he asked, before affirming the group’s commitment to their cause.
Following the February attack, AFC/M23 vowed to continue targeting DRC government assets, including Bangoka airport in Kisangani, aiming to destroy drones used against its bases and hold the DRC government accountable for the deaths of its soldiers, including Lt Col Ngoma.
The clashes in North Kivu and South Kivu, particularly in Masisi, continue to highlight the intense conflict between AFC/M23 and DRC forces, with each side asserting its operational capabilities in self-defense and territorial control.

title: AFC/M23 Confirms Deployment of Commandos Near Kisangani
excerpt: On March 5, 2026, the AFC/M23 coalition announced the deployment of specialized commando units near Bangoka International Airport in Kisangani, DRC, aimed at targeting drone operations used by the DRC army and its allies. The coalition confirmed that it had carried out drone atta
title_en: AFC/M23 Confirms Deployment of Commandos Near Kisangani
excerpt_en: On March 5, 2026, the AFC/M23 coalition announced the deployment of specialized commando units near Bangoka International Airport in Kisangani, DRC, aimed at targeting drone operations used by the DRC army and its allies. The coalition confirmed that it had carried out drone atta
body_en:
On March 5, 2026, the AFC/M23 coalition announced the deployment of specialized commando units near Bangoka International Airport in Kisangani, DRC, aimed at targeting drone operations used by the DRC army and its allies.
The coalition confirmed that it had carried out drone attacks on the airport on February 1 and March 1, 2026, intending to destroy facilities used to launch attacks on AFC/M23 bases and civilians in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces.
Deputy Spokesperson Dr. Oscar Balinda explained:
“The commando forces travel day and night, they go to do their work and then return. So they went and worked, and then returned. This is the terror we want to stop so that we can respect the ceasefire, return to the negotiating table, and achieve lasting peace.”
On March 2, 2026, AFC/M23 inducted 1,518 new fighters at the Rumangabo military base in Rutshuru Territory, defining them as specialized commando units trained to operate while mobile, rather than maintaining permanent bases.
Yannick Tshisola, Director of the Office of the AFC/M23 Commander-in-Chief, indicated that these commandos could play a decisive role in operations targeting Bangoka airport.
This deployment highlights AFC/M23’s focus on mobile, tactical operations to protect its controlled areas while signaling readiness for continued self-defense amidst the ongoing conflict in eastern DRC.

title: Museveni Rejects US and UK Military Bases in Uganda
excerpt: On March 5, 2026, Ugandan President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni stated that he rejected proposals by the United States and the United Kingdom to establish military bases in Uganda, despite offers to strengthen military cooperation. Museveni explained that Uganda’s army is already well
title_en: Museveni Rejects US and UK Military Bases in Uganda
excerpt_en: On March 5, 2026, Ugandan President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni stated that he rejected proposals by the United States and the United Kingdom to establish military bases in Uganda, despite offers to strengthen military cooperation. Museveni explained that Uganda’s army is already well
body_en:
On March 5, 2026, Ugandan President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni stated that he rejected proposals by the United States and the United Kingdom to establish military bases in Uganda, despite offers to strengthen military cooperation.
Museveni explained that Uganda’s army is already well-built and capable of defending the country independently. He referenced Uganda’s military history, highlighting the army’s success in defeating Milton Obote’s forces in 1986, as a foundation for self-reliance.
“Foreign troops? What? We can defend ourselves, we don’t need help from others. If we want knowledge, we can come, learn, and come back,” Museveni said.
He also emphasized concerns over legal accountability, noting that agreements in other countries often require foreign soldiers accused of crimes to be tried in their home countries, which he would not accept for Ugandans.
The announcement comes amid Iranian attacks on US military bases in the Middle East, showing vulnerabilities for countries hosting foreign bases. Museveni highlighted that security in West African nations with foreign bases like Niger, Burkina Faso, and Mali has improved, but Uganda prefers self-reliance and national control over military matters.
Currently, the US maintains bases in African countries including Djibouti, Somalia, Cameroon, Seychelles, and Kenya, while the UK has a base in Nanyuki, Laikipia Region.
This decision reinforces Uganda’s stance on sovereignty and independent defense capabilities.

excerpt_en: Rumangabo, North Kivu, March 8, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition, engaged in conflict with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government, announced the handover of more than 5,000 captured Wazalendo fighters and FARDC soldiers to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC
body_en:
Rumangabo, North Kivu, March 8, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition, engaged in conflict with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) government, announced the handover of more than 5,000 captured Wazalendo fighters and FARDC soldiers to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). The handover ceremony took place on March 2, 2026, in Rumangabo, North Kivu, and the prisoners are to be transported to Kinshasa and returned to the DRC government, according to AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka.
The coalition described the move as a demonstration of its commitment to humanitarian principles, building trust between warring parties, and reducing hostilities.
However, Kanyuka criticized the Kinshasa government, claiming it has refused to release some fighters and other individuals allegedly detained illegally. “Although AFC/M23 is taking concrete measures to reduce the atmosphere of war, the Kinshasa government remains stubborn. It continues to refuse to release our comrades, arrested simply because of their appearance,” he said.
The coalition accused the government of violating the ceasefire agreement and targeting civilians and their property, urging peace negotiators and domestic and international partners to closely monitor compliance. Kanyu

title: Rwanda’s Warnings Ignored Before Uvira Battle
excerpt: Kigali, March 8, 2026 - President Paul Kagame said that Rwanda had repeatedly warned the international community about escalating violence in Uvira, South Kivu, prior to the AFC/M23 coalition capturing parts of the territory in the Democratic Republic of Congo. In a meeting with
title_en: Rwanda’s Warnings Ignored Before Uvira Battle
excerpt_en: Kigali, March 8, 2026 - President Paul Kagame said that Rwanda had repeatedly warned the international community about escalating violence in Uvira, South Kivu, prior to the AFC/M23 coalition capturing parts of the territory in the Democratic Republic of Congo. In a meeting with
body_en:
Kigali, March 8, 2026 - President Paul Kagame said that Rwanda had repeatedly warned the international community about escalating violence in Uvira, South Kivu, prior to the AFC/M23 coalition capturing parts of the territory in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
In a meeting with his counterparts in Rwanda on March 6, 2026, Kagame explained that the Washington peace talks had created a temporary lull and established a framework for resolving security concerns. Despite this, clashes continued between the DRC government, Burundian troops, FDLR, and Wazalendo armed groups, which blocked civilian access and launched ground and air attacks in South Kivu.
“Despite the ongoing talks, forces continued to clash in eastern DRC. Thousands of Burundian troops and pro-government forces remained in line and launched attacks, blocking civilians and striking relentlessly,” Kagame said.
The President stated that these ongoing attacks prompted the AFC/M23 to act against government forces to stop the assaults and reopen civilian access. On December 9, 2025, AFC/M23 fighters captured the town of Uvira, forcing DRC, Burundian, FDLR, and Wazalendo forces to retreat to Bujumbura, Fizi territory, and Kalemie in Tanganyika province.
“That’s what happened in Uvira. Rwanda had been sounding the alarm for months,” Kagame emphasized, noting that the United States and European countries condemned Rwanda, accusing it of violating the ceasefire. Kagame added that Rwanda had long been burdened by responsibilities that were not its own.
Conclusion
The period from February 22 to March 8, 2026, was marked by a complex interplay of diplomatic tensions, regional security challenges, and domestic progress for Rwanda. The ongoing conflict in eastern DRC-underscored by the death of AFC/M23 spokesperson Col. Willy Ngoma and heated exchanges at the United Nations-continues to strain regional relations, highlighting the persistent need for adherence to the Washington Peace Accords and inclusive dialogue.
Despite these external pressures, Rwanda has maintained a firm commitment to long-term development and modernization. Key initiatives include the national electronic ID program, the strategic pursuit of nuclear energy to strengthen electricity supply, and the integration of thousands of refugee children into the national education system, all reflecting a focus on social and economic stability.
In addition, Rwanda has strengthened international partnerships, notably with Singapore and India, and expanded trade licenses for domestic industries under Pan-African standards, positioning the country as an emerging hub for innovation and regional commerce.
Looking ahead, the successful implementation of the 7th East African Community (EAC) Development Plan and the resolution of cross-border challenges, particularly with Burundi, will be essential to fostering deeper regional integration and ensuring sustainable peace in the Great Lakes region.
In conclusion, Rwanda’s strategic initiatives and international engagement demonstrate resilience and forward-looking governance, balancing domestic progress with regional stability in a challenging geopolitical environment.
By Jeff Buleli

Despite these external pressures, Rwanda has maintained a firm commitment to long-term development and modernization. Key initiatives include the national electronic ID program, the strategic pursuit of nuclear energy to strengthen electricity supply, and the integration of thousands of refugee children into the national education system, all reflecting a focus on social and economic stability.
In addition, Rwanda has strengthened international partnerships, notably with Singapore and India, and expanded trade licenses for domestic industries under Pan-African standards, positioning the country as an emerging hub for innovation and regional commerce.
Looking ahead, the successful implementation of the 7th East African Community (EAC) Development Plan and the resolution of cross-border challenges, particularly with Burundi, will be essential to fostering deeper regional integration and ensuring sustainable peace in the Great Lakes region.
In conclusion, Rwanda’s strategic initiatives and international engagement demonstrate resilience and forward-looking governance, balancing domestic progress with regional stability in a challenging geopolitical environment.
By Jeff Buleli

title: Rwanda-Burundi: Catholic Bishops Express Hope for Reopening of Closed Borders
excerpt: Kigali March 12, 2026 - Catholic bishops from Rwanda and Burundi have expressed hope that land borders between the two countries, closed since January 2024, will soon reopen, allowing the resumption of cross-border travel and trade. The remarks came during a joint meeting of the
title_en: Rwanda-Burundi: Catholic Bishops Express Hope for Reopening of Closed Borders
excerpt_en: Kigali March 12, 2026 - Catholic bishops from Rwanda and Burundi have expressed hope that land borders between the two countries, closed since January 2024, will soon reopen, allowing the resumption of cross-border travel and trade. The remarks came during a joint meeting of the
body_en:
Kigali March 12, 2026 - Catholic bishops from Rwanda and Burundi have expressed hope that land borders between the two countries, closed since January 2024, will soon reopen, allowing the resumption of cross-border travel and trade.
The remarks came during a joint meeting of the two countries’ episcopal conferences held in Kigali from March 9 to 11, 2026. Discussions focused on strengthening cooperation and addressing challenges facing local populations, particularly Christian communities.
Speaking to the press, Joachim Ntahondereye, Bishop of Muyinga Diocese and President of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Burundi, urged believers not to lose hope despite the prolonged border closure. He emphasized that the situation is temporary, noting that “the reasons behind the closure will eventually come to an end,” and that people will once again be able to “travel and cooperate as before.”
He also encouraged those with the means to continue using air travel, which remains operational, as a way to maintain exchanges of ideas and promote development and peace between the two nations.
Meanwhile, Antoine Kambanda, Archbishop of Kigali and President of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Rwanda, highlighted the symbolic importance of the meeting. He noted that the Burundian delegation had arrived in Kigali by air, demonstrating that ties between the two countries remain intact despite ongoing tensions.
“This is strong evidence that we must work together to find solutions, in a spirit of understanding, because it is in our interest to live in harmony rather than in conflict,” he said.
Burundi closed its land borders citing security concerns. Although air traffic between the two countries has since resumed, trade and the movement of people remain significantly disrupted.

title: Rwanda, Israel Hold Talks to Strengthen Military Cooperation
excerpt: Kigali, March 12, 2026 - Rwanda and Israel have held high-level discussions aimed at deepening military cooperation, as both countries seek to reinforce security partnerships amid evolving regional challenges. The talks, held on March 11, brought together Rwanda’s Minister of Def
title_en: Rwanda, Israel Hold Talks to Strengthen Military Cooperation
excerpt_en: Kigali, March 12, 2026 - Rwanda and Israel have held high-level discussions aimed at deepening military cooperation, as both countries seek to reinforce security partnerships amid evolving regional challenges. The talks, held on March 11, brought together Rwanda’s Minister of Def
body_en:
Kigali, March 12, 2026 - Rwanda and Israel have held high-level discussions aimed at deepening military cooperation, as both countries seek to reinforce security partnerships amid evolving regional challenges.
The talks, held on March 11, brought together Rwanda’s Minister of Defense Juvenal Marizamunda and Chief of Defence Staff Mubarakh Muganga with Einat Weiss, Israel’s ambassador to Rwanda. The meeting was also attended by Brig. Gen. Patrick Karuretwa, Director General for International Military Cooperation at Rwanda’s Ministry of Defense.
According to the Rwandan Defence Force, discussions focused on issues of mutual interest and explored ways to further strengthen existing military ties between the two nations.
Rwanda and Israel maintain longstanding cooperation in defense and security, including joint training programs, knowledge sharing, and collaboration aimed at promoting regional and international stability. Their partnership also extends beyond the military sector into areas such as technology, education, healthcare, investment, and agriculture.
The renewed engagement comes at a time of heightened security concerns for both countries. Israel continues to face tensions in the Middle East, including conflict involving Hamas and broader regional dynamics linked to Iran.
For Rwanda, security challenges remain tied to instability in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, where authorities have repeatedly raised concerns over cooperation between Congolese forces and the FDLR armed group.
Officials from both sides emphasized the importance of sustained cooperation to address shared security concerns and contribute to broader peace and stability efforts.

title: Minister Nduhungirehe Condemns International Hypocrisy Over DRC Conflict
excerpt: Kigali, 12 March 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has denounced what he described as the bias and hypocrisy of the international community regarding the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Speakin
title_en: Minister Nduhungirehe Condemns International Hypocrisy Over DRC Conflict
excerpt_en: Kigali, 12 March 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has denounced what he described as the bias and hypocrisy of the international community regarding the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Speakin
body_en:
Kigali, 12 March 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, has denounced what he described as the bias and hypocrisy of the international community regarding the ongoing war in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
Speaking after the death of French national Karine Buisset in a drone strike in Goma on 11 March 2026, Minister Nduhungirehe criticized the global response, noting that while many countries and organizations expressed sorrow, no accountability was demanded from those responsible.
“The international community stood united, blaming all parties and calling on the DRC government to establish an independent commission of inquiry,” he said, highlighting that the attack was carried out by DRC forces.
Minister Nduhungirehe questioned why, in other instances where DRC forces conducted attacks against civilians, particularly in Minembwe and Banyamulenge, the international community often remained silent. He added that even when calls for investigations were made, such as after the January 3, 2026 drone strike in Masisi that killed and injured many civilians, inquiries were never conducted.
“It is sad to see that today, not only have the principles of the United Nations and international law lost value, but human lives are sacrificed when powerful interests are threatened,” he stated.
The Minister further condemned the selective nature of international scrutiny. He pointed out that while attacks targeting Congolese Tutsi communities continue, and threats against Rwanda are made, the international community often chooses silence or partiality. Conversely, when Rwanda is accused of involvement in alleged killings, such claims are often amplified without verification.
Minister Nduhungirehe concluded by affirming Rwanda’s stance: while drone attacks and cross-border threats persist, the Rwandan army will continue to protect the nation and its citizens.

title: Rwanda Partners with Japan to Strengthen Disaster Management
excerpt: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - Rwanda is learning from Japan to improve its ability to prevent and respond to disasters including earthquakes, floods, landslides, and lightning, which have historically caused loss of life, damaged infrastructure, and cost the country heavily in repairs.
title_en: Rwanda Partners with Japan to Strengthen Disaster Management
excerpt_en: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - Rwanda is learning from Japan to improve its ability to prevent and respond to disasters including earthquakes, floods, landslides, and lightning, which have historically caused loss of life, damaged infrastructure, and cost the country heavily in repairs.
body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 - Rwanda is learning from Japan to improve its ability to prevent and respond to disasters including earthquakes, floods, landslides, and lightning, which have historically caused loss of life, damaged infrastructure, and cost the country heavily in repairs.
The knowledge exchange is taking place through a two-day conference in Kigali, which began on 12 March 2026. Activities showcased 12 Japanese companies offering technologies designed to prevent disasters before they occur and respond efficiently when they do.
Japan, situated near the Pacific Ocean, is among the world’s most disaster-prone nations, regularly affected by tsunamis and earthquakes. The conference also commemorates the over 15,900 people who died and the 2,500 still missing from the 11 March 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan.
According to Gen. Maj. (Rtd) Albert Murasira, Rwanda’s Minister of Disaster Management, researchers attending the conference, including those from the University of Rwanda, are studying Japanese approaches to early disaster detection, evacuation planning, and preventive measures. “These two days are for us to meet and learn how they work, but now the advantage is that schools and university researchers have also come, so they can continue research for Rwanda’s needs,” he said.
Japanese Ambassador to Rwanda, Kazuya Nakajo, emphasized the potential impact of Japanese technology on saving lives and supporting Rwanda’s economic growth. “I believe that Japanese technology and the NST2 development plan will play a role in preventing disasters and promoting continued economic growth in Rwanda. Together, we can deal with these disasters effectively,” he said.
Rwanda is already implementing programs such as tree planting to reduce landslides and erosion, alongside initiatives to combat deforestation. Japanese company Jibu Gaz One Ltd. showcased an innovative solution for providing affordable gas to low-income households. Traditionally sold in six-kilo cylinders, Jibu Gaz now offers 1, 2, or 3-kilo cylinders, costing 1,600 Rwandan francs per kilo, helping households avoid returning to charcoal or firewood, a key contributor to deforestation.

title: Investor Abdul Samad Rabiu Praises President Kagame’s Leadership
excerpt: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - Abdul Samad Rabiu, one of Africa’s wealthiest investors, has praised President Paul Kagame for his visionary leadership and commitment to Rwanda’s development, calling him an example for Africa and beyond. Rabiu made the remarks following talks with Presid
title_en: Investor Abdul Samad Rabiu Praises President Kagame’s Leadership
excerpt_en: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - Abdul Samad Rabiu, one of Africa’s wealthiest investors, has praised President Paul Kagame for his visionary leadership and commitment to Rwanda’s development, calling him an example for Africa and beyond. Rabiu made the remarks following talks with Presid
body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 - Abdul Samad Rabiu, one of Africa’s wealthiest investors, has praised President Paul Kagame for his visionary leadership and commitment to Rwanda’s development, calling him an example for Africa and beyond.
Rabiu made the remarks following talks with President Kagame at an international conference on civilian nuclear energy, which brought together heads of state, government officials, and energy experts.
“His visionary leadership, commitment to development, and determination to advance Rwanda continue to serve as an example for Africa and beyond. President Kagame is a great example of leaders dedicated to Africa’s future and the continent’s opportunities,” Rabiu said.
President Kagame, who served as Head of Institutional Reforms of the African Union from 2016 to 2024, strengthened the organization’s functionality and economic stability, including the revival of the Peace Fund, which has raised $400 million.
Under Kagame’s leadership, Rwanda has become one of the fastest-growing economies in Africa, maintaining annual growth rates of over 8%. Poverty has significantly declined due to targeted programs, with the Seventh Rwandan Population and Housing Survey (EICV7) showing poverty falling from 39.8% in 2017 to 27.4% in 2024, and extreme poverty dropping from 11.3% to 5.4%.
Rabiu highlighted that these achievements reflect good governance that prioritizes the people and positions Rwanda as a model for sustainable development on the continent.

title: Rwanda Continues Efforts to Finalize Border Demarcation with Neighbors
excerpt: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - Rwanda is continuing a long-standing process to confirm its official borders with neighboring countries, more than two decades after the initiative was first launched, the Ministry of Environment has said. Speaking before Parliament, Minister of Environmen
title_en: Rwanda Continues Efforts to Finalize Border Demarcation with Neighbors
excerpt_en: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - Rwanda is continuing a long-standing process to confirm its official borders with neighboring countries, more than two decades after the initiative was first launched, the Ministry of Environment has said. Speaking before Parliament, Minister of Environmen
body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 - Rwanda is continuing a long-standing process to confirm its official borders with neighboring countries, more than two decades after the initiative was first launched, the Ministry of Environment has said.
Speaking before Parliament, Minister of Environment Dr. Bernadette Arap explained that the process began in 2000, when the Cabinet approved the creation of a national commission to oversee border negotiations and demarcation with neighboring states. The commission officially started work in February 2001, supported by a technical team.
“Significant progress has been made, including demarcation work with the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda,” the Minister said. However, she noted that the process remains incomplete, as some borders have not yet been formally approved by all parties involved.
As a precaution, during the national land registration program (2009-2013), authorities instructed residents living within 200 meters of international borders not to register their land, in order to avoid potential disputes. As a result, some land in these areas remains unregistered to date.
Negotiations are ongoing. Recent engagements include meetings with Tanzania and a February 2025 session with Uganda, where both sides agreed to resume border demarcation efforts.
Land Boundary Disputes Persist
In addition to international borders, Rwanda is also addressing internal land boundary discrepancies identified during the nationwide land registration process.
Minister Arap revealed that 222,423 land plots have already been corrected, while efforts continue to resolve outstanding cases across 582 villages. Challenges included unclear boundaries due to terrain such as forests, pastures, and farmland, as well as instances where landowners were absent during the initial mapping.
To address this, authorities are now using modern mapping technologies to finalize corrections, with the goal of completing the process within the year.
The government is working with development partners to support boundary corrections in districts such as Kirehe, Nyagatare, and Kayonza, with plans to expand the effort to 10 additional districts.
Officials noted that while some residents can hire private land surveyors, others are being supported through local administrative structures to ensure fair representation and resolution.
The ongoing efforts reflect Rwanda’s commitment to clarifying territorial boundaries, strengthening land governance, and preventing future disputes both domestically and across its borders.

title_en: Bobi Wine Emerges from Hiding, Announces Temporary Move Abroad
excerpt_en: Kampala, 14 March 2026 - Ugandan opposition leader Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, widely known as Bobi Wine, has announced that he has emerged from nearly two months in hiding and will temporarily leave the country for engagements abroad. Kyagulanyi said he went into hiding on Janua
body_en:
Kampala, 14 March 2026 - Ugandan opposition leader Robert Kyagulanyi Ssentamu, widely known as Bobi Wine, has announced that he has emerged from nearly two months in hiding and will temporarily leave the country for engagements abroad.
Kyagulanyi said he went into hiding on January 15, 2026, shortly after the conclusion of presidential and parliamentary elections, citing security concerns and alleged targeting by government forces.
He accused authorities of conducting raids, setting up checkpoints, and targeting his associates, claiming that his supporters helped shield him during that period. “They did not find me because the people of Uganda protected me,” he said.
The opposition leader, who contested under the National Unity Platform (NUP), has rejected the election results, which saw incumbent President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni declared the winner. Official figures from the Electoral Commission showed Museveni securing 71.65% of the vote, while Kyagulanyi received 24.72%.
Bobi Wine stated that his trip abroad is temporary and work-related, aimed at engaging with international partners and allies. “I will be speaking with our friends around the world before returning to Uganda to continue the fight for freedom and democracy,” he said.
His announcement comes amid ongoing political tensions in Uganda, with the opposition continuing to contest the credibility of the electoral process and raising concerns over political freedoms and security.

title: Rwanda and Djibouti Explore Expanded Bilateral Cooperation
excerpt: Djibouti, 16 March 2026 - Rwanda and Djibouti have held high-level talks aimed at strengthening and expanding bilateral cooperation across key sectors. Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, was received by his Djiboutian counterpar
title_en: Rwanda and Djibouti Explore Expanded Bilateral Cooperation
excerpt_en: Djibouti, 16 March 2026 - Rwanda and Djibouti have held high-level talks aimed at strengthening and expanding bilateral cooperation across key sectors. Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, was received by his Djiboutian counterpar
body_en:
Djibouti, 16 March 2026 - Rwanda and Djibouti have held high-level talks aimed at strengthening and expanding bilateral cooperation across key sectors.
Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Ambassador Olivier Nduhungirehe, was received by his Djiboutian counterpart, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, where both sides discussed opportunities to deepen collaboration in areas of mutual interest.
According to Djibouti’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Rwandan minister is also expected to meet the President of Djibouti and deliver a special message from President Paul Kagame.
Relations between the two countries have remained stable over the years, supported by a joint ministerial commission that meets regularly to explore new avenues of cooperation.
In November 2025, Rwanda and Djibouti signed nine cooperation agreements covering sectors such as sports, health, family development, and diplomatic training. Existing agreements also span trade, air transport, technology, investment protection, and visa facilitation for diplomats.
As part of this partnership, Djibouti has allocated 60 hectares of land to Rwanda, including plots near the port and in a commercial zone, while Rwanda has provided Djibouti with 10 hectares in an industrial zone in Masoro.

title: Denis Sassou Nguesso Re-Elected President of Congo-Brazzaville
excerpt: Brazzaville, 18 March 2026 - Denis Sassou Nguesso has been re-elected president of the Republic of Congo, securing a fifth term with 94.82% of the vote following elections held on 15 March 2026. The 82-year-old leader, representing the Congolese Labour Party, defeated six other c
title_en: Denis Sassou Nguesso Re-Elected President of Congo-Brazzaville
excerpt_en: Brazzaville, 18 March 2026 - Denis Sassou Nguesso has been re-elected president of the Republic of Congo, securing a fifth term with 94.82% of the vote following elections held on 15 March 2026. The 82-year-old leader, representing the Congolese Labour Party, defeated six other c
body_en:
Brazzaville, 18 March 2026 - Denis Sassou Nguesso has been re-elected president of the Republic of Congo, securing a fifth term with 94.82% of the vote following elections held on 15 March 2026.
The 82-year-old leader, representing the Congolese Labour Party, defeated six other candidates. His closest challenger, Mabio Mavoungou Zinga, received 1.48% of the vote.
The results, announced by national authorities, extend Sassou Nguesso’s rule, which has spanned nearly four decades since he first came to power in 1979. Although he briefly lost power in 1992, he returned to leadership in 1997 following a civil war.
Opposition candidates have a five-day window to file appeals, which will be reviewed by the Constitutional Court before the final results are confirmed.
A constitutional amendment adopted in 2015 removed presidential term limits and age restrictions, enabling Sassou Nguesso to run for additional terms.
The Republic of Congo, located in Central Africa, borders Gabon, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and has a population of over six million people.

body_en:
Dakar, 18 March 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Sports, Nelly Mukazayire, has delivered a message from President Paul Kagame to Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye during an official visit aimed at strengthening bilateral and multilateral cooperation.
According to Senegal’s presidency, the meeting focused on shared priorities within the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), particularly in the areas of youth and economic development.
Discussions also highlighted efforts to support the candidacy of Louise Mushikiwabo for another term as Secretary-General of the OIF. Rwanda has been actively engaging partners to back her re-election bid.
Prior to her visit to Senegal, Minister Mukazayire traveled to Mauritania, where she met President Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani to seek support for the same candidacy.
President Kagame re-nominated Mushikiwabo in January 2026. She has led the OIF since 2019 and began her second term in November 2022, positioning her for a potential third term.
Rwanda and Senegal maintain longstanding diplomatic ties, reinforced by regular high-level exchanges. In recent months, both countries have signed cooperation agreements covering sectors such as agriculture, health, and development.
The latest diplomatic engagement underscores Rwanda’s continued efforts to consolidate regional and international partnerships, particularly within Francophone institutions.

title: Dr. Iyamuremye Criticizes Support for Sanctions Against Rwanda
excerpt: Kigali, 18 March 2026 - Former Senate President Augustin Iyamuremye has criticized Rwandans who express support for international sanctions against their own country, warning of the broader impact on ordinary citizens. Speaking on 18 March, Iyamuremye said he could not understand
title_en: Dr. Iyamuremye Criticizes Support for Sanctions Against Rwanda
excerpt_en: Kigali, 18 March 2026 - Former Senate President Augustin Iyamuremye has criticized Rwandans who express support for international sanctions against their own country, warning of the broader impact on ordinary citizens. Speaking on 18 March, Iyamuremye said he could not understand
body_en:
Kigali, 18 March 2026 - Former Senate President Augustin Iyamuremye has criticized Rwandans who express support for international sanctions against their own country, warning of the broader impact on ordinary citizens.
Speaking on 18 March, Iyamuremye said he could not understand why some Rwandans-particularly those living abroad-appear to welcome measures such as the suspension of foreign aid and other restrictions.
His remarks come amid strained relations between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo, which have prompted some international partners, including the United Kingdom and Canada, to suspend parts of their cooperation with Kigali.
Earlier in March 2026, the United States also imposed sanctions on members of the Rwandan Armed Forces, further intensifying the debate.
Iyamuremye argued that such measures primarily affect citizens rather than political leaders, citing potential disruptions to essential services and development projects.
“I cannot understand how a Rwandan could be happy that their country is being sanctioned,” he said. “These are services meant for citizens-roads, water, electricity and health facilities.”
He added that those who support such measures fail to distinguish between the government and the broader population, emphasizing the need for national cohesion during challenging times.
The comments highlight ongoing divisions among Rwandans regarding the impact and legitimacy of external pressure linked to regional security tensions.

title: Rwanda and DRC Agree to Advance Implementation of Washington Peace Accords
excerpt: Washington, 19 March 2026 - Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo have agreed to take concrete steps to implement the Washington Peace Accords, in a renewed effort to ease tensions and promote regional stability. The agreement, initially signed on 27 June 2025 with the
title_en: Rwanda and DRC Agree to Advance Implementation of Washington Peace Accords
excerpt_en: Washington, 19 March 2026 - Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo have agreed to take concrete steps to implement the Washington Peace Accords, in a renewed effort to ease tensions and promote regional stability. The agreement, initially signed on 27 June 2025 with the
body_en:
Washington, 19 March 2026 - Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo have agreed to take concrete steps to implement the Washington Peace Accords, in a renewed effort to ease tensions and promote regional stability.
The agreement, initially signed on 27 June 2025 with the support of the United States, focuses on addressing security concerns, including the dismantling of the FDLR armed group and the removal of Rwanda’s defensive measures along the border.
Although the accord was ratified by both countries in December 2025-along with provisions on economic cooperation in trade, mining, and infrastructure-implementation has remained limited.
Rwanda has maintained that it cannot lift its security measures while the FDLR and allied groups remain active near its borders. Kigali has also accused the Congolese government of continuing to support the group, including through integration into local armed forces and allied militias.
Against this backdrop, delegations from both countries met in Washington from 17 to 18 March 2026, where they committed to advancing implementation of the agreement.
According to U.S. officials, the parties agreed on measures aimed at de-escalation, including respect for each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Additional steps include the neutralization of the FDLR, a phased withdrawal of Rwanda’s security measures, and the protection of civilians affected by the conflict.
The renewed commitment signals a shared intention to achieve lasting peace and stability in eastern DRC and the wider Great Lakes region, though significant challenges to full implementation remain.

excerpt_en: Victoria, 20 March 2026 - Rwanda and Seychelles have held high-level discussions aimed at expanding cooperation across key sectors, including education, tourism, and agriculture. Seychelles Vice President Sebastien Pillay received Rwanda’s Minister of Labor and Employment, Christ
body_en:
Victoria, 20 March 2026 - Rwanda and Seychelles have held high-level discussions aimed at expanding cooperation across key sectors, including education, tourism, and agriculture.
Seychelles Vice President Sebastien Pillay received Rwanda’s Minister of Labor and Employment, Christine Nkulikiyinka, who delivered greetings from President Paul Kagame and reaffirmed Rwanda’s commitment to closer ties.
According to the Seychelles Presidential Office, the talks focused on strengthening collaboration in priority sectors while exploring new opportunities in trade, including plans for Seychelles to export seafood to the Rwandan market.
Both sides also discussed improving service delivery, building institutional capacity, and sharing development experiences to advance sustainable development goals.
Vice President Pillay proposed the establishment of a joint mechanism to monitor the implementation of bilateral agreements and ensure effective follow-up.
The discussions build on existing cooperation between the two countries, including agreements reached during President Kagame’s 2023 visit to Seychelles, which covered areas such as health, investment, and security.
A visa waiver agreement between Rwanda and Seychelles also remains in place, facilitating travel and economic exchange between the two nations.

title: Joseph Kabila Calls for the Removal of Tshisekedi’s Regime
excerpt: Goma, North Kivu March 23, 2026 - Former President Joseph Kabila Kabange, who led the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) from 2001 to 2019, has publicly called for the removal of President Félix Tshisekedi’s government, denouncing it as acting illegally. The statement came during
title_en: Joseph Kabila Calls for the Removal of Tshisekedi’s Regime
excerpt_en: Goma, North Kivu March 23, 2026 - Former President Joseph Kabila Kabange, who led the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) from 2001 to 2019, has publicly called for the removal of President Félix Tshisekedi’s government, denouncing it as acting illegally. The statement came during
body_en:
Goma, North Kivu March 23, 2026 - Former President Joseph Kabila Kabange, who led the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) from 2001 to 2019, has publicly called for the removal of President Félix Tshisekedi’s government, denouncing it as acting illegally. The statement came during an interview on March 20 with journalist Hubert Leclercq of Le Libre, conducted at Kabila’s residence in Goma, North Kivu province.
Kabila, who has been in eastern DRC since May 2025, has been accused by the authorities of collaborating with the AFC/M23 coalition, which controls Goma, and of undermining national security. He was sentenced to death in absentia by the Kinshasa government.
“When asked why I am in Goma, I said it is home. I received you in a house I bought in 1999. The relentless attacks on me and my political family began in 2019, before the birth of AFC/M23. I believe I have the right to work and communicate with all Congolese, with the aim of uniting the population and achieving peace,” Kabila told Le Libre.
He condemned the recent drone strike launched by DRC government forces on March 11, 2026, targeting Goma, which he said aimed to eliminate him and senior AFC/M23 leaders, including Corneille Nangaa, Bertrand Bisimwa, Freddy Kaniki, and Maj. Gen. Sultani Makenga. Kabila further accused government forces of continuing to kill civilians in eastern regions such as Masisi and the Minembwe commune in South Kivu, often employing drones.
Kabila sharply criticized Tshisekedi’s government, asserting it has repeatedly disregarded the law and is now attempting to amend the Constitution to extend presidential terms. “I said it in May last year, we must stop this dictatorship that has been established. To achieve this, we must unite our forces, mobilize all Congolese, whether in exile or inside the country,” he said.
He cited Article 64 of the DRC Constitution, which he interprets as giving every Congolese the responsibility to punish individuals or groups who violate the law, as the legal basis for the planned removal of Tshisekedi’s regime.
Kabila’s statements are likely to further heighten tensions in an already volatile eastern DRC, where political divisions and ongoing armed conflicts continue to destabilize civilian populations.

title: Kagame Urges Kigali Leaders to Eliminate Corruption and Improve Service Delivery
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda March 23, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has called on leaders in the City of Kigali and across public institutions to urgently address persistent problems related to pollution, poor service delivery, and corruption, warning that failure to act will have serious cons
title_en: Kagame Urges Kigali Leaders to Eliminate Corruption and Improve Service Delivery
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda March 23, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has called on leaders in the City of Kigali and across public institutions to urgently address persistent problems related to pollution, poor service delivery, and corruption, warning that failure to act will have serious cons
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda March 23, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has called on leaders in the City of Kigali and across public institutions to urgently address persistent problems related to pollution, poor service delivery, and corruption, warning that failure to act will have serious consequences.
Speaking on Monday, March 23, at the conclusion of a high-level consultative meeting with government and local leaders, Kagame criticized what he described as a tolerance for “reduced” corruption rather than its total elimination.
“Why compare ourselves to countries where corruption is worse? Why accept so-called ‘petty corruption’?” he asked. “If you see services not being delivered properly and remain silent, you are complicit.”
The Rwandan leader stressed that silence in the face of corruption amounts to participation, urging officials to take responsibility and act decisively. He warned that negligence in public service delivery can have fatal consequences, citing the case of a woman who died after being denied care at a hospital due to administrative issues with her health insurance.
Kagame also highlighted visible shortcomings in urban management, pointing to poor sanitation, unmaintained public spaces, and unregulated construction in Kigali. He said he had personally observed dirt along roads and inconsistent urban planning, calling for immediate corrective measures.
“I still see dirt on the roads. I stop and ask those with me to remove it,” he said, emphasizing the need for practical, low-cost solutions, such as landscaping and better organization of residential and commercial areas.
The president urged city authorities to establish dedicated task forces, involving security services and urban planning officials, to ensure consistent enforcement and follow-up on identified issues. He expressed frustration at the slow pace of implementation, noting that similar directives had been issued for years.
Beyond urban governance, Kagame addressed broader social and economic challenges, including school dropouts, family instability, and agricultural productivity. He questioned why Rwanda has not yet achieved food self-sufficiency, pointing to gaps in awareness, production, and post-harvest management, particularly the lack of systems to preserve perishable goods.
He concluded with a firm warning: all identified problems must be resolved, or authorities themselves will be held accountable for inaction.

title: Rwanda Warns Against Repeating “Mistakes of 1994” Over Violence in Eastern DRC
excerpt: Kigali March 23, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has called on the international community to act decisively to prevent atrocities in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, warning against a repeat of the failures that led to the
title_en: Rwanda Warns Against Repeating “Mistakes of 1994” Over Violence in Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: Kigali March 23, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has called on the international community to act decisively to prevent atrocities in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, warning against a repeat of the failures that led to the
body_en:
Kigali March 23, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation, Olivier Nduhungirehe, has called on the international community to act decisively to prevent atrocities in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, warning against a repeat of the failures that led to the Genocide against the Tutsi.
Speaking at an international conference focused on remembrance, reconciliation, and reconstruction, Nduhungirehe emphasized the need to draw lessons from past tragedies to address current risks. He pointed to ongoing violence in eastern DRC, alleging that communities, particularly Tutsi populations including the Banyamulenge, are being targeted.
“In the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, those driven by an ideology targeting Tutsi communities continue to perpetrate violence, killings, and displacement,” he said.
The minister warned that silence in the face of such warning signs amounts to complicity, urging the international community to respond before the situation escalates further. “We must bring this to light. Remaining silent when such signs are visible is complicity,” he stated.
Nduhungirehe also referenced previous global commitments made after major atrocities, including the Holocaust, noting that despite the pledge of “never again,” similar tragedies have occurred.
He further linked the current situation in eastern DRC to the aftermath of the 1994 genocide, particularly the presence of armed groups such as the FDLR, which Rwanda accuses of perpetuating violence in the region.
According to Kigali, attacks against Kinyarwanda-speaking Congolese communities continue, with allegations that multiple armed actors are involved. Rwanda has repeatedly called on the international community to acknowledge and respond to these developments, arguing that early warning signs should not be ignored.
These remarks come amid ongoing tensions between Rwanda and the DRC, with Kinshasa accusing Kigali of supporting the AFC/M23 rebellion-an allegation Rwanda denies-further complicating efforts to stabilize the region.

title: Rwanda Earns Over Rwf236.8 Billion from Tourism in Three Months
excerpt: Kigali, March 12, 2026 - Rwanda generated more than Rwf236.8 billion (approximately $161.5 million) in tourism revenue over a three-month period from November 2025 to January 2026, according to data from the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda. The figures highlight touris
title_en: Rwanda Earns Over Rwf236.8 Billion from Tourism in Three Months
excerpt_en: Kigali, March 12, 2026 - Rwanda generated more than Rwf236.8 billion (approximately $161.5 million) in tourism revenue over a three-month period from November 2025 to January 2026, according to data from the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda. The figures highlight touris
body_en:
Kigali, March 12, 2026 - Rwanda generated more than Rwf236.8 billion (approximately $161.5 million) in tourism revenue over a three-month period from November 2025 to January 2026, according to data from the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda.
The figures highlight tourism as a key driver of the country’s economy, with significant contributions from both air and land arrivals. Visitors entering Rwanda by air accounted for the largest share of revenue, generating $136.7 million. Leisure travelers, including those visiting for holidays and tourism activities, contributed more than $65 million, with gorilla tourism alone accounting for at least 71.4% of that segment.
Regionally, visitors from North America were the top contributors, generating $40.8 million. This performance is partly attributed to Rwanda’s strategic international marketing efforts, including partnerships with major U.S. sports teams such as the Los Angeles Clippers and the Los Angeles Rams under the “Visit Rwanda” campaign. The initiative builds on earlier collaborations with European football clubs including Arsenal FC, Paris Saint-Germain, and FC Bayern Munich.
These partnerships aim to boost Rwanda’s global visibility and attract high-value tourists and investors, particularly from the United States, a major source market for international travel.
Land border entries also contributed to tourism earnings, generating $24.9 million, largely from visitors traveling for family and social purposes. Most land arrivals came through key border points linking Rwanda with neighboring countries including Uganda, Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Tanzania.
The report further indicates that Rwandans traveling abroad spent over $95.9 million during the same period, with air travelers accounting for the largest share of expenditures. Countries within the East African Community remained the primary destinations.
Education emerged as a leading reason for travel, both for visitors entering Rwanda and Rwandans traveling abroad, with students typically recording the longest stays.
Tourism remains a cornerstone of Rwanda’s economic strategy. In 2024, the country welcomed 1.36 million international visitors, generating $647 million in revenue. Authorities are now targeting $1 billion in annual tourism revenue by 2029, as part of broader efforts to expand the sector and strengthen its contribution to national growth.

title: Rwanda and Kenya Sign MoU to Boost Cross-Border Payments
excerpt: Kigali, 11 March 2026 - The Central Bank of Rwanda (BNR) and the Bank of Kenya have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to facilitate cross-border payments and strengthen regional financial integration. The agreement, inked on the sidelines of the Inclusive Fintech Forum i
title_en: Rwanda and Kenya Sign MoU to Boost Cross-Border Payments
excerpt_en: Kigali, 11 March 2026 - The Central Bank of Rwanda (BNR) and the Bank of Kenya have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to facilitate cross-border payments and strengthen regional financial integration. The agreement, inked on the sidelines of the Inclusive Fintech Forum i
body_en:
Kigali, 11 March 2026 - The Central Bank of Rwanda (BNR) and the Bank of Kenya have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to facilitate cross-border payments and strengthen regional financial integration.
The agreement, inked on the sidelines of the Inclusive Fintech Forum in Kigali, establishes a ‘License Passporting Framework for Payment Service Providers (PSPs)’, allowing licensed PSPs to operate seamlessly in either Rwanda or Kenya.
Officials said the MoU is expected to promote competition, encourage innovation, and accelerate technology-driven financial services across East Africa. It aligns with the East African Community (EAC) Cross-Border Payment System Masterplan, which seeks to create a common, efficient, and inclusive regional payment system.
A key objective of the agreement is to address regulatory fragmentation by ensuring that a license issued in one EAC country is recognized across member states, enabling broader access to cross-border financial services.
The BNR described the MoU as a significant step toward market growth, innovation, and digital financial integration, all under strict regulatory oversight. The Bank of Kenya reaffirmed its commitment to continued regional cooperation in the financial sector.

title: Rwandan Parliament Calls for Stronger Measures Against Illegal Mining
excerpt: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - The House of Representatives has urged authorities to address illegal mining in a lasting and comprehensive manner, citing its growing threat to public safety and the environment. The issue was raised during the presentation of an analytical report by the
title_en: Rwandan Parliament Calls for Stronger Measures Against Illegal Mining
excerpt_en: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - The House of Representatives has urged authorities to address illegal mining in a lasting and comprehensive manner, citing its growing threat to public safety and the environment. The issue was raised during the presentation of an analytical report by the
body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 - The House of Representatives has urged authorities to address illegal mining in a lasting and comprehensive manner, citing its growing threat to public safety and the environment.
The issue was raised during the presentation of an analytical report by the Committee on Foreign Affairs and Security, which highlighted theft and illegal mining as key security challenges.
Deputy Tumukunde Hope Gasatura, Chairperson of the Committee, revealed that between 2020 and 2025, 1,335 cases of illegal mining were reported. Miners have been found operating in people’s fields, rivers, state forests, abandoned mines, and old mine sites, causing environmental damage and loss of property.
He identified several causes of illegal mining, including:
Growth of the mineral market and fraudulent traders
Residents with traditional knowledge of mineral locations
Mining in licensed areas without authorization
Unprotected abandoned or old mines
Youth dropping out of school and joining illegal mining due to financial incentives
Insufficient security personnel by mining companies
Minerals found in private fields and homes
Unauthorized local leaders or former workers exploiting mines
Lack of compliance with labor management and monitoring systems
Gasatura also noted that there are currently 994 unregulated mines across the country, posing risks of accidents, injuries, and deaths.
Deputy Niyorurema Jean Rene recommended the expedited cancellation of mining permits to curb illegal operations. Deputy Uwamahoro raised concerns about markets buying illegally mined minerals, calling for proper monitoring of the chain of custody.
MP Mukabunani Christine proposed the creation of a mining sector unit within the Private Sector Union to strengthen oversight, while MP Kanyandekwe Christine emphasized balancing worker health and safety in legally operating mines.
The Parliament has requested the Ministry of Local Government to present strategies to improve the Mining Task Force, and asked the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) to:
Expedite issuance of mining licenses
Improve monitoring of RMB contracts with companies
Prevent use of unethical subcontractors
Leverage the Inkomane system to track mining activities
The parliamentary push reflects a growing effort to curb illegal mining, protect communities, and ensure the responsible development of Rwanda’s mineral resources.

title: Rwanda Cooperation Initiative Generates Rwf19 Billion from Study Tours
excerpt: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - The Rwanda Cooperation Initiative (RCI) has generated nearly Rwf19 billion since its establishment in 2018, driven by thousands of international visitors seeking to learn from Rwanda’s development model and innovations. The announcement was made by RCI Dir
title_en: Rwanda Cooperation Initiative Generates Rwf19 Billion from Study Tours
excerpt_en: Kigali, 13 March 2026 - The Rwanda Cooperation Initiative (RCI) has generated nearly Rwf19 billion since its establishment in 2018, driven by thousands of international visitors seeking to learn from Rwanda’s development model and innovations. The announcement was made by RCI Dir
body_en:
Kigali, 13 March 2026 - The Rwanda Cooperation Initiative (RCI) has generated nearly Rwf19 billion since its establishment in 2018, driven by thousands of international visitors seeking to learn from Rwanda’s development model and innovations.
The announcement was made by RCI Director General Patricie Uwase during a partners’ meeting aimed at improving the quality of services offered to visiting delegations.
Uwase revealed that around 10,000 visitors from over 70 countries, including 45 African nations, have participated in study tours in Rwanda. These visits, which combine knowledge exchange and tourism, have become a growing source of revenue and international engagement.
“In Rwanda, we have many solutions others can learn from, but we must improve how we present and package them,” Uwase said, emphasizing the need to integrate practical demonstrations and business components into presentations.
However, an internal audit found that only 15% of the 297 partner institutions were able to clearly present their services. Gaps included weak program design, limited practical exposure, and insufficient integration of tourism experiences for visitors.
Dr. Willy Mugenzi, Director of Operations at RCI, noted that some visitors expressed dissatisfaction due to a mismatch between expectations and delivery. He stressed the importance of moving beyond theory: “It is not enough to explain achievements; visitors need to see how solutions work in practice, including the challenges faced and how they were overcome.”
Partners are now being encouraged to adopt a more transparent and hands-on approach, showcasing both successes and challenges to enhance credibility and learning outcomes.
Vividi Karangwa Immaculée, Director General of Hope and Homes for Children, acknowledged that institutions previously focused mainly on positive outcomes, often overlooking challenges. “Visitors come to learn, not just to admire success. We are now committed to sharing our experiences more fully, while maintaining a constructive approach,” she said.
Established in 2018, the RCI serves as a platform to promote Rwanda’s homegrown solutions, particularly across Africa, by facilitating knowledge sharing, innovation transfer, and capacity building.

title: Fitch Affirms Rwanda’s Economic Outlook Despite Regional Tensions
excerpt: Kigali, 14 March 2026 - Fitch Ratings, the American-British credit rating agency, has reaffirmed confidence in Rwanda’s economy, maintaining its ‘B+ rating with a stable outlook’ and projecting continued growth despite regional security and political challenges. In its latest ass
title_en: Fitch Affirms Rwanda’s Economic Outlook Despite Regional Tensions
excerpt_en: Kigali, 14 March 2026 - Fitch Ratings, the American-British credit rating agency, has reaffirmed confidence in Rwanda’s economy, maintaining its ‘B+ rating with a stable outlook’ and projecting continued growth despite regional security and political challenges. In its latest ass
body_en:
Kigali, 14 March 2026 - Fitch Ratings, the American-British credit rating agency, has reaffirmed confidence in Rwanda’s economy, maintaining its ‘B+ rating with a stable outlook’ and projecting continued growth despite regional security and political challenges.
In its latest assessment released on 13 March 2026, Fitch indicated that Rwanda’s economy is expected to remain resilient, with growth projected to exceed 7% in the 2026/2027 fiscal year.
The agency acknowledged that earlier concerns over reduced external financing, driven by regional tensions and strained diplomatic relations with countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada, and Belgium, had weighed on the outlook. However, it noted that confidence has rebounded since April 2025.
According to the report, international partners continued to support Rwanda, providing nearly $1 billion in funding by June 2025. Fitch expects external financing to remain strong, with foreign loans projected to approach $1 billion in 2026/2027, largely on low-interest, long-term terms.
Fitch also downplayed the potential economic impact of recent U.S. sanctions on the Rwandan military, stating that these measures are unlikely to significantly affect the broader economy. “The loans are directed to the government, not the military, and are concessional in nature,” the agency noted.
However, the report highlighted rising public debt, which could reach 79% of GDP by 2027, driven by major investments such as the Bugesera International Airport project and the expansion of RwandAir.
Key sectors expected to sustain growth include infrastructure development, agriculture, and tourism, with the new airport seen as a critical driver of economic expansion.
Fitch further commended Rwanda’s efforts to reduce the budget deficit, noting that fiscal reforms, including the introduction of new tax measures, are improving domestic revenue. The deficit is projected to decline to 3.6% of GDP by 2026/2027, down from 5.9% in 2024/2025.
Overall, the agency concluded that Rwanda’s economic fundamentals remain strong, supported by prudent fiscal management and sustained international support, even as regional uncertainties persist.

title: Rwanda Targets Data-Driven Governance by 2030, Says Minister Ingabire
excerpt: Kigali, 15 March 2026 - Rwanda is aiming to become a fully data-driven government by 2030, with technology and innovation at the core of decision-making across all sectors, Minister of ICT and Innovation Paula Ingabire has said. Speaking in a recent media interview, Ingabire outl
title_en: Rwanda Targets Data-Driven Governance by 2030, Says Minister Ingabire
excerpt_en: Kigali, 15 March 2026 - Rwanda is aiming to become a fully data-driven government by 2030, with technology and innovation at the core of decision-making across all sectors, Minister of ICT and Innovation Paula Ingabire has said. Speaking in a recent media interview, Ingabire outl
body_en:
Kigali, 15 March 2026 - Rwanda is aiming to become a fully data-driven government by 2030, with technology and innovation at the core of decision-making across all sectors, Minister of ICT and Innovation Paula Ingabire has said.
Speaking in a recent media interview, Ingabire outlined the country’s ambition to ensure that every government action is based on real-time data and evidence, positioning Rwanda among global leaders in digital transformation.
“We want to be a government where every decision is based on information and evidence,” she said, emphasizing that technology is central to solving national challenges.
Empowering Youth as Innovators
The Minister stressed the importance of transforming Rwanda’s youth from technology users into creators, noting that young people must be given opportunities to develop solutions rather than simply consume digital tools.
To address barriers, the government has introduced reforms in public procurement, allowing tenders to be framed around problems rather than predefined solutions. This approach enables start-ups and young innovators to propose creative responses and compete alongside established companies.
“We have tested this approach and seen a wealth of ideas from young innovators,” Ingabire noted, adding that local entrepreneurs often have a deeper understanding of community challenges.
Expanding Opportunities in Public Markets
Public procurement remains a significant economic driver, with contracts valued at over 1,000 billion Rwandan francs annually in recent years. The reforms are expected to increase access for local businesses and youth-led enterprises, unlocking new opportunities in government projects.
Scaling Artificial Intelligence
Rwanda is also accelerating the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across key sectors such as healthcare, education, and agriculture. The AI Scaling Hub, hosted at the Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution (C4IR) in partnership with the Gates Foundation, is spearheading these efforts.
The initiative focuses on:
Raising public awareness about AI, including its benefits and risks
Building local expertise to develop homegrown AI solutions tailored to Rwanda’s needs
Bridging the Digital Access Gap
Despite 95% internet coverage, the Minister acknowledged that access alone is not enough. Many citizens still lack the devices needed to fully benefit from digital services.
To address this, the government, with support from the World Bank, is identifying vulnerable groups and developing financing solutions to help them acquire essential technology such as smartphones.
“These efforts will ensure that no one is left behind as Rwanda advances toward a digital and inclusive economy,” Ingabire said.

“We have tested this approach and seen a wealth of ideas from young innovators,” Ingabire noted, adding that local entrepreneurs often have a deeper understanding of community challenges.
Expanding Opportunities in Public Markets
Public procurement remains a significant economic driver, with contracts valued at over 1,000 billion Rwandan francs annually in recent years. The reforms are expected to increase access for local businesses and youth-led enterprises, unlocking new opportunities in government projects.
Scaling Artificial Intelligence
Rwanda is also accelerating the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across key sectors such as healthcare, education, and agriculture. The AI Scaling Hub, hosted at the Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution (C4IR) in partnership with the Gates Foundation, is spearheading these efforts.
The initiative focuses on:
Raising public awareness about AI, including its benefits and risks
Building local expertise to develop homegrown AI solutions tailored to Rwanda’s needs
Bridging the Digital Access Gap
Despite 95% internet coverage, the Minister acknowledged that access alone is not enough. Many citizens still lack the devices needed to fully benefit from digital services.
To address this, the government, with support from the World Bank, is identifying vulnerable groups and developing financing solutions to help them acquire essential technology such as smartphones.
“These efforts will ensure that no one is left behind as Rwanda advances toward a digital and inclusive economy,” Ingabire said.

body_en:
Kigali, 16 March 2026 - The Rwanda Stock Exchange (RSE), in partnership with the Ministry of Sports, has launched a campaign to encourage athletes to invest in financial markets and secure their long-term financial future.
The initiative began with a training session bringing together sports stakeholders, focusing on how athletes can leverage the stock exchange for savings, investment, and financial stability beyond their careers.
The program emphasized the importance of financial literacy, highlighting how stocks and other financial products can offer sustainable income and long-term security, particularly for athletes whose earnings may fluctuate during and after their careers.
Rwego Ngarambe, Secretary of State in the Ministry of Sports, underscored the need for athletes to build strong financial foundations. “Athletes dedicate years to their careers. It is essential that they invest with the same commitment to secure their future and contribute to the country’s economic transformation,” he said.
The CEO of the Rwanda Stock Exchange, Pierre Célestin Rwabukumba, noted that the initiative aims to provide athletes with reliable and regulated investment opportunities. “Athletes can transform their future by investing gradually in approved financial products, gaining confidence while benefiting both during and after their careers,” he said.
Participants welcomed the campaign, saying it aligns with their need to plan for life after sports and achieve financial independence.
The initiative comes at a time when Rwanda’s sports sector is expanding, alongside growing attention to the financial well-being of athletes. Regulators and partners emphasized that improving access to investment opportunities and strengthening financial education will be key to helping athletes make informed financial decisions.
